Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Full)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.
Dr. Byoung Choh immigrated to the United States in 1972, when he was 43 years old. He could come to the states after he passed the ECFMG exam, coming to work at a mental health hospital. Working as both a resident and intern in Cleveland, Ohio, he had learned to adjust to a new environment with his wife. Originally from North Korea, Choh had a rough time during the Korean War, escaping and getting separated from his family. Although he was able to get in contact with them, he was not able to see them ever again because of the corrupt government in North Korea. Choh despises the corruption in Korea and believes that it is best for him and his family to live in America, with freedom. In terms of conserving his Korean culture, Choh believes that it is very important to know how to speak one’s native language, which is why he encourages his grandchildren to do the same. As a Korean immigrant, he feels proud of his accomplishments and hard work and believes that his home is now America.
Keywords: United States; Korea; War; ECFMG examination; Resident; Intern; Cuyahoga Falls; Ohio; Wife; Seoul; Family; Children; Education; English language; North Korea; Money; School; Stepmother; Corruption; Communism

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

My name is Byoung Cho. I am now 83 years old. That was 1950. 1950. At the time I was a college student in the North part. My family had a very hard time because the North Korean government, so-called Red government, they don't like and they suppressed people who lived somewhat wealthy, more than the usual standard.

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

They hate such people. So we were one of the group they hate. I refused to be taken to their army. I said, no, I never served in your army. It was called enlistment. I refused. And then finally I smuggled into underground for at least two weeks. Two weeks.

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

So now my family also didn't know where I am. They should not know about it because police were looking for me. If they pressed my family, "Where is your son?" If they do know where I am, eventually they may talk about that. But my family, they don't know because I didn't tell where I will go. So finally that was the 8th army and Korean 3rd infant division and capital infantry division came to my hometown and then are

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

"Wow!" - So-called liberation. And then Chinese army invaded from the north to the North Korea. In the east coast there was a big seaport by the name of is Heungnam (흥남시) near to my hometown. There were a lot of ships came to transport UN forces, but they didn't know how many refugees were there and how many more ships were needed. They put Korean refugees in between the

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

choke, between the tank, between in their supplies, put them and then so many people come. But why my family couldn't come there? They shut down between port and my hometown because the Red Army guerrilla smuggled into the refugee group just like refugees crossing, visiting. So they don't know who is refugees, who is Red Army guerrilla. So no more refugee. That's why many you see, you know my uncles, two uncles, their family, my family,

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

they come down the stop lines and then returned home... So how did you get to the port first? Oh, I was young at the time. The Korean army needed young men. They so-called new soldier. A new soldier. They called recruit. So the Korean army took us onto their truck and covered with something and then checkpoint in the US Army MP (military police). What is this? Korean army office. "Oh, they are the recruits."

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

Also, "Okay." So we got a chance to pass. The Korean army has no power. The US army had all the power. So we became a regular army personnel. For South Korea? So I became a so-called what? What's the PFC? Private First Class. Private. First Class. First Class. Beneath that, private second class, say freshmen. They say just new soldier or

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

we trained our ship, got the part of some area in Gangwon-do (강원도) area. And then we became a trainee. And then many officers told me, "Hey, how come nobody know how soon this war is going to end? So how come you continue that soldier life? It's very difficult. Why didn't you become an officer?" So I took some examination and then I become

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

an officer lieutenant and then I became a lieutenant colonel in the army. And then after that, I got out of the army. So retired from the army and then I established the private practice in Seoul. When I came over here to United States, I think I was probably 43 years old. Right? In what year? In 1972, I became one of employees in the state of

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

Ohio. State Hospital. The date was October 1st. I want to visit my North Korea. Is it okay? if it's not good for you? I don't go. So he, my stepmother said, "Ah, now it became much better." But before it was so bad because my home, originally my home wasn't good to them. And then in addition to that, I went to the south. They said such people, counter activist, counter activist.

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

But now much is relaxed. So come over if you want, come over, that's fine. And then that was in 1988 when the Olympic game is processing in Seoul. In September, in early September. So I went to Japan and then changed my flight to Beijing, China. My cousin, Mr. Kim came to the Beijing by train. He took three days to train

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

with his wife. We took a train, night train at that time only night train. In the daytime, there have no train for foreigners. They don't like foreigners. Look around, they don't like that. Next morning, we got out of the train at my hometown Hamheung (함흥) and then we met my stepmother and my stepbrother, stepsisters. And then my original hometown,

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

rural area village, home village. When I was born there in rural area, everything changed more. My mother's tomb was moved to somewhere. I don't know who did it. Why did it? Nobody knew? This is your mom's tomb. I am now 83-year-old. Do you know where is the longest place I lived? Here. More than forty years now. I lived in South Korea between 1950 and 1972. It is only 22 years.

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

And then you lived in North Korea only 18 years or... Maybe. I don't know how old I was. I forgot. So when I drove my car to Pennsylvania over Pittsburgh or somewhere else, and then came back to Ohio, Pennsylvania is the mountain side. Like this. And then in once passed the borderline of the Ohio. The road was wide and straight, direct way, rectified everything.

Dr. Byoung G. Choh (Edited)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung G.

And now I can't come back to Ohio. I feel just like my hometown.

Jung S. Choh (Full)
Interviewee: Choh, Jung S.
Mrs. Jungsook Choh was born in 1935 in Uhrae-Jin, Hamkyung-Namdo, which is now in North Korea. She recalls her life immediately after the Korean Independence from Japan and the subsequent events during the Korean War which separated her younger brother from the rest of the family.
Keywords: Uhrae-jin, Hamkyung-namdo, Korea; North Korea; Father; Mother; Brother; Middle School; Korean War; Seoul; Tempura business

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky
Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee came to New York in 1973, in hopes of beginning a new chapter of his life in the United States. Leaving his life behind in Korea, he shares his challenges of starting over through the same, repetitive process, from intern to resident, and how he came to change and adapt to the ways and cultures of America. Growing up in a poor family in Daegu, South Korea, Dr. Lee shares his stories of living through a period of war and how those wars helped to shape the man he is today. Moreover, he comes to express his true opinions on high expectations and the importance of having a strong, connected family. He holds great love for his children and his grandchildren and hopes that they know that God is always by their side.
Keywords: New York; Vietnam War; Korean War; Japanese Occupation; Second World War; God; Religion; Korea; Grandchildren; Doctor; Family; United States

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

My name is Sang Gook Lee. I came to this country in 1973. I'm 76, almost 77 now. What is the happiest moment in your life? I don't know. When I met your mother for the first time. And then getting married. Yeah. And you guys married, especially you were the last one. And when the grandchildren come out, I was very happy. Grandchildren is very important things. And then when they're children, they grow up. I look down and I feel like so different from the Korean in Korea

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

and some part, a lot of this missing, respecting the elderly. And then I realized the life is different, way of thinking is different, education different. But in my heart, what I feel, the lovely grandchildren, that is nothing different. What is the saddest? Saddest. When I heard my father died, I couldn't attend. We are very poor and he work hard. That's all I know. What did he do?

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

Partly he was a farmer and he was also doing small, the bicycle job and repair and just shop. Yeah. I don't remember that much about him either, other than he was sick most of the time. Yeah, he was sick. And I feel like if somebody ask you start all your life again, how do you live? I would say I cannot live better than now, but I lived until now. Except what I have told to my parents. My mother died early. That's your biggest regret. But we didn't have time. Life's very short.

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

(gentle piano music) My name is Samuel Lee, Lee Sang Gook in Korean. I was born Daegu, Korea at 1935, so I'm 87 years old now. I was born in Japanese occupation in Korea. Something I remember about Japanese, so far, go back to my primary school years. I have seen so many Japanese around our town. Certainly principal of the school was Japanese and a lot of teachers, they are Japanese but mixed with some Korean teachers. Every morning we are together in early morning, in schoolyard,

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

we have to memorize the 황국신민선서, that in Korean. We have to loudly speak all together in the morning, "Pray to the Emperor and I will do my best with my life," or something like that. Teachers try to brainwash us, and every house, they have a small kamidana, small like a temple shape things on the wall. And you forced to pray there. And also teachers told us, "If you pray what you wishes, you can reward it." So I was learn, I did that things. As a Christian later, I found out myself, I was so much regret that things,

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

so much ashamed. And my house where I was grown, my father's house was just next to the Japanese police station. And also, I have seen the sticks they hit. That's made with the cow's sexual organ. Dried. That is not broken when hit the people. Everybody afraid, and if someone to pass front of the police station, they didn't want, they turn around. Everywhere we go, they have police power or military soldiers. The end of the Japanese occupation, that time was the Second World War. So they took everything. The big houses where something make money is belong to the Japanese,

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

and the Koreans lost everything. In 1943, '44, that time, agricultural things, they took it, especially rice. They have forced to change our surname, everybody. I have seen once or twice who kept the Korean name. Unless they have changed their name, they can not survive in that situation I think. My name was in Japanese Iwamoto Soukoku. In Korean, Ambon Sanguk. We cannot speak in Korean at school. And they forced to speak in Japanese at home. And at the church at that time, a very small members in our church. A small country church, and we have a Sunday school

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

and the teachers try to teach us Korean. Korean. But I didn't know why they doing that. But the church was the only place I still have a positive peeling. My mother, she was a very sensitive person. Actually, I believe my depression was from her. Her was the youngest in family and her, she had two brothers and two sisters. She was very religious, so I remember that. I remember her prayer and some reason, whenever she pray at the church, she was crying all the time. I don't know why. I think that all family things or national problems. She is passed away.

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

I think '41. I was a junior. I was junior in college. I went to my friend house at Jinhe, and I come back, she was unconscious. She was very attractive to everybody at the countryside church. 전도사님 who was attend when she was passed away, he remember her when she come as a new revert, and song, that hymn, that was. (Samuel sings in Korean) That song, still we have that.

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

That's a very, not hymn for the new revert. He remember that she sung that. So, for few days where she was in coma we sung that hymn all the time. And I remember that still that make me cry. [HJ] During the Korean War, you talk about being a houseboy. Yeah, I was house boy. [HJ] Tell me about what that was like. Yeah, that is one of the independent construction battalion. Our company did the construction of the Han River, the bridge. So, it's not really frontline in shooting things. I did for two person, one is a major, one is a colonel.

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

The commander at that battalion. I did wash their clothes and the cleaning. I was 15, 16. So I was away from home for three years. The first one and half years there, then I had depression attack. I didn't know I was in depression, but my friend who come together there, they thought I'm a little funny, just talk himself, and not communicate well and they think there's something wrong with me. So, they pushed me away from there to back to home. So, stay I think one or two years.

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

No, one or two months at home. I was go back to the high school. That time I was finished middle school and I go up to the high school. I was too late to come back to school. Out of school so long. So, you have to stay one more year. I was upset and I didn't want that. So I back to the military, as house boy. Now thinking back, my depression was really bad, but I can survive with my faith. That inside. Still, I can survive with that. That was the first time and the last time. But all my life I had some part of symptoms. When I think back, I had it, all through my life.

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

Anxiety, bad anxiety, all time. But I had a prayer, and when you do work as a doctor, it's one of the best stressful things I can tell. So, that's always give me anxiety. After grown up, most people didn't know I have that problems. And also I thought to myself, "Everyone has the same kind of reaction and symptoms." When I think back carefully, I was in depression. [HJ] So were you surprised when Nina came and asked about that? One of the first things when we put her in therapy was her therapist said, "Is there a history of depression in your family?" I said, "No." And then she came and talked to you, and that's when I started to realize maybe we just didn't talk about it, and we didn't know. I don't wanna talk about.

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Edited)
Interviewee: Lee, Rocky

It's my mother, myself, and I think about Nina. It's too much to me. But I'm praying for her. All the time, every morning. I didn't mean she's something wrong, or she's weak. I just pray for her. "God, please accept her prayer." That all I pray. My name is Samuel Lee. This is my Korean American story. (gentle piano music)

Kwon Sook Young (Full)
Interviewee: Kwon, Sook Young
Ms. Kwon Sook Young, born and raised in Korea, came to New York in 1973. Expressing the pain and fear she felt while raising her children kids in an unfamiliar country, she comes to highlight many obstacles she had faced due to language barriers and her process of growing and adapting to her new surroundings. Working as a volunteer at the YWCA for over 20 years, she helped many young kids whose parents were too busy to watch over them. Moreover, as the wife of a soldier who fought in the Vietnam War, she expresses her hardships of raising her children alone amidst her fear for her husband's safety. As all of her kids are currently married to non-Koreans, she expresses her opinions on mixed races and her love for her grandchildren, who bring her great happiness. Always looking up to God, she hopes and prays for the best for her family and grandchildren. She hopes to share the beauty of the Korean culture someday and hopes to be remembered as a beautiful and kind grandma.
Keywords: Grandchildren; Korea; Vietnam; Children; Mother; God; Volunteer; Korean culture/language; Non-Korean; Mixed Races

Kwon Sook Young (Edited)
Interviewee: Kwon, Sook Young

My name is Kwon Sook Young. I'm 72 years old. I came here in 1973. Two d ays ago after dinner, Nina and I sat down at the dining table and I was Korean myeolchi (anchovy) and then Nina take a dinner, a late dinner, or she took the, what is it, exercise. After that, she called me, "Halmoni, I love you." I was so cry. I was so happy. This happiest time. I love her. She's a teenager now and I think she has so much stress.

Kwon Sook Young (Edited)
Interviewee: Kwon, Sook Young

Then every day I prayed for her. Her mind is very comfortable and no stress, and maybe God help her. A couple of years ago I tried to teach them Korean language, but they're so busy. They don't have enough time and they don't like it. I think someday they'll like it. If I have time, I can take all the grandchildren to Korea and visit Korea and show them everything.

Kwon Sook Young (Edited)
Interviewee: Kwon, Sook Young

I really want the children to always get together and not argue if we are not in here. We passed away after that. Always think about each other. Love each o ther and in God. That's my hope. What do you want your grandchildren and your great-grandchildren and their kids to know about you? What do you want them to remember about you? Just beautiful halmoni.

Kwon Sook Young (Edited)
Interviewee: Kwon, Sook Young

Nice and beautiful, halmoni. That's it.

Kwon Sook Young (Edited)
Interviewee: Kwon, Sook Young

﻿My name is Kwon Sook-young. I was born in Bonghwa-gun, Gyeongsangbuk-do. I was about 10 when the Korean War started and we began to evacuate. I was with my mom and I had two younger brothers but one passed away soon after being born. We evacuated to Andong. But from there, they told us to evacuate again. And at that time, my grandfather's son, my father's cousin, was working at a nearby train station as an assistant station master or something. He took us to the train's freight car, not a passenger car, and told us to be in there with bags of rice from my grandfather. And began to evacuate. As we were going from Andong to Busan, the bombing was so bad that the train rolled back. We had bags of rice on the sides of the car and people sitting in the middle of the freight car. And in addition to rice, we also needed water. So we placed a big kettle full of water on top of the rice.

Kwon Sook Young (Edited)
Interviewee: Kwon, Sook Young

When the train rattled, the kettle dropped on me. I couldn't do anything about it even though I was wet. After that, the night passed and the bombing stopped. We arrived at some station in the morning. But they said I was dead. Totally motionless. 00:00:95,000 --> 00:00:100,000 my grandfather brought a station employee with him. 00:00:100,000 --> 00:00:105,000 He told the employee since the rest are alive and it's morning, they should eat something since they've starved the entire trip. 00:00:105,000 --> 00:00:110,000 Even my mom, who had to nurse my younger brother, said they should go eat then bury me before leaving again. 00:00:110,000 --> 00:00:115,000 So after that, while they were talking about where to bury me, I came out crawling. 00:00:115,000 --> 00:00:120,000 My whole family ran away. 00:00:120,000 --> 00:00:125,000 There's an old saying if you leave a dead body alone, it will be possessed. 00:00:125,000 --> 00:00:130,000 I crawled out alive. 00:00:130,000 --> 00:00:135,000 After all that, we finally settled somewhere near Busan. 00:00:135,000 --> 00:00:140,000 But there was nothing for us to do. 00:00:140,000 --> 00:00:145,000 Our grandfather told us that we can't just play around here. 00:00:145,000 --> 00:00:150,000 He told us to go work. 00:00:150,000 --> 00:00:155,000 We asked him what kind of work we should do? 00:00:155,000 --> 00:00:160,000 He told us there's a lot of Korean pears nearby. 00:00:160,000 --> 00:00:165,000 He directed us to go to the orchard and buy some and go to the train station nearby. 00:00:165,000 --> 00:00:170,000 And sell it to the soldiers who are around that station. 00:00:170,000 --> 00:00:175,000 So we'd sit at the station and go up to the soldiers asking them to buy some pears. 00:00:175,000 --> 00:00:180,000 But who would buy them from kids? 00:00:180,000 --> 00:00:185,000 They were buying them from adults and not from us. 00:00:185,000 --> 00:00:190,000 We were tired and hungry. 00:00:190,000 --> 00:00:195,000 So my older cousin told us we should stop and just eat the pears ourselves. 00:00:195,000 --> 00:00:200,000 So the three of us, all little girls, ate the whole thing. 00:00:200,000 --> 00:00:205,000 Despite having younger siblings, we didn't leave any for them and ate everything. 00:00:205,000 --> 00:00:210,000 Our grandfather kicked us out of the house and the three of us went to the mountains thinking what we should do. 00:00:210,000 --> 00:00:215,000 There's one bad memory I have from that time. 00:00:215,000 --> 00:00:220,000 My grandmother stayed behind to watch our family's brewery and property and told us the communists wouldn't do anything to an old lady. 00:00:220,000 --> 00:00:225,000 So while she watched, every night soldiers from the opposition would come from the mountains and ask her for food. 00:00:225,000 --> 00:00:230,000 Since we had a farm, we did have lots of provisions. 00:00:230,000 --> 00:00:235,000 And it was hard to say no to them - so she did. 00:00:235,000 --> 00:00:240,000 So my father and our family returned to the brewery after everything and a new government took place. 00:00:240,000 --> 00:00:245,000 But because we provided food to the communist party, they had to execute my father. 00:00:245,000 --> 00:00:250,000 So they took my father away. 00:00:250,000 --> 00:00:255,000 I still remember they put blindfolds on them and lined them against a wall. 00:00:255,000 --> 00:00:260,000 But my grandfather was generous and helped a lot of people thoughout the years. 00:00:260,000 --> 00:00:265,000 He would give financial support to those who couldn't afford education. 00:00:265,000 --> 00:00:270,000 And there was one person who received scholarship from my grandfather. 00:00:270,000 --> 00:00:275,000 And there was one person who received scholarship from my grandfather. 00:00:275,000 --> 00:00:280,000 He was the chief of police of that squad. 00:00:280,000 --> 00:00:285,000 He was there to oversee the execution. 00:00:285,000 --> 00:00:290,000 He would go down the line one by one asking who they were. 00:00:290,000 --> 00:00:295,000 Then he saw my father there. 00:00:295,000 --> 00:00:300,000 He asked the squad who he was and they told him he's the son of so and so. 00:00:300,000 --> 00:00:305,000 He told them to take my father out. 00:00:305,000 --> 00:00:310,000 My father's fate changed just 5 minutes before the execution. 00:00:310,000 --> 00:00:315,000 Everyone else on that line were shot dead at that spot. 00:00:315,000 --> 00:00:320,000 Literally escaped death at the last minute. 00:00:320,000 --> 00:00:325,000 I wanted to go to Seoul but my family wouldn't let me. 00:00:325,000 --> 00:00:330,000 I got angry so I looked at Kyungbok University which was nearby. 00:00:330,000 --> 00:00:335,000 I applied to the nursing school in there and got accepted. 00:00:335,000 --> 00:00:340,000 That school offered dorms and I didn't have to go home. 00:00:340,000 --> 00:00:345,000 Sol attended that school. 00:00:345,000 --> 00:00:350,000 I was there for only one semester. 00:00:350,000 --> 00:00:355,000 But within that semester, I learned a lot and even did field work. 00:00:355,000 --> 00:00:360,000 And that's where I met your father. 00:00:360,000 --> 00:00:365,000 That's when I met my husband. 00:00:365,000 --> 00:00:370,000 Then I got married. 00:00:370,000 --> 00:00:375,000 Gave birth to HJ, Roky and Yoon. 00:00:375,000 --> 00:00:380,000 Soon after that, your father went to Vietnam for 10 months or so. 00:00:380,000 --> 00:00:385,000 When he came back, he went back to the hospital and was the chief of surgery. 00:00:385,000 --> 00:00:390,000 He was a chief despite his young age because at that time, there was someone in charge, but he was American. 00:00:390,000 --> 00:00:395,000 He didn't have a license in Korea even though he had one in the U.S. 00:00:395,000 --> 00:00:400,000 So he couldn't be chief by law. 00:00:400,000 --> 00:00:405,000 That's why your father was chief because he was Korean and a surgeon. 00:00:405,000 --> 00:00:410,000 The hospital he worked at, which was in Pyeong-dong, gave us a house and we all lived there. 00:00:410,000 --> 00:00:415,000 But all of a sudden, pediatricians, OBGYNs, and everyone at the hospital were saying they were preparing to move to the U.S. 00:00:415,000 --> 00:00:420,000 Then one day your father comes home and says he took the ECFMC exam and passed. 00:00:420,000 --> 00:00:425,000 I asked him what that was and he told me it was to move to the U.S. 00:00:425,000 --> 00:00:430,000 I asked why do we have to move to the U.S.? 00:00:430,000 --> 00:00:435,000 Don't we have to stay here? 00:00:435,000 --> 00:00:440,000 We knew nothing about the U.S. 00:00:440,000 --> 00:00:445,000 at that time. 00:00:445,000 --> 00:00:450,000 All I can think about was how much we will struggle if we went there. 00:00:450,000 --> 00:00:455,000 We can't even speak the language there. 00:00:455,000 --> 00:00:460,000 So I told him we can't go. 00:00:460,000 --> 00:00:465,000 He said he has to go. 00:00:465,000 --> 00:00:470,000 He tells me that he doesn't like the work with the patients here. 00:00:470,000 --> 00:00:475,000 What choice do I have? 00:00:475,000 --> 00:00:480,000 So we moved to the U.S. 00:00:480,000 --> 00:00:485,000 We moved to New York in 1973. 00:00:485,000 --> 00:00:490,000 We felt so out of place. 00:00:490,000 --> 00:00:495,000 It was hard and I cried every night. 00:00:495,000 --> 00:00:500,000 There was this one time when you, HJ, brought homework from school and that was one of my saddest days. 00:00:500,000 --> 00:00:505,000 It was math homework and if it was a simple math equation, it would've been easy. 00:00:505,000 --> 00:00:510,000 But I couldn't help at all because they were math problems in English. 00:00:510,000 --> 00:00:515,000 I couldn't understand any of it. 00:00:515,000 --> 00:00:520,000 I sat there and cried a lot that day. Myung Hee Jun (Full)
Interviewee: Jun, Myung Hee
Born as the fifth of seven children in Longjing, China Jun Myung Hee's life journey began in 1932. He fled to Seoul at the age of 11 in 1943 to escape communism, traversing the 38th parallel. In a harrowing incident, he nearly perished falling into a frozen river but resolved to survive in free land. Life in Korea during that time was marked by poverty and limited educational opportunities, leading him to work and struggle to attend school. He entered school late during his last year of middle school and the June 25th War lead to a seven-year military service stint, interrupted by a hospitalization due to injury. Reflecting on his upbringing, he recalls the difficulties faced in China under Japanese occupation, where his family struggled despite his grandfather's profession as a doctor. The family's political involvement, particularly through his mother's activism against discrimination, led to her imprisonment during the March 1 uprising. Despite their hardships, his parents played significant roles in aiding the Korean Independence movement in China, resulting in ongoing financial support from the Korean Government. However, his grandfather met a tragic end under Mao's regime, facing execution for his collaboration with the Japanese. His grandfather worked as a doctor, and was only allowed to keep his hospital open in exchange for examining comfort women for STDs. After the Korean War, he embarked on entrepreneurship, which, amidst a challenging economic climate, eventually failed. Following the footsteps of his siblings, many of whom had immigrated to the United States as students and immigrants, he too found his way to America in 1990 at the age of 62. Initially settling in Dallas, Texas, he eventually made New York his permanent home, where he has resided ever since, reflecting on a life marked by resilience, sacrifice, and the pursuit of freedom and opportunity.

Jun Jinhee (Full)
Interviewee: Jun, Jinhee
Jinhee Jun (Jinhee Choi) was born on December 6th, 1927 in Sincheon, Seoul, under colonial rule. When she was around six, her family relocated to Manchuria, where she attended elementary school (Hong-joong Elementary School) and middle school (Gang-myeong Girls’ Middle School). Up until liberation, she received her education in Japanese, and went by the Japanese name “Takada Jenshin.” Following graduation, she worked as an elementary school’s teacher in Manchuria, where all of her students were Korean, though she instructed them in Chinese and Korean, teaching most subjects. She recalls being neither poor nor wealthy in her youth. Some members of her family were involved with the independence movement; her father, a doctor who had opened a practice in Manchuria, secretly treated independence activists who passed through. His clinic also saw comfort women, though Korean doctors were not allowed to conduct checkups on them, with Japanese medics treating them instead. She also remembers how a family member on her maternal side (Mother? Uncle?) who was heavily involved with the independence movement was imprisoned, and how upon their release they couldn’t see too well because it had been too dark in their cell. Following the end of WWII, many of her friends fled to Japan as sympathizers, but she and her family stayed in Manchuria for a little while longer until moving to Seoul in 1947; she recounts how the few Japanese still living in Manchuria at the time were mostly farmers who did not have the means to go back to their country, and how she felt sorry for them as many ended up moving to the Soviet Union. When the Korean War broke out, she and her family followed the military down to Daegu, where they had no relations, before moving back to Seoul, where she married in Supyo (Supyo Church). Following her sister, she immigrated to the United States in 1979 at the age of 52, living first in Tulsa, Oklahoma, where she made a Japanese friend named Hiroki who helped with her English. She became an American citizen in Tulsa, taking English lessons to pass the citizenship test, and worked at American Airlines for 16 years. When asked if she ever missed Korea, or anyone still in Korea, she said that everyone had already come to America, and that she as well as her children enjoyed life in the U.S. When asked whether she identified as Korean or as Korean American, she said she hadn’t given it much thought, and thought of herself as Korean.

Theresa K. Rhee (Full)

Theresa K Rhee, born Jun Kyunghee was born on Jaunary 14, 1935 in China (Manchuria). She was the sixth of seven children; she had three sisters and three brothers. Her father practiced medicine, with his clinic having around a dozen beds, and her mother used to be an independence activist. When her mother was 19, she became a leader of the independence movement, and was subsequently jailed for a year by Japanese authorities. Her father, who had graduated from medical school, proposed to her after her release, to which she replied that she couldn’t marry him because she was a “criminal.” Upon learning of her illicit activities, however, Theresa’s father chose to marry her mother because she was an “honorable criminal.” Her mother married when she was 22, and the family moved to Southern Manchuria, where there were Korean communities. Theresa’s family lived there until she was 12, after which they moved to Ganghwa Island, modern-day South Korea; she recounts taking a truck to the Peninsula, then a train at the Tumen River to Seoul, then to Incheon, where they boarded a ferry to Ganghwa Island where her family was originally from. This was her first time in Korea. In 1948, speaking little Korean (interesting), she passed an examination to be placed into Ewha Middle School. When she was 15, the Korean War broke out and the family moved temporarily to Daegu, where she enrolled in Hyosang Catholic High School. At the war’s end, the family moved back to Seoul where she graduated from Ewha High School before beginning studies in English at Ewha University. She settled in West Virginia in 1962, most of her friends Caucasian. She begins the interview by recounting her family’s history with the Christian faith, which began in the 1800s when the first Protestant missions arrived on the Peninsula. In the 1890s, her grandfather, a successful self-made man who had amassed enormous wealth, founded a school in his village with these missionaries, believing that education could be a means for the students to have better lives. While living under Japanese rule, many members of her family were engaged with Korean independence movements. She remembers how her father, educated abroad in New York, was an independence activist who worked alongside the likes of Kim Gu and Rhee Syngman during his time in the United States, and how upon his return to Korea he was imprisoned twice by the Japanese. Her husband began his academic career in Japan studying at an Imperial University, before obtaining professorship at Seoul National University after liberation. She remembers with pride how her during independence movements, her husband was a staunch supporter of Korean independence (she points out, despite his education at an imperial university, he was loyal to the cause of liberation). However, following independence from colonial rule, her husband was kidnapped and taken to North Korea, potentially to work at Kim Il Sung University with which her family had some kind of connection. Despite the hardship of raising six children alone, she takes pride in their perseverance and success, remembering how her kids would pursue schooling rigorously, walking to school no matter the outside conditions. In 1982, she moved to the United States (one of her sons had moved ten years prior, in 1972), and continues to lead a life of faith, crediting her health, children, and satisfaction to God.

Byoung Choh (Full)
Interviewee: Choh, Byoung
Byoung Choh was born in 1929 in what is now North Korea, during the Japanese occupation. He faced the prohibition of the Korean language at his primary school, which was enforced by both Korean and Japanese teachers. Despite this, he continued speaking Korean at home. Byoung's teenage years were marked by compulsory military training in high school, a reflection of the turbulent times. The landscape of his homeland dramatically changed in August 1945 when the US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, leading to Japan's surrender. Shortly thereafter, the Soviet army occupied northern Korea, introducing communism, while the southern part saw the US army bringing democracy after the Japanese withdrawal. Byoung witnessed the harshness of the Soviet regime, including the treatment of Korean women and the theft of resources. This contrasted with the gentler approach of the American forces. In October 1945, Kim Il Sung was installed by the Soviets as the leader of North Korea. The establishment of the 38th parallel soon followed, setting the stage for the Korean War in 1950. During the conflict, Byoung, realizing the dangers of staying in the North, made a harrowing escape to the South by ship in December 1950. Tragically, he was separated from his family when the US destroyed infrastructure, preventing their planned reunion. Byoung then joined the South Korean army, where he began his military life amidst scarce resources. His service lasted until 1964, during which time he admired General MacArthur for his role in the conflict, despite MacArthur's eventual dismissal by President Truman. Post-military, Byoung married Jung Sook and opened a medical practice in Seoul. Seeking a better life, Byoung moved to the United States in 1972 after passing a special exam for foreign medical doctors. He settled in Cleveland, Ohio, where he has lived ever since. It was only after witnessing the successful establishment of his children in America that he felt reassured about his decision to immigrate. Throughout these challenges, Byoung's faith in God provided him with strength and perseverance.

So my brother and I rode the train to different destinations. He went to our grandmother's home, and I went to our aunt's. I spent about six months at my aunt's place. Jung S. Choh (Full)
Interviewee: Jung S. Choh
Jung Sook Choh was born in 1935 in Hangyeonnamdo, near the East Sea (동해 바다). She and her father fled to Shinpo to escape the increasing violence of the Japanese occupation. Despite learning Japanese as a child, she no longer remembers the language. To distance themselves from conflict, they moved further south before liberation. After liberation, her father sought a new place to settle and went to Hwanghaedo, where he taught villagers Hangeul in exchange for food. They later joined him and acquired a small home. Her father then served the Cheondoist church in Gaenipo while Jung Sook and her mother farmed. Due to financial constraints, Jung Sook could not initially attend school, but later, her aunt helped her get into middle school. She returned to her mother's home when they had more money, but the Korean War began, preventing them from reuniting with her brother. During the war, the North Koreans issued new currency, rendering the old money useless. Her father sent the old money to Cheondoists in Seoul, which led to his imprisonment when someone was caught. Rumors spread that prisoners were drowned by communists, but her father survived an attempted poisoning in prison by not drinking the soup provided. Her father's colleagues warned them to flee, and they escaped to Seoul, facing hardships such as riding on the roof of a train to Osan. Seeking valid identification, a kind police officer from their hometown provided IDs and housing, allowing them to start a tempura business. They later moved to Chuncheon to be closer to her brother and started a bookstore. During the 1988 Olympics, they located her brother, who had posed as an orphan for special benefits in North Korea. Jung Sook attended school in Seoul, where she met her future husband. Her mother was reluctant to send her to college, but eventually did, though Jung Sook got engaged and did not finish her education. They immigrated to Akron, Ohio, where her husband found a residency at St. Thomas Hospital. Initially poor, their situation improved once her husband became a doctor. They bought a house near the hospital and established a stable life. Jung Sook is grateful for immigrating to the United States, as her children have had good lives and found good partners.

Namsun Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, Namsun
Namsun Lee got sick with tuberculosis at 24 and was sent to a sanatorium in South Korea. While there, she encountered a man praying in the hospital church, later to become her husband. They moved to the United States with their three children, settling in Richmond, VA. She supported the family financially while her husband was studying to be a pastor. She worked at a sewing factory for three years, despite physical pain and racial barriers at work, Namsun remained resilient. She eventually found work at the General Electric company, initially on an assembly line and later in a higher-paying "man's job" assembling TVs. Her happiest memory occurred during a moment of deep despair in Albany, NY. Feeling overwhelmed being a pastor's wife, she ran into the broken bathroom stall of the children’s ministry building. She found solace in hearing children sing praise songs. She walked outside and asked God to to give her joy which lead her to a profound spiritual experience. The feeling of joy washed over her like an ocean wave, sadness was gone and everything felt different. Namsun's faith sustained her through adversity. She imparted its importance to her children, reassuring them in the face of hardship and maintaining a strong family prayer routine. She now cherishes her role as a grandmother, aiming to pass on the wisdom and joy she finds in her faith.

Reverend Jong Hyung Lee was born in 1941 in South Korea. He arrived in the US in 1974 at the age 33. After earning his PhD in the US, he returned to Korea to teach in seminaries and churches. He founded Korean Overseas Missions Inc. to train church and community leaders and send missionaries abroad. Notable among his missions was establishing spiritual ministry at Myungsung Medical College in Ethiopia. He taught ethics and world view to students, helped establish spiritual ministry, and laid the foundation to train students on whole person medical care. His belief in God stemmed at a young age seeing his grandmother's deep devotion to Christianity and overcoming his personal near-death experience at 23. Grateful for his wife's support, he raised three daughters and now has three grandchildren. After 35 years of ministry, he leaves a legacy of service and faith as a pastor. He seeks to tell his grandchildren the importance of inner character, fostering meaningful relationships, and the transformative power of God. He emphasizes the interconnectedness of humanity, highlighting the potential for personal growth and spiritual change.

Han Sung Park (Full)
Interviewee: Park, Han Sung
Park Han Sung was born on January 7, 1935, in Andong, a rural countryside without buses or electricity raised by a single mother after her father's premature death. She fondly remembers foraging as a child and cherishes her connection to nature during her childhood. Her grandmother was incredibly kind and loving, and her older sisters often sacrificed for her as the youngest sibling. Her mother, though a woman of few words, was a strong homemaker who could make a meal from a single jujube, ensuring the family never felt the lack despite their father's early death. Han Sung learned to cook from her mother, who maintained a sense of stability and self-esteem in the family. She attended Japanese school as a child and remembers the pain of being unable to perform jesa, a Korean ancestral rite, due to Japanese interference. The Korean War began when she was in 3rd grade, forcing her family to flee to Suwon, then Daegu, and ultimately Busan. During the war, her family faced many hardships, including the theft of heirlooms by communists and the abduction of relatives by the People's Army. Despite the turmoil, Hang Sung formed a close bond with her sister, especially after their brother-in-law was sent to the military. After the war, Han Sung resumed her education in Daegu, experiencing happiness and frequent visits with her mother. Han Sung decided to become a pharmacist to support her mother, and she took pride in being a good daughter, helping with household chores whenever she visited home. After marrying, she got her first job at a wonderful pharmacy with supportive bosses, where she learned financial literacy and gained independence. However, her life took another turn when her husband decided to move to America. Despite her mother's sadness and pleas for her to stay, Han Sung eventually joined her husband, bringing their children. In America, they lived in an apartment with other Koreans, which mitigated her loneliness, but she also recalls being poor during that time. Concerned about her children's future and language skills, she prioritized their English education. Her children eventually attended medical school, and Hang Sung feels that all her sacrifices were worth it for their success. Though she sometimes regrets moving to America and believes she might have been happier in Korea, she finds solace in her children's happiness and achievements.

Yun Hoon Chung, born in China in April 1938 to a lineage of scholars, moved to China in 1918 during the Japanese occupation. Inspired by a photo of the Empire State Building, he taught himself English with the help of a Japanese American tutor. His family's privileged life in Manchuria shielded them from immediate oppression, thanks to his father's successful import-export business, of soybeans, corn and rice. Despite societal challenges, Yun Hoon's father instilled in him a strong sense of Korean identity and resilience against discrimination. Once back in North Korea, realizing the limitations of education under the dictatorship, Yun Hoon attempted to assassinate Kim Il-sung before fleeing to South Korea with nothing but a 10 won note. Encountering the US and CIA due to his English proficiency, he prioritized education over offers of employment. Struggling to survive, he secured a scholarship for weather forecasting training through a fake college certificate. A few months later, the Korean War broke out and hid from being drafted by North Korea. He was caught often while looking for food but eventually escaped. Once the war endedUpon arriving in the United States, he attended Michigan University, working various jobs to support his family. Despite immense pressure, he compared his previous life in North Korea as more difficult. While working at a packaging company, he was tasked with making improvements on a sugar packaging machine. When the company went under he took it upon himself to create the product and eventually ventured into entrepreneurship. His successful ventures led to the development of innovative products, notably impacting packaging supply systems. He has currently been working on building a new commercial product that will impact the supply chain system and help to eliminate waste.Yun Hoon instilled in his children the same values of freedom, equality, and resilience he was taught by his father. He aspires to contribute to global welfare and Korean unification, embracing his identity as an engineer and inventor. Throughout his journey, he learned to embrace challenges, encourage imagination, and view failure as a stepping stone to growth.

Kim J Chung (Full)
Interviewee: Chung, Kim J
Kim J. Chung was born in October 1935 in Pyongyang. In 1946, at age 11, her family fled to Ongjin, pretending to attend a wedding, with money sewn into their clothes by her mother. They moved to Incheon and then Seattle. She recalls this escape as similar to a scene from The Sound of Music. Within six months, their money was gone due to her father’s frivolous spending. He eventually abandoned the family to work in a gold mine, losing his wife’s trust. Her mother began sewing scarves to sell to soldiers, and Jung Sook helped, improving their living conditions. Her mother was politically active in the North-West Youth Association, opposing communists. During the Korean War, communists imprisoned her mother. Jung Sook’s bravery and the presence of her infant sibling secured her mother’s release. They fled to Kangwondo and then to Jeju, where Jung Sook, at age 13, enjoyed singing in a church choir. After the war, Jung Sook had a tutor with whom she developed a relationship. When he immigrated to the US, she was promised to him. She struggled with immigration exams but eventually passed, cheating on the English test, and traveled by boat to Seattle at age 18. She cared for seasick passengers during the journey. In the US, she faced initial disappointment with her living conditions but pursued her GED at Ann Arbor High School. She married her tutor because she didn't want to live with a man unmarried. She was the first Korean many Americans had seen and received many gifts. Despite poverty, she was grateful to escape the Korean War’s atrocities. Jung Sook and her husband had three children. They faced housing discrimination but borrowed money to start a hasuk (boarding house). They later bought and renovated a seven-bedroom house. Her husband invented and sold a sugar packing machine, prompting their move to Toledo for better business opportunities. Jung Sook has no regrets and attributes her life's comfort to her faith. Initially skeptical of charismatic Christian practices, she experienced a deep faith revival after a pastor's sermon, believing her life is a miracle from God.

Chong Taek An (Full)
Interviewee: Chong, Taek An
Chong Taek An was born in 1929 in Hwanghae Province, Korea, which today is situated in the southwestern region of North Korea, bordering the 38th parallel. His childhood was spent in the deep and rural mountainsides, and he recalls how he had to make arduous mountain crossings to get to elementary school. In the winters, he and his friends would ride logs down the mountain slopes to get to and from school. His family lived in Hwanghae until he was in 3rd grade, when they moved to Seoul following a relative who was in the oil-pressing business. In order to make ends meet, An worked instead of continuing school to support his family, working in both the fields and in the oil-press. His family eventually worked in a rice-cake business, but because rice was a commodity during the Japanese occupation, they had to discreetly smuggle grains to be turned into rice cake, and their business was often subject to inspections by the imperial police. Often, the family had to eat millet, corn, or red beans instead of rice because of how scarce it was. During this time, An’s mother worked in food preparation for the Japanese, and An himself was able to be trained as an electrical technician, working on the railroad crossing signals. It was here where he was introduced to Christianity by a fellow contractor. His mother was opposed to him attending church, as this would mean he wouldn’t be able to perform jesa (ancestral rites) for his parents. After liberation, he met his wife (she was at the railroad station), and encouraged by his mother, took her out on a date. They married after the Korean War came to an end, and he recalls how because the bridges across the Han river were still destroyed, he had to ferry across the river to the wedding site. After the war, he found work in a factory, before working in the import-export business. But because of various export quotas that such businesses were subject to during the Park Chung-hee administration, he found himself deeply in debt to the point of contemplating suicide, but stood down, attributing his courage to his faith. After paying his debts, he immigrated to the United States, where he had a relative, and arrived with $500. He worked for an electronics company for a while but was injured one day (electric shock?), which put him in the hospital. After recovering, he moved to New York, where he first worked at a grocery store (potentially greengrocer) before borrowing money from his brother-in-law to open a dry cleaners. His business was in a run-down neighborhood filled with abandoned buildings, and so after a few years he and his wife sold the dry-cleaners to a Jewish businessman and moved to a different part of the city. When asked what he would tell future generations, he said that his generation doesn’t expect of their descendants to struggle as they did, but that they should focus on keeping their faith, and the hope that comes with it.

Jeong Ae Choi (Full)

Jeong Ae Choi, born in Gyeongui-do to parents from Gwajun, grew up in a family marked by hardship and resilience. Her father, who lost his own father at the age of nine, was raised by his grandfather in poverty and loneliness. Despite these challenges, he excelled in school, and his teacher funded his education, leading him to become a government worker. Jeong Ae's mother, despite living in poverty, managed to send all her sons through college by making the best of their situation. In the sixth grade, Jeong Ae experienced the liberation from Japan, but soon after, her grandmother sold their house to pay for her brothers' education. Unfortunately, they were scammed out of the money, leaving Jeong Ae unable to attend school. When the Korean War broke out, her brother was drafted but did not serve due to his height. Jeong Ae witnessed the war's brutal violence and believes she survived by the grace of God, attributing this to her family's strong Christian faith. Jeong Ae married a man who was caring for his deceased brother's two children. Living in poverty, she worked at handiworks and embroidery, earning the love of her mother-in-law. She emphasizes the importance of family unity, believing that becoming a family requires everyone to work together and live for others. Encouraged by a church member in LA and with family already in the US, Jeong Ae and her husband decided to immigrate. After arriving in America, her husband worked in a factory but was severely injured in an electrocution accident. The Gwangju Uprisings in Korea, which they initially thought were a North Korean invasion, made her fear for the safety of her children left behind in Korea. She eventually brought her children to the US. Jeong Ae began working part-time sewing, which allowed all her children to attend college, for which she is grateful to God. Jeong Ae later started a laundry business, opening earlier than other businesses and running it successfully. Eventually, they bought a retirement home in Jacksonville, where she now enjoys yoga and golf daily. Reflecting on her life, she acknowledges the hardships in Korea but also recognizes the times of peace that followed. Despite her limited English, due to having many Korean friends in the States, she emphasizes the importance of family and faith, values that have guided her throughout her life.

His humanitarian instincts prompted him to confront North Korean soldiers and advocate for the welfare of the vulnerable, underscoring his compassion and courage. With over 50 visits to North Korea, Hanshik remains a steadfast advocate for reunification, emphasizing the common humanity shared by North and South Koreans. She said, "You're right, but it would be better if you came. 00:00:185,000 --> 00:00:190,000 Let's pray together and look for a way!" Back then, it took longer to fly to the U.S. 00:00:190,000 --> 00:00:195,000 than it does today I think it took me around 17 hours because I had a 3 hour layover in Chicago on my way to Atlanta. 00:00:195,000 --> 00:00:200,000 I have no memory other than sleeping. 00:00:200,000 --> 00:00:205,000 My sister took me to a lawyer's office, in order to get me employed. 00:00:205,000 --> 00:00:210,000 I was very glad, but also scared. 00:00:210,000 --> 00:00:215,000 I had never spoken English before. 00:00:215,000 --> 00:00:220,000 The (Korean) lawyer said, "Hyejoo, your major was English literature." It was true. 00:00:220,000 --> 00:00:225,000 But I felt embarrassed when people say, "You should be good at English because you majored in it." To that, I would say, "I chose the major because I wasn't good at English and wanted to improve." Among my friends, there were even some who joked that we had majored in Korean-English literature, because we read English books in Korean. 00:00:225,000 --> 00:00:230,000 While living in the US, I felt like other widows or divorced women all experience something similar. 00:00:230,000 --> 00:00:235,000 Whenever I told someone, "My husband's passed away and I live alone with my young daughter" I noticed their facial expressions and attitudes changed. 00:00:235,000 --> 00:00:240,000 For one thing, men treated me less respectfully. 00:00:240,000 --> 00:00:245,000 I know it could just be my personal opinion. 00:00:245,000 --> 00:00:250,000 People also treated me thoughtlessly, because I had no husband to take care of me. 00:00:250,000 --> 00:00:255,000 Although I had my sister and my daughter, I felt lonely. 00:00:255,000 --> 00:00:260,000 The loneliness resulted from feeling the need to have a partner by my side so desperately. 00:00:260,000 --> 00:00:265,000 In that difficult time, (I met my present husband.) He came to the U.S. 00:00:265,000 --> 00:00:270,000 as a student and visited the lawyer's office that I was working for in order to change his visa. 00:00:270,000 --> 00:00:275,000 He was single. 00:00:275,000 --> 00:00:280,000 Back then, he was struggling to establish his own business. 00:00:280,000 --> 00:00:285,000 He looked so young, like a high school student. 00:00:285,000 --> 00:00:290,000 We didn't intend on dating in the beginning, but he was so kind to me while I was in such difficult circumstances. 00:00:290,000 --> 00:00:295,000 One day, my other female colleagues and I planned to set up a date for him, since he was single. 00:00:295,000 --> 00:00:300,000 After his date with the girl, we asked him how he liked her. 00:00:300,000 --> 00:00:305,000 He said he didn't like her, and, as a passing comment, he said, "I'd rather date Hyejoo from this office!" My husband might deny that he had ever said that, but I clearly remember. 00:00:305,000 --> 00:00:310,000 So, I thought, I may have a chance.... 00:00:310,000 --> 00:00:315,000 he sees me as a woman, although I have a daughter and I'm 2 years older than him. 00:00:315,000 --> 00:00:320,000 Could it be possible?' I started to get my hopes up. 00:00:320,000 --> 00:00:325,000 As you can assume, it wasn't an easy relationship. 00:00:325,000 --> 00:00:330,000 Even if I had been a mother of a son, it wouldn't have been an easily approved marriage. 00:00:330,000 --> 00:00:335,000 My husband's family including his mother strongly disapproved of our relationship, but, my husband resolved everything by himself. 00:00:335,000 --> 00:00:340,000 He never mentioned his mother's opinion of me, and after he had resolved everything on his own, we managed to marry. 00:00:340,000 --> 00:00:345,000 I'm so thankful to him. 00:00:345,000 --> 00:00:350,000 He gave me and my daughter a home. 00:00:350,000 --> 00:00:355,000 We married in 2003 and really wanted to have a baby, but we weren't able to have one, causing us to worry. 00:00:355,000 --> 00:00:360,000 Since I was 2 years older than my husband, the chances of having a baby grew slimmer as I got older. 00:00:360,000 --> 00:00:365,000 I also miscarried three times. 00:00:365,000 --> 00:00:370,000 To make matters worse, I got hypertension at 39 years old, due to my family history. 00:00:370,000 --> 00:00:375,000 When it came time to start taking medication for hypertension, my doctor told me that I couldn't take too much of the medication considering the possibility of my pregnancy. 00:00:375,000 --> 00:00:380,000 After getting diagnosed with hypertension at 39, I gave birth to my baby at 45. 00:00:380,000 --> 00:00:385,000 That six-year period from 39 to 45 was extremely challenging to me physically. 00:00:385,000 --> 00:00:390,000 Although I was taking medication for hypertension, it didn't keep my symptoms perfectly under control. 00:00:390,000 --> 00:00:395,000 I had a very hard time. 00:00:395,000 --> 00:00:400,000 There were many moments I thought I was going to die. 00:00:400,000 --> 00:00:405,000 I gave up on having a baby, but it's when I gave up that I got pregnant. 00:00:405,000 --> 00:00:410,000 Due to my old age and body condition, I had to be hospitalized for 9 weeks. 00:00:410,000 --> 00:00:415,000 It was hard staying at an American hospital, eating American food. 00:00:415,000 --> 00:00:420,000 Now looking back, I don't know how I survived those 9 weeks. 00:00:420,000 --> 00:00:425,000 It seemed surreal. 00:00:425,000 --> 00:00:430,000 I guess I persevered because I desperately wanted a baby. 00:00:430,000 --> 00:00:435,000 After being in labor for a long time, I eventually had to get a C-section. 00:00:435,000 --> 00:00:440,000 The next morning, I couldn't wait to see my baby who was born the previous night. 00:00:440,000 --> 00:00:445,000 I didn't have that kind of feeling when my first baby was born. 00:00:445,000 --> 00:00:450,000 But, when I looked at my baby, she was so beautiful. 00:00:450,000 --> 00:00:455,000 'How could I give a birth to such a beautiful baby!' I was so grateful. 00:00:455,000 --> 00:00:460,000 I thank God for so many things. 00:00:460,000 --> 00:00:465,000 For giving me good parents and being able to meet my husband. 00:00:465,000 --> 00:00:470,000 However, if someone asked me what I am most thankful for since coming to the U.S., However, if someone asked me what I am most thankful for since coming to the U.S., I would say that it's being given my second daughter. 00:00:470,000 --> 00:00:475,000 When I heard that my first husband was seriously ill, I had so many thoughts. 00:00:475,000 --> 00:00:480,000 'This is not something that only happens in TV dramas." 'I can also have a husband who gets sick and becomes a cancer patient.' 'I can become a widow.' It was agonizing, but I've learned a lot about the world, thanks to my husband. 00:00:480,000 --> 00:00:485,000 During his last 3 months, my first husband was bedridden because his body was becoming paralyzed. 00:00:485,000 --> 00:00:490,000 I sort of jokingly asked, "You might die soon, so why don't you say some final words to your daughter?" He was Catholic, and he said, "I regret one thing in front of God. 00:00:490,000 --> 00:00:495,000 Thinking of the Ten Commandments, I haven't killed someone or committed theft, but I haven't kept the commandment 'love your neighbor as yourself.' I kept the passive commandments, like abstaining from adultery or theft, but didn't keep the active commandments. 00:00:495,000 --> 00:00:500,000 I was told to love my neighbors like myself, but I didn't love them. 00:00:500,000 --> 00:00:505,000 I regret that so much.” He said, "Time never waits for you, so whatever you want to do today, don't push it off to tomorrow. 00:00:505,000 --> 00:00:510,000 Do it today!" I'd like to say to my children, "Time never waits. 00:00:510,000 --> 00:00:515,000 Do what you want!" I don't expect my two daughters to do very great things like saving mankind, but I want them to do at least one thing to make the world better than it was before they were born. 00:00:515,000 --> 00:00:520,000 "There are still many people suffering from hunger in the world, but you're not. 00:00:520,000 --> 00:00:525,000 You've been given the option of good education and good food. 00:00:525,000 --> 00:00:530,000 So, after you graduate from college, don't try to do something for me. 00:00:530,000 --> 00:00:535,000 Instead, please try to make the world a little bit better! 00:00:535,000 --> 00:00:540,000 Not later after you retire or after you become rich! 00:00:540,000 --> 00:00:545,000 Time never waits for you, as I have already experienced." "Act today!" I'm Hyejoo Jeong. 00:00:545,000 --> 00:00:550,000 This is my Korean American Story.

Sungwon Park's life is marked by a blend of privilege, love, and resilience, shaped by her upbringing as the daughter of a renowned doctor. Despite her father's early passing, Sungwon remembers their life as blessed and wealthy, surrounded by love and admiration. Her husband, a unique man with complex thoughts, had experiences in North Korea that kept her anxious and restless, unable to communicate with him directly. While her husband traversed between South and North Korea, Sungwon single-handedly raised their five children, crediting her unwavering faith in God for their well-being and safety. Despite the challenges, her husband eventually earned his doctorate in the United States, further enriching their lives. Marrying a well-off professor, Sungwon embarked on a new chapter in America with limited resources but with the support of her brother who had already immigrated.  Reflecting on her children's choices to marry non-Koreans, Sungwon finds solace in their happiness and the quality of their family lives, prioritizing love and fulfillment above cultural differences. Sungwon's journey embodies strength, love, and gratitude, navigating life's ups and downs with resilience and unwavering faith.

Woonhye Jeong (Full)

Jeong Woonhye, born on May 4th, 1959, in Haenam and raised as the second of five children in a pastor's family, reflects on a life shaped by love, sacrifice, and resilience. Growing up, she grappled with the expectations of serving the congregation and the challenges of her father's pastoral duties, yet gained a newfound appreciation for his wisdom in her later years. Despite never wanting to marry a pastor, fate intervened when her husband's family, influenced by her father's church, pursued a match between them. They married a month later, embarking on a journey marked by missionary work in Chile and various church positions before settling in Atlanta. Throughout her life, Woonhye confronted financial struggles but shielded her children from their reality until college. She prioritized their education, teaching them Korean to preserve their heritage and journaling to capture their memories. Despite her mother's illness and her grandmother's wisdom, Woonhye cherished the simple joys of her childhood in Haenam, marked by mud flat adventures and communal meals. Her pursuit of education defied expectations, culminating in a move to Seoul with her beloved grandmother, a cherished memory that remains her happiest. Yet, it was her grandmother's passing that taught her the true depth of loss and the enduring impact of wisdom and love, transcending literacy and leaving an indelible mark on her soul.

Woonhye Jeong (Edited)
Interviewee: Jeong, Woonhye

I thought I could marry any man but a pastor. Why? I admired my father who was a pastor, but his life was so difficult. There were a variety of difficulties. My father served a rural church. Sometimes, people that seemed less respectable than my father came and complained bitterly to him, but my father humbly listened to their complaints. Now I know he did it out of love and faith, but back then I thought, "Why does my father have to put up with this? This is probably the life of any pastor. I could marry any man in the world but a pastor!" When I first met my husband, his family was attending my father's church. As children, he and I attended the same church for three years, and then his family moved to another city, Goon-san. Since my father was their pastor when they first became Christians, even after they moved away, they came to my father for support and advice on their difficulties. In the sixteen years since his family moved away, we grew up and went separate ways. One day, I encountered my husband's sister again when she was paying a visit to my father. The topic of marriage came up, and she set up a date for me and my husband. I had no interest at all. I went to the meeting place in order to say no. My husband said he had a prayer list of what he wanted in his future wife. One day, after his morning prayer, it struck him that I was above and beyond the best fit for his prayer list. I even had a bonus for him. So, he gathered his courage to call me and ask me out on a date. We met and talked. It might have been God's guidance. Despite my former negative feelings about marrying a pastor, I really ended up marrying one, only a month after our first date.

Woonhye Jeong (Edited)
Interviewee: Jeong, Woonhye

After the Japanese occupation and the Korean War, my grandmother was among the many Koreans who were very poor and had very little food. She became a widow at age thirty-eight with five children to care for. Food was scarce and beggars were everywhere. When I was little, I saw many handicapped soldiers with hooks instead of hands, begging door to door in groups of six or seven or ten. When those soldiers came to my grandmother, she always had something for them to eat. She would invite them in to eat at the table that she brought in from the kitchen. I always ended up having to help her. I remember being scared of their hooks hurting me. So it became routine that whenever she stayed over at our home, beggars would always come to eat. Graduating from college, I thought long and hard about my future and decided to become a teacher. To become a teacher, you had to pass an exam. If I wanted to teach in a small town, I could have easily passed the exam. However, I wanted to teach in Seoul, despite having studied in a small-town college. Both my parents and my professors discouraged my dreams. They said that Seoul was too competitive for me to apply. However, my grandmother, who I adored so much and was living with my family at the time, told me that night while lying in bed—we always slept in the same bed— "If you teach in Seoul, I would love to live in Seoul with you. That would mean so much to me." I thought, "Oh, this is something that would make my grandma happy, and also something I want to do. If my grandma wants to go to Seoul that much, I have to go no matter what!"

Woonhye Jeong (Edited)
Interviewee: Jeong, Woonhye

I studied so hard for the exam. Before my graduation, I took the exam. Just one day before the graduation date, I received news that I had passed. So right after my graduation, we packed our bags and went to Seoul. When my grandma and I lay in bed that night, she could not contain her excitement. "Is this a dream or reality that you and I have come to Seoul to stay like this?" The first reason my grandma loved living in Seoul was being closer to her daughter, who was financially struggling and living near the area. Her daughter was so poor that she could not afford to have my grandmother stay with her. However, living with her granddaughter (me) now, she could visit her daughter every day. She was so happy to be able to spend time with her daughter. Every morning when my grandma got up early, she would always say, "The body will decay." She would open the windows to let fresh air in, saying, "The body will decay. Why treat it sparingly? Wherever one goes, one should work hard and serve wholeheartedly." It was her attitude towards life. I'm Woonhye Jeong. This is my Korean American Story.

Sang Gyun Kim (Full)
Interviewee: Kim, Sang Gyun
Sang Gyun Kim, a 49-year-old Korean immigrant who has spent 25 years in America, reflects on his experiences navigating cultural differences, discrimination, and the challenges of raising a daughter in a foreign land. Having immigrated with his parents due to the South Korean IMF crisis, Sang pursued education at Georgia State University before establishing his own accounting business as a CPA. Despite his success, Sang faced discrimination while working at his sister-in-law's business and witnessed the tragic consequences of gun violence within his community with his father's close friend passing away after being hospitalised for three years. While tensions between Asian and Black communities once existed, Sang notes a decline in conflict as Korean businesses in predominantly Black neighborhoods have dwindled since the 90s. However, Sang grapples with feelings of isolation in America, missing the sense of community he had in Korea while also reflecting on the freedom that being in the States allows. Sang's own journey is marked by personal loss, including the passing of his mother and the absence of familial support during her eight years of illness. Seeking to instill resilience and conviction in his daughter, Sang reflects on the meaning of home and belonging, yearning to find a place of safety and connection. Despite challenges, he remains committed to preserving his cultural identity, attending Korean mass and seeking community support, albeit with a sense of longing for deeper understanding and solidarity among Korean Americans.

Sang Gyun Kim (Edited)
Interviewee: Kim, Sang Gyun

I came to the U.S. when I was 23 years old, and I've been here for 25 years. I lived in Seoul, Korea before I immigrated to Atlanta, where I've been living for 25 years. My parents immigrated to the U.S., so I came with them. When I first came to this country, there was nothing I could do. My uncle ran a coin laundry in a Black neighborhood in downtown Atlanta. It was a very dangerous place. As my aunt managed the store alone in the evening, she thought she needed a man to keep her safe. So, I worked there only at night. Then, I went to Georgia State University and took classes, because I wanted to study. Now, I'm a certified public accountant who runs my own company. Of course, it was very sad when my mother died. Living in America is very different from living in Korea in many ways. I can't get help around, because I have no relatives here. My mother had been sick for a long time—for about eight years. I tried to take care of her by myself, but it was very hard. For an immigrant like me, it is one of the most difficult things. If there are relatives like aunts or uncles nearby, they will be very helpful. If you can talk with them, you will be comforted. You can tell them how hard it is for you. But here I had to take care of her all by myself, and that was very difficult. It's not easy for older Koreans to find a proper nursing home around here. It is difficult for them to stay with Americans. There was a nursing home for Koreans nearby, but it was built just a few years ago. Before that, there was no nursing home for Koreans only. The Korean-only nursing home was built in South Carolina three or four years ago.

Sang Gyun Kim (Edited)
Interviewee: Kim, Sang Gyun

My friend's mother got dementia and entered the nursing home. It takes two to three hours to get there, and two to three hours to come back home. He drives two to three hours each way so he can spend time with his mother. But when she asks, "Who are you?" he feels incredibly sad. He drives two to three hours to see her because he misses her, but she doesn't even recognize him. But sometimes she recognizes him while they are talking. So he talks with her and feeds her with food. He said he feels very sad when going back home. I think that would be the case. It is hard to explain in one word what it's like to live in this country. While I was living in Korea, I could easily find myself socially connected without special effort. There are many relatives and friends, and also work colleagues if I were working there. However, if I live here, all such social connections are cut off. It's not easy to make new friends here. Even if I work, I do not get along with my colleagues like in Korea. Being cut off from many relationships, I feel lonely in isolation. However, I have more freedom here in many ways. If I were in Korea, I would have to be concerned about "saving face" and take care of such things. However, there is almost no such thing here. So there are advantages and disadvantages. When I first came to America, I experienced it with no expectations. Of course, I was embarrassed and felt a lot of loneliness. Now it has improved a lot because I understand all the situations. Now that I know the pros and cons, I have fun now. Still, this place does not feel like home to me. Then, does Korea feel like home? No, Korea does not feel like home either. I think it is not a place like America or Korea that makes you feel home. Home is a place where you feel psychological stability. But I don't think it's the place where I live now. Even if I go to Korea, it seems hard to find. I just need to keep trying to find it.

Sang Soo Park (Full)
Interviewee: Kim, Park, Sang Soo
Sang Soo Park was born on January 4, 1929, in Kyungsangnamdo. His early years were marked by severe hardship, including extreme hunger that led him to eat dog food, acorns, and foraged shrubbery. Growing up in a community where starvation was rampant, people would greet each other by asking if they had eaten. Despite the harsh conditions, Sang Soo remembers his father as kind and generous, though without a stable trade, which placed a significant responsibility on Sang Soo as the firstborn son to take care of his family. Determined and brave, Sang Soo worked various jobs to support his family. He initially worked in a factory making baskets, then became a carpenter, making tables and chairs for the Sacheon Air Force. During the Korean War, he fled from Sacheon right before his military service. After liberation from Japanese colonization, he faced the ideological conflict between communism and capitalism. He almost joined the communists but was advised by a family friend to stay in the south, a decision that saved his life as many of his friends who went north perished. After the war, Sang Soo became a vegetable salesman, then traded wheat and rice, and eventually ran a restaurant. He took pride in his entrepreneurial spirit, never working under anyone. He even tried cattle ranching, believing it could be profitable. Despite not finishing his education in childhood, he later pursued schooling under Park Chung Hee's regime and eventually earned a master's degree. Sang Soo's younger brother, who was prospering in America, invited him to move to the states in 1965. Sang Soo provided his brother with $20,000 in seed money, encouraging him to start his own company. As the eldest son, Sang Soo bore significant financial responsibility, putting his siblings through school and taking pride in their success. One of his greatest regrets was not allowing his youngest sibling to pursue acting, insisting on architecture instead. In America, Sang Soo faced new challenges. He initially worked at a factory that eventually burned down, leading to a year and a half of hospitalization. After recovering, he moved to Atlanta, ran a grocery store, and converted a movie theater into another grocery store. However, he lost everything during the Rodney King riots, lamenting the lack of police support for Koreans. Fortunately, business owner's insurance allowed him to rebuild. Sang Soo emphasizes the importance of political involvement to ensure the safety and prosperity of the Korean community. Reflecting on his life, he believes that if he had come to America under more challenging circumstances, he might have built a more substantial career. Despite the ups and downs, Sang Soo remains proud of his resilience and the legacy of support and success he fostered within his family.
