Sang Soo Park (Edited)
Interviewee: Kim, Park, Sang Soo

I'm Sang Soo Park, and I was born on January 4, 1929 in Kyungsangnam-do province, Jinyang-gun, Geumgok-myun, Songgok-ri. If a guest visits us from a distant town, he stays at my home. When we serve him a meal, he is supposed to leave a spoonful of food. It was our table manners and culture. The leftovers were what women in the kitchen would eat. It was said that a guest who was eating food at his host's house poured water into the bowl because he was so hungry. When the host's kid nagged his mom for food, she promised that she would feed him with the guest's leftovers. However, the guest poured water into his bowl because he was hungry. So the kid burst out crying because the guest didn't leave any food for him. Whenever we saw someone older, we would ask, "Did you eat breakfast? Did you eat lunch? Did you eat dinner?" That was our greeting, because, back then, we all starved. When I visited the U.S., my brother was working at a chemical factory. He urged me to come to America, saying that he was living a good life and this country is great.

Sang Soo Park (Edited)
Interviewee: Kim, Park, Sang Soo

I told my brother, "Why don't you manage the factory yourself?" My brother responded, "Where can I get the money (to buy the company)?" So, I decided to provide him with the money. And I eventually ended up working with him at the chemical factory. After I started working there, a fire broke out. The chemical factory was totally burned down from the fire. Since then, I was hospitalized for a year and a half. My brother was also sick, at the same time. He used to receive kidney dialysis, and then later he received our sister's kidney to survive. He extended his life a little bit longer, but finally died at the hospital. After my brother died, I moved to Chicago, and then came to Atlanta. I managed a small grocery, and one day, I found a theater was placed on sale. So I bought the theater. After buying it, since I liked managing a large scale business, I transformed it into a grocery store.

Sang Soo Park (Edited)
Interviewee: Kim, Park, Sang Soo

Then the Rodney King riots broke out there. That was my fate. LA was where the Rodney King riots broke out. Although the Rodney King riots happened in LA, it affected the black students in Atlanta. My store was in midst of five colleges, and the students let loose their anger on me a weak Korean. The demonstrators marched to my store. The police squadrons set up a barricade 500m away from us, to prevent the rioters from going further into the city. I closed the steel door of my store. Although I closed the steel door, they kept invading. They broke down the steel door with big clubs, and came into the store. They set a fire inside the store, and I ran upstairs. My wife and me, and the couple who owned the liquor store next door, escaped together to the 2nd floor (the rooftop). So, I called 911, asking for help. I called them several times. However, they were just saying yes and never came to help. If I were a Jewish man or someone else, the police chief would have protected us from the rioters. Weak people are treated the same way wherever they go.

Sang Soo Park (Edited)
Interviewee: Kim, Park, Sang Soo

No matter what country, weak people never get protected. The rioters were destroying my store, but there was nothing I could do. A helicopter was flying over my building. People from the helicopter kept calling me, and I called 911. However, nobody really came to help us. Then, on top of the building, I thought, 'I almost died before, so I'm as good as dead. Despite these hardships, he believes that earlier immigrants faced even greater challenges. As the vice president of the Korean Association in Atlanta, Lee played a crucial role in addressing safety concerns during the riots that followed the LA riots. With the help of a Jewish woman named Frank, he secured a meeting with Mayor Jackson, during which he demanded better protection for Korean American stores. Pastor Ji's moving speech at the subsequent press conference left a lasting impression on Lee. During the Atlanta Olympics, Lee made a point to welcome the North Korean team, despite being labeled a communist for years afterward. He expressed his belief that Koreans, whether from the North or South, should support each other. One of the hardest aspects of immigration for Lee was leaving his friends behind, especially given the high costs of communication and lack of flights to Korea at the time. He views Korea's development fondly and urges second-generation immigrants not to endure the same struggles as their parents. I have three children. An hourly earning wasn't enough to provide a strong future for my kids. So I thought about obtaining a license for a better job. I found out that a realtor license was relatively easy for me to study and obtain, and good for building my career. I've been working as a realtor for thirteen years since then. Back then, my sense of direction was very poor. After driving around a subdivision, I would be completely lost, not knowing where North, East, South, and West were. MapQuest was not available then, so I would be breaking out in a sweat trying to find my way. I had heard that places like Chicago or LA are easier to navigate than Georgia, because those cities are mapped like grids. The streets in Georgia are meandering and have many dead ends. One time the sun had gone down while I was still lost, so I barely found my way home in the darkness. I don't really look like the type of person who cries often, do I? In fact, I don't cry that much. I generally tend to suppress my emotions. Ever since I immigrated to the U.S., I had a hard time adapting to a series of new circumstances, including my in-laws and my marriage life. Time flew by, and I ended up having my third baby. After my third baby was born, I began to suffer from panic attacks, a disorder that many Koreans are afflicted by these days. It was a year after my youngest child was born that I suddenly had difficulty breathing while driving my car. I also felt all strength leaving my body, similar to the symptoms of low blood sugar. I couldn't even lift my fingers. I wondered why and opened the window to breathe better, but it didn't work. It took every ounce of energy I had left to get home and finally lie down on my sofa. I was told to go to the emergency room, but I had no insurance back then, so I was worried about how high the examination charges would be. It's hard to believe that at the time I felt like I was suffocating but still worrying over the medical bills.

Kelly Choi (Edited)
Interviewee: Choi, Kelly

Luckily I survived the night and went to a clinic the next morning. I had a blood test done, as well as some other tests, but no problem was found. The doctor said, "I think your symptoms resulted from emotional stress." I asked how stress could trigger the symptoms and he said, "It happens when a certain chemical from your brain attacks your body. In Korean, it's called kwa-ro-sa (death from overwork). In fact, you could have died." It was then that I realized how much I had been suppressing my emotions. Until then, I was juggling adapting to life in the U.S., fulfilling my responsibilities as a mom, working to make a living, and struggling with a language barrier. But I didn't realize the gravity of how stressed I was until my symptoms hit me. It was eight to nine years into my marriage when I started taking medication for depression. I tried to overcome my depression by seeking faith in God. A pastor said to me, "You should lay all your burdens on God. Psychotherapy will be necessary, but why don't you try that as well?" I really felt like I would die soon. Although I was taking medication, I was still anxious about dying from the panic attacks. One day I went inside my closet and openly confessed to God all the hardships that weighed on my heart. I cried so much. Inside my closet, I confessed to God about all the stressful times when I needed to cry but didn't during my early life as an immigrant. I cried from 2:00 p.m. until 6:00 p.m., until I felt it was enough. Through that, I was able to dispel my stress and overcome my panic disorder without medication. Letting stress accumulate inside you is very unhealthy. You have to grapple with it by all means. Looking back, I think all the difficulties I have experienced from my work have made me stronger. The small things used to easily frustrate me, but now I'm more optimistic and willing to take action.

Yung Duk Kim (Full)
Interviewee: Kim, Yung Duk
Kim Yung Duk was born in 1934 in Changjeon, a small fishing harbor in North Korea. During his early education under Japanese colonization, he attended public school until the 5th grade, where speaking Korean was penalized, and students were often pitted against each other. His upbringing in a Japanese-dominated system left a lasting impression, as he still counts in Japanese. Kim's father ran a successful sardine business, but the rise of the North Korean Communist Party in the late 1940s led to persecution of landlords, business owners, and Christians. In 1947, to escape the Soviet influence and imminent danger, Kim's family fled to South Korea, settling first in Kangwondo and later in Daejeon. As a teenager, Kim supported his family by collecting and selling firewood in the local market. Due to the turmoil and displacement, Kim missed formal education in Hangul, the Korean alphabet. His mother, despite having no formal education herself, taught him to read and write Korean. Kim attended an unaccredited school run by poet Hoon Jung, who instilled in him a love for poetry, literature, and music. This period, enriched by dedicated teachers, was the best time of his life and pivotal in shaping his future. Kim's education continued through various relocations caused by political unrest, including the Yeosu-Suncheon Rebellion in 1948, where his brohter was assigned to investigate the incident by the government. His family him him to avoid guerilla recruitment during the Korean War. His older brother's assignment with the US on the POW exchange at Guje Island eventually brought the family to Guje, where Kim attended high school. Kim then attended Seoul National University and served as a civil engineer in the Navy. His exemplary service led to an opportunity to study in the United States. In 1963, he enrolled at the University of Western Ontario, earning a PhD. In 1974, he moved to New York, supported by a missionary scholarship he had received in Korea. Kim's wife, a PhD in medicine and an anesthesiologist, interned in New York, allowing Kim to join her. For four years, he put his career on hold to care for their children, an experience he highly recommends to other fathers. After completing his PhD, he found a job in New York and was soon offered a role as an engineering advisor in Saudi Arabia. There, he learned about Hyundai's contract for an offshore loading station and was recruited to work for Hyundai in Korea. Kim worked for Hyundai for 25 years. After retiring in 1997, he dedicated himself to improving the lives of Koreans in America. He joined the Korea Society board, helped establish Korean language classes in public schools, joined the voter's council, created the Research Center for Korean Community at Queens College, and founded the Korea Chamber of Commerce. His efforts have significantly contributed to the Korean community's development in the United States.

Holding great stereotypes on what a pastor should be-male, old, and wise-Aram hopes to find a community where her young, woman self is accepted and a place where the true meaning behind religious passages is studied and interpreted.

Reverend Jean Kim (Full)
Interviewee: Kim, Jean
Rev. Jean Kim was born in Hamhung City, North Korea. Living through the Japanese occupation of Korea and also the Korean War, she faced many hardships growing up, as she had to move around from place to place and also work to earn money. As she and her family escaped from Communist North Korea, they lived in Seoul, where one of her brothers joined the army to get an apartment to live in. However, after the breakout of the Korean War, Jean Kim never heard from her brother again. Her family ended up taking the train to Busan, where they lived homeless for three years until Jean moved to America in 1970. She was hoping to get her master’s degree in social work and also worked as a social worker at a mental health community center. She later formed her own Presbyterian Women’s Church and founded foundations to increase awareness for the homeless. She went from place to place, talking about this topic, and published five books. As one of the last things she wants to accomplish, she hopes to make one book in Korean and English, advocating to help out the homeless.

Unzu Lee, born during the Korean War to North Korean refugees, embarked on a journey marked by faith and advocacy. Her family immigrated to Brazil before settling in the US in 1968, where she encountered challenges stemming from language barriers. Despite these obstacles, she found her calling and was ordained in the Presbyterian Church USA in 1995. For two decades in Kentucky, she led a committee dedicated to women's advocacy. Ahn's full feature film, "Spa Night," garnered wide support, reflecting his aspiration to foster a sense of belonging and community while promoting solidarity through his work.

Heeja Park Pai (Full)
Interviewee: Pai, Heeja Park
Heeja Park Pai was born on June 7, 1945, in Seoul, Korea, living in Changshin-dong. She was the fifth child born in her family, and had one younger sister, and she recalls being a rather frail child, often the subject of teasing and bullying by her older siblings. It didn’t help that she didn’t like to eat rice, preferring bread instead, which in retrospect she attributes to an early desire to immigrate to the United States. She was five years old when the Korean War broke out, and though she doesn’t have many memories of this part of her childhood, she does remember how the family’s evacuation from Seoul felt more like a camping trip than an evacuation. She completed her primary and secondary education in Korea before immigrating to the United States on July 15, 1972, when she arrived in San Francisco on a student visa to attend SFU. After completing a semester of schooling, she met President Kim Dae Jung in San Francisco, and upon hearing that he’d be traveling to Washington D.C., traveled to DC as well at the behest of her uncle, who was working as a “trader” and had connections in the East Coast. After arriving in DC, she took a taxi to New York where she’d been offered a job at Korean Airlines, but was shortly laid off. Realizing she wouldn’t be able to stay in the United States for much longer without obtaining a more permanent visa, she opted to search for a sponsor when she came across the announcer Lee Kwan-gae, who said he’d offer sponsorship to someone who’d look over his children. She found an unexpected sponsor under a Jewish physician named Dr. Leslie, who had taken an interest in her art (calligraphy), and had been operating a kind of “boarding house” at his residence for students, fully sponsoring their tuition and lodging. Graced with this opportunity, Pai continued her schooling in New York, attending English classes at NYU for two years before matriculating into the Brooklyn Museum Art School, where she studied for 3 years. Soon, she met her husband, and had one daughter and one son; together, the family lived in the Leslie residence for a number of years. Around this time, too, her husband became ill, as did Dr. Leslie, and were in and out of the hospital for a number of years—she attributes her husband’s failing health to his commitment to his business, which required of him long work hours and many business trips which she took in his stead later into his life. Both her husband and Dr. Leslie passed within a short time span; at the time of her husband’s passing, Pai was in Korea and had to quickly secure a ticket back to New York, which had recently experienced 9/11. Both of her kids began families of their own, and Pai recounts a funny anecdote where she went with her son and her daughter-in-law to go apartment-hunting, assuming that she would live with his family, to her son’s (and daughter-in-law’s) surprise: she admits that this was something she wouldn’t ask of him today.

Yoon Soo Park (Full)
Interviewee: Park, Yoon Soo
Yoon Soo Park was born on July 4, 1929, in Gimcheon, Korea. His parents, originally from North Korea, were involved in the Korean independence movement during the Japanese occupation before settling in Gimcheon. He and his six siblings grew up during this occupation, experiencing the imposition of Japanese language and military training in school, and working in rice fields. His teachers and parents, who were Christians, instilled in him a strong sense of the Korean language by reading the Korean Bible. When the Korean War began, Park was a student at Seoul National University. He and his brothers escaped and took 10 days to reach their hometown, surviving on potatoes. His family relocated to Busan and later settled in Seoul after their home in Gimcheon was bombed.His academic excellence led him to new opportunities abroad. In 1952, he moved to Canada through a scholarship program by a Canadian missionary organization, earning a master’s degree in nuclear physics from the University of Alberta. He later obtained a PhD in solid-state and semiconductor physics from the University of Cincinnati in the US. He was recruited by the Aerospace Research Laboratory in Dayton, Ohio, becoming the head of the semiconductor research lab. Sponsored by UNIDO, he worked with the Korean Institute of Science and Technology (KIST) to advance Korea’s technological development.Despite his decision to stay in the US, Park continually sought ways to support Korea and share his expertise through training and fundraising for Korean students and professors. In the US, he was active in Korean churches and served as chairman of organizations like the Korean American Scholarship Foundation (KASF) and the Korean-U.S. Science Cooperation Center (KUSCO). He remains grateful for his family, career, and the successes of his children and grandchildren.

Young Hae Han (Full)
Interviewee: Han, Young Hae
Young Hae Han was born in Busan in 1952, the youngest of six siblings. Her oldest sister was twelve years older. Her parents were musicians, and she grew up in a large house with a kiddie house and slides, enjoying a happy childhood. Her maternal grandfather, born in 1890, studied medicine at the University of Chicago and became a doctor in Hawaii, where he provided free services to Koreans and supported the Korean independence movement during the Japanese occupation. He was later exiled to Shanghai, where he died in 1941 after being tortured by the Japanese. Posthumously, he was honored by the Korean government in 1968 and is buried in the Korean National Cemetery in Seoul. Her mother, inspired by her father's legacy, became a famous singer and always wore a hanbok, representing her country with pride. Young Hae started playing the piano as a child and initially loved it, but her enthusiasm waned after beginning formal lessons. In 1975, at age 23, she moved to America from Gimpo, with her father renting a bus for family and friends to see her off. She settled in San Francisco, having chosen the United States over Germany due to the opportunity and the presence of her sister and many European musicians in the States. She attended the San Francisco Conservatory for her master’s degree, enjoying a close relationship with her professors. Despite being very homesick and crying daily, she immersed herself in studies and social activities. At Ewha University, frequent student protests closed the school often, allowing her to bond with friends. In San Francisco, however, she found the city lonely and boring, focusing on studying, practicing, and spending time with her nieces. Young Hae later attended the Eastman School of Music at Rochester University, where the small number of Korean students forced her to learn English. She felt lonely and became sick, but this isolation allowed her to improve significantly as a musician. She didn't experience much racism, as the focus in her community was solely on music. After having two children, Young Hae moved back to Korea in 1985, twenty years after first leaving. Concerned more about her children’s safety than her career, she encouraged them to adapt to their new environment without comparing it to America. Her children, initially enthusiastic about their Korean heritage, attended international school, with her daughter choosing an American name upon arrival in Korea. In America, her daughter faced racial bullying, prompting Young Hae to address the issue by educating her daughter’s classmates about Korea, which had a positive impact. Although she felt her career might have been stunted by motherhood, she believed her life experiences enriched her musical skills. Young Hae values freedom for her students and children, sometimes wondering if she should have pushed them harder academically. She allowed them to experience failure, believing it was an important part of their growth.

Born in 1953, Yun Jong Sun's early memories are tinged with happiness, especially his fond recollections of playing soccer during his elementary school days. Starting anew in Argentina, Yun Jong Sun found employment in textiles, a stepping stone toward eventually reaching America. The decision to settle in Argentina had the unintended but welcome outcome of ensuring his children became trilingual, a source of pride for him. However, the transition to life in the States proved challenging, marking the beginning of a difficult period for him. Despite facing adversities, including a stroke at a young age, his unwavering faith in Christ and the support of social services aided in his recovery and ongoing health care. As his children have grown and flourished, Yun Jong Sun now yearns for the opportunity to travel and explore the world. Reflecting on his life, he expresses regret for having worked too tirelessly, often failing to appreciate the beauty and blessings surrounding him. Above all, Yun Jong Sun hopes to be remembered as a man of deep faith, whose journey embodies perseverance, resilience, and an unwavering commitment to his family's well-being. He now serves as pastor at the Love Mission Church of New York.

Inha Cho (Full)
Interviewee: Cho, Inha
Inha Cho was born in South Pyongan Province in what is today North Korea, and spent his childhood there before crossing the 38th parallel, arriving in the South. His daughter is in the room as the interview is taking place to clarify/ask questions. In 1965, Cho was sent to Vietnam as part of the Korean Marine Corps under the Park Chung-hee administration; although he recalls how many civilians and soldiers at the time were against deployment, many went to fight anyway, as the government promised good pay and benefits. In Vietnam, he sympathized with the villagers, and saw atrocities committed against them by the government; it was here that Cho says his support for the defenseless was turn into a strong sense of conviction against injustices. Upon his return, Cho was trained in traditional Korean medicine, and had a practice before moving to the United States in 1978, where he continued work with acupuncture. He was shocked at how many “bad” Koreans there were in America, or Koreans who extorted and blackmailed fellow destitute Koreans, and took it upon himself to prevent such actions from happening. Much later, during the Saigu Uprising, he heard on the new Korean-language radio channel, “Radio Korea,” that Koreatown was the site of uprising and looting following the acquittal of the LAPD officers involved with the beating of Rodney King. With a couple other Korean men, many younger than he, Cho and his crew drove five cars, each with one to three armed individuals, to wherever Radio Korea communicated was in need of backup. He told his crew not to shoot live rounds at anyone, but Cho himself was shot twice, in the thigh and ankle. He recounts how he wrapped his thigh in a plastic grocery store bag while the driver tried to get him to a hospital, but found Koreatown to have been barricaded off, with police moving away from the neighborhood to protect the “white” neighborhoods. Eventually the crew arrived at the ER, only for none of the hospital staff to give him care until he yelled at the staff that he was bleeding profusely. He credits God for saving his life that night, as well as his wife’s sincere prayers. Upon reflection, he found it difficult to accept how a country which boasts strength in diversity could also be the site of intolerable systemic injustice, although 25 years after the Uprising, he states that he continues to believe in the innate goodness of people, though he regrets how the mass media at the time of the Uprising portrayed it as a race conflict between the Korean and Black communities in Los Angeles; he believes that responsibility fell on everyone.

Jinho Lee's journey into journalism began when he moved to the U.S. in 1980 and later joined Radio Korea in 1991. Initially aspiring to attend law school, Lee's career took a pivotal turn during the Los Angeles riots of 1992, a period that offered him an unexpected crash course in journalism. The scarcity of manpower at Radio Korea during the riots provided Lee with the freedom to cover a wide range of stories, significantly shaping his decision to pursue journalism as a career. This experience allowed him to witness firsthand the complexities of racial tensions and economic disparities within the city. Lee's reporting during the riots revealed a multifaceted narrative that extended beyond the surface-level racial conflicts between Black and Korean communities. Through interviews with Black individuals, Asians, and the LAPD, Lee uncovered a consensus that the root causes of the unrest lay in governmental neglect, economic hardship, and a lack of educational and job training opportunities in the area. Despite the racial dynamics highlighted by the media, Lee believed the core issues were more closely tied to systemic neglect by the city government, affecting both Black and Korean residents, rather than a simple racial animosity. One of Lee's significant observations was the frequent violence against store owners, a reality that underscored the daily risks faced by Korean Americans in certain neighborhoods. The conditions he encountered upon moving to LA, reminiscent of a "third-world country," with prevalent trash and graffiti, further emphasized the city's neglect. The situation was so dire that Radio Korea staff, including Lee, had to take extraordinary precautions, sharing a single bulletproof vest for reporting in dangerous areas and driving old cars that they could afford to lose to damage. The Rodney King incident and the subsequent trial, which highlighted police brutality and the systemic injustices faced by African Americans, also impacted Lee's perception, making him feel that Koreans too were victims of the city's failures. Lee's experiences during the LA riots transformed Radio Korea into a critical community resource, acting as a makeshift command center that provided Korean Americans with vital information and support in the absence of adequate police or fire department responses. Reflecting on the riots, Lee acknowledges the deep-seated issues of government neglect in South Central LA but remains hopeful that lessons have been learned. He emphasizes the importance of political engagement and education for Korean Americans, urging them to draw inspiration from the Black community's resilience and advocacy for a stronger collective voice. Through his career and insights, Jinho Lee exemplifies the role of journalism in bridging communities and fostering understanding amidst adversity.

TC Kim’s family immigrated from Korea to the U.S. in the mid-70s when he was just 14. These experiences were compounded by frequent moves due to his father's church-building efforts, forcing TC to adapt to new environments repeatedly, from adopting and then dropping a Southern accent, to adjusting to the diverse cultural landscape of Los Angeles. Education played a significant role in TC's life, with expectations set high for him as the eldest son. At UCLA, he pursued majors in Psychology and Anthropology, diverging from the traditional career paths expected of him. His father's influence was profound, inspiring TC to become a journalist through involvement with the Christian Press, a newspaper publication his father started. The Los Angeles riots of 1992 were a pivotal moment in TC's life, occurring shortly after the death of his father. The chaos and violence of the riots brought significant loss and fear into his life, with his family's bookstore being looted. TC's response to the crisis—capturing the events through photography, assisting in translation for victims, and his subsequent involvement with the LAPD's Community Police Advisory Board (CPAB)—demonstrates his deep commitment to his community and to fostering understanding and cooperation between the police and the community. TC's personal life has been marked by both tragedy and resilience. The loss of his wife to breast cancer, his experiences as a single parent to five boys, three of whom serve in the military, and his engagements with single-family ministries and support for the divorced and widowed, reflect his enduring strength and commitment to family and community. His founding of the United Taekwondo Organization, with its emphasis on Christian faith and responsible use of skills, along with his work to support victims of crime, illustrates his ongoing efforts to contribute positively to society. Despite the hardships and losses, TC Kim's story is one of hope and progress. His involvement in initiatives like the CPAB and his efforts to improve police-community relations highlight the potential for positive change.

Meg Campbell, a 38-year-old nurse at Camp Sejong, was born in Seoul, South Korea, and adopted at the age of five. She grew up in Upstate New York alongside three older adoptee sisters, navigating the complexities of adoptee life. The isolation of her environment often weighed heavily on her, yet her relationship with her sisters, especially her oldest sister Joy, provided a stabilizing force. During her middle school years, Meg grappled with her identity and experienced a notable strain in her relationship with her parents. She perceived that they favored her over her sister Beth, which led to significant familial tension and resulted in Meg not speaking to her parents for six months. This strain was evident even years later, as her parents did not attend her wedding, which occurred 8 or 9 years ago. Despite these challenges, Meg has forged strong bonds with her adoptee sisters, who have been a constant source of support. These relationships have instilled in her a desire to connect with her birth siblings, preferring this connection over discovering who her birth parents are. Currently, Meg is married with two children and has no interest in searching for her birth parents. Identifying more with her American upbringing than her Korean heritage, Meg considers the relationships with her adoptee sisters as pivotal in shaping her life. Her experiences have left her curious about potential siblings but content with the family dynamics she has cultivated with those around her.

Michael Mullen, a 47-year-old from Seoul, South Korea, has a poignant narrative marked by complex family dynamics and personal discovery. Adopted at the age of three from an orphanage, he grew up in Spokane, Washington—a predominantly white area—alongside three domestically adopted siblings who are white. Michael remains close with his adoptive family, although one of his adoptive sisters has ceased contact due to personal issues. Despite several moves back to Korea as an adult, Michael initially refrained from searching for his birth parents to avoid potentially painful revelations. Recently, he accessed his adoption papers for the first time, learning that his biological mother had been killed and his aunt, unable to care for him, had left him at a police station. This information discouraged him from further inquiries to avoid the emotional toll of confirming these details. Michael is married with two sons, ages 12 and 15. Growing up, he struggled to connect with his Korean identity but has embraced it more as an adult, particularly after engaging with other adoptees. His turning point came when he gave a presentation on his adoption story at Queens College, where he found comfort and community among fellow adoptees, leading him to realize the importance of this connection in his life. Now, Michael is keen to share his adoptee story more broadly, participating in the Legacy Project's Love/Hate series, which explores the Korean adoptee experience and its ties to mental health. Through sharing his journey, Michael aims to lessen the stigma around discussing adoption and to foster understanding and solidarity among adoptees.

Nellie Sung's life journey epitomizes the complexity and depth of the adoptee experience. Born in Seoul, South Korea, Nellie was adopted by an American family when she was only 7-8 months old and raised in the twin cities of Minnesota. Despite the love and middle-class comforts provided by her family, including an older biological sister, Nellie grappled with a profound sense of alienation. Being the only person of color in her Catholic school further intensified her feelings of not belonging—a sentiment echoed throughout her youth. Nellie's parents encouraged her connection to her Korean heritage, evident from their thoughtful gifts like a Hanbok for Christmas and her involvement in Korean School and Korean adoptee camps. However, she faced significant challenges, including battling depression triggered by harsh bullying during her formative years. College marked a pivotal shift in Nellie's life. She embarked on a journey of self-discovery, pursuing a major in Women's Studies and later a master's degree in Racial and Ethnic Studies from Trinity College Dublin. Her senior year took her back to South Korea for a semester at Yonsei University, a challenging but ultimately transformative experience that allowed her to blend into a crowd for the first time. Nellie's professional life flourished upon her return to the United States, writing for the Korea Times and teaching in Korea before settling in large cities like New York. Her personal life also prospered, marrying in 2004 and starting a family. Throughout, she remained deeply engaged in social justice, particularly through her involvement in an Asian Women's Organization. A poignant moment in her life was when, at age 22, she escorted an adoptee on a flight to the U.S., reuniting with this individual years later through social media. This encounter stirred a mix of emotions about Korea's adoption practices, reflecting her complicated relationship with her birth country. Nellie's journey underscores a powerful narrative of searching for identity, facing cultural dissonance, and ultimately forging a path that honors both her origins and her own unique life story.

Seungjin Lee, born in 1978 in South Korea, immigrated to the United States in 1988 at the age of ten with his family after a decade-long process initiated when he was born. Settling in the Bronx, New York rather than Flushing, his parents chose this to encourage quicker assimilation into American culture. They sought a better life away from the political instability of South Korea during its dictatorship era, fearing their children might be influenced by communist ideologies. Seungjin's father, who had previously run a glassmaking factory near the DMZ, ventured into owning a dry cleaners in the U.S. despite the family's initial financial struggles with only $2,000 to their name. The cultural shift included exploring American cuisine, with his father experimenting with various foods, from Vienna sausages to clam chowder. While Seungjin's older sisters faced challenges integrating into American society, Seungjin himself adapted quickly, seemingly oblivious to any discrimination, and was indifferent about the move. At home, religious and ideological differences presented challenges, with his mother being very religious and his father critical of the church. Unique among Korean immigrant stories, Seungjin’s father encouraged his children to pursue arts rather than conventional paths like law or medicine. Seungjin himself graduated with a double major in Fine Arts and Management Throughout his life, Seungjin has felt blessed. He is now a father to three children and values the sacrifices his own father made, which he reflects upon deeply, especially during familial events like the burial of his grandfather in Korea, a moment that connected him physically and emotionally to his heritage. In his Legacy Project reflections, Seungjin recounts the arduous transitions and sacrifices, highlighting his father’s journey from North to South Korea during wartime and their shared struggles and resilience upon moving to the U.S. These narratives underscore the profound impact of his family’s migration on his personal and professional life.

Yung Kim, born in 1960, has a rich history shaped by his family's experience through various governmental changes in Korea. His grandfather witnessed the transition from Korea's Imperial government established in 1903 to Japanese occupation, and the subsequent division of Korea post-WWII. Yung’s parents, originally from different parts of Korea, met in Seoul, influencing Yung's sense of identity, which was further shaped during college when he received a scholarship from a North Korean organization. In 1982, Yung moved to the U.S., where he has since been an active member of his local Korean church for 35 years, engaging deeply in various roles from teaching youth about Korean culture and biblical studies to participating in the choir. His commitment extends beyond the church as he volunteers at a senior center and is involved in Korean civil movement organizations advocating for justice in Korean society. Professionally, Yung’s journey began with a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering in Korea, followed by a transition to computer science in the U.S. where he eventually worked for IBM for 15 years. Post-IBM, he explored international opportunities, connecting with a Korean company and the Mexican state department on projects related to waste water treatment. Throughout his life in the U.S., Yung has focused on human rights and societal justice, inspired by the respect he received upon his arrival. His early years in the U.S. were challenging, marked by depression and struggles with language and cultural integration, but support from his wife and work colleagues, as well as his faith community, provided him with a strong support system. Yung's commitment to social change is also evident in his involvement with Father’s School, a program that encourages Korean fathers to abandon authoritarian roles for deeper emotional connections with their families. His niece, Nina Joung, interviewed him for the Legacy Project, highlighting his efforts to bridge cultural gaps within the Korean-American community. Yung's story is a testament to his dedication to his heritage, community service, and the pursuit of justice.

Hyun Joon Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, Hyun Joon
Hyun Joon Lee, born in Seoul and raised in Indonesia, embarked on a richly diverse educational and cultural journey before settling in the Bronx, New York. Her path to the U.S. began unexpectedly when she met her future husband at Yonsei Medical School in 1991. It was love at first sight; they dated for 10 months before getting engaged, and she moved to the U.S. the day after their wedding in 2000, primarily motivated by her relationship. Despite her initial lack of intention to move to the U.S., Hyun adapted quickly to life in New York, bringing with her a deep-rooted value system influenced by her Korean upbringing. Growing up in Indonesia, she attended an international school and was fluent in Indonesian, but the core of her community and values remained distinctly Korean. This foundation was further reinforced during her time in Korea for college, making her transition there seamless. Hyun’s professional journey is as multifaceted as her personal life. She initially attended Cornell for summer schools, despite her father's reservations about her becoming too Americanized, and eventually pursued a career in integrative medicine and aesthetics in the U.S. Over the past 10 years, she has not only practiced but also founded a nonprofit organization aimed at combating obesity in America, seeking to make a significant impact beyond her clinical work. Her life in America has been the longest she has spent in any country, and she views herself as highly adaptable, capable of assimilating under any circumstances. This adaptability was tested during a challenging 2.5-year period in her marriage, which was particularly difficult as her move to the U.S. was motivated by her relationship. Despite these challenges, she and her husband worked through their issues, reinforcing her belief in resilience. Hyun identifies strongly with her Korean heritage, yet her views are progressive, supporting gay rights and abortion rights, which she feels align with her humanity and values rather than national identity. This sometimes puts her at odds with her conservative, Republican, and Christian parents. Nonetheless, her relationship with her parents remains strong; they have been a constant source of support, with her mother visiting frequently to help with her children—aged 16, 14, and 4. In this Legacy Project feature, Hyun Joon Lee reflects on how her unique experiences—from Seoul to the Bronx, from Yonsei to Cornell—have shaped her life's mission to leave a lasting impact on public health in America.

Lillian Chung's journey reflects the intertwining of cultural heritage and personal discovery. Born in Seoul in 1969, her family's immigration to San Diego in 1971 marked the beginning of her American experience, guided by the presence of her aunt and uncle. Her father's pursuit of education in the Philippines redirected their family's path, away from the traditional family business in Korea. Lillian's immersion in Korean American culture blossomed at Camp Conifer, where she found a community of Americanized Korean American youths. While racism was not a predominant memory from her childhood, Lillian's cultural awakening came during a Yonsei summer program in college, offering her a deeper understanding of her Korean roots. Her journey took a romantic turn when her mother and her future mother-in-law orchestrated a meeting with her now-husband while they both resided in Boston. Professionally, Lillian pursued educational psychology, finding fulfillment as a school psychologist. Since moving back to the West Coast from the East Coast, she finds solace in the slower pace of life. Reflecting on her experiences, Lillian acknowledges the evolving landscape of Asian representation, particularly noting the differences her children encounter compared to her own upbringing.

At 37 years old, Sylvia has cultivated a diverse and impactful career, transitioning from practicing law to spearheading innovative philanthropic efforts. She was born into a Korean family in the multicultural neighborhood of Scarborough, where she was the only Korean until 8th grade. Her father owned a convenience and later a video store, embedding early experiences of community and entrepreneurship in her life. Sylvia’s educational and career trajectory led her from studying Criminal Law to roles as a public defender and prosecutor, before moving into policy research and access to justice within the nonprofit sector. She currently holds a significant position as the Chief Innovation Officer at the Asian Pacific Community Fund, where her primary responsibility is to incubate the first national Asian American Community Foundation. The shift to philanthropy aligns with Sylvia's realization of the unique challenges and opportunities facing Asian Americans, the fastest-growing population group in the US. This demographic shift, she notes, has created a disconnect between institutions and the community, something she aims to address in her work. Sylvia's personal journey into her cultural identity began following an inquiry into her Korean American background, which led her to visit Korea for the first time as an adult. Discovering that her family roots trace back to North Korea, she learned more about her family's history, including her father's role in founding one of the first Korean Presbyterian churches in Canada. Inspired by her heritage, Sylvia co-founded HanVoice, a nonprofit focused on North Korean refugee rights, which has been a significant part of her life’s purpose. On a more personal note, Sylvia has faced family challenges, notably a strained relationship with her brother, which led to emotional and physical confrontations. These incidents have shaped her commitment to being open about her struggles, using her platform to promote authenticity and healing. Sylvia’s story also intertwines with her professional and personal life, highlighting her desire to reclaim and pass on her Korean identity to her children, reflecting on her regrets about not being more available to them due to her demanding career. Her story was captured in a Legacy Project video recording, hosted by Suzan Lee Paek in Newport Beach, CA, providing a platform for Sylvia to share her multifaceted experiences and insights.

Jessica, a 26-year-old born and raised in Los Angeles, has led a life marked by diverse experiences and a continuous search for personal fulfillment. Spending most of her early life in Orange County, she enjoyed the benefits of growing up in a multicultural community, where she largely escaped the pains of racism. Her educational journey included a stint at a boarding school near Akron, Ohio, for 1.5 years, which broadened her perspectives further. Initially, Jessica ventured into the world of fashion, interning at Saks Fifth Avenue's marketing department before college. This experience sparked an early interest in a fashion career. However, her academic pursuits led her to study African history in college, where she initially thought she would become a historian and then a teacher. After completing her thesis, she realized that academia was not her calling and shifted her focus to writing, particularly within the esports and gaming industry. Jessica’s career in gaming evolved as she began working in developer relations and business development for a game discovery platform. Her journey through the professional world has been fulfilling, reflecting her desire to engage deeply with her passions. On a more personal note, Jessica embraces her identity as a tattooed Korean American, challenging the traditional taboos against body art in Korean culture. She has extensive tattoos, including a significant piece around her thigh, which was met with unexpected support from her parents. These tattoos, alongside her Asian heritage, have sometimes led to uncomfortable invasions of personal space, prompting Jessica to learn to assert herself and occupy her space confidently, despite occasionally feeling the need to cover up around family. Jessica has also navigated challenges with mental health, including high-functioning depression, OCD, and anxiety, exacerbated by her birth control. Through therapy and self-exploration, she has learned to find happiness amidst these struggles. In a recorded Legacy Project video hosted by Suzan Lee Paek in Newport Beach, CA, Jessica discusses her tattoos and career transitions, from pursuing a degree in Historical Linguistics, engaging in linguistics research, to embracing her role in the gaming world. Her story is one of resilience, adaptation, and the ongoing quest to live authentically.

At 18, she made the significant decision to leave home with her then-boyfriend, who would later become her husband. By 20, she was married, and by 21, she had bought a house. Choosing to delay parenthood, Sung didn’t have children until she was 31, a decision born from a deep desire to be intentional about her life choices. She longed for and was blessed with a daughter, who later transitioned and identified as transmasculine. This experience profoundly shaped Sung's understanding of identity, prompting her to learn about nonbinary identities and fully accept her child. Her son's transition was a pivotal moment for Sung, challenging her to confront and question her deeply held Christian beliefs. The struggle was initially met with resistance from her church community, which suggested "praying the trans away." However, Sung and her husband embarked on a journey to understand and navigate the gender spectrum, eventually finding support in an LGBTQ+ Christian community that taught them the meaning of grace. Sung's reflections on her family’s experiences underscore the importance of living authentically. Her son's poignant question, "What if I never get to live as the person I was meant to be?" resonated deeply with her, catalyzing a shift from a conservative to a more progressive Christian viewpoint. This transformation was not just about accepting her son but also embracing the change within herself. Today, Sung is an advocate for her children to live their true, authentic selves, cherishing the personal growth and new perspectives her family's journey has afforded her. She holds her faith and love for her children as central to her identity, a testament to her resilience and evolving understanding of what it means to truly love and accept.

Doug Kim (Full)
Interviewee: Kim, Doug
Doug Kim, born in 1956 in Minnesota, embodies a narrative of cultural resilience and identity exploration. Growing up in a Midwestern American environment, his early years were marked by significant challenges due to his Korean heritage. His childhood was shaped by frequent bullying in Minnesota until his family relocated to Muenster, Indiana, when he was in fourth grade. This move highlighted his cultural differences even more, escalating conflicts with peers to the extent that his father enrolled him and his siblings in Judo school to learn self-defense. The cultural disconnect was exacerbated by his parents’ lack of communication about their cultural struggles, leaving Doug feeling isolated and misunderstood. During his junior year of high school, another relocation brought Doug and his family to Detroit, Michigan, where he finally found a sense of community within a local Korean population. Despite excelling in extracurricular activities, including roles as Sophomore and Senior Class President, a member of the marching band, and Editor-in-Chief of the school newspaper, Doug’s parents prioritized academic excellence above all else. This focus on academics was a source of tension, as Doug felt pressured to fulfill traditional expectations over his own interests. Doug’s understanding of his cultural identity deepened over time, particularly regarding his parents' insistence on marrying within the Korean community—a stance rooted in their historical experience of cultural suppression during the Japanese Occupation. Their desire to preserve Korean heritage led his mother to found Saejong Camp, aimed at helping Korean-American children connect with their heritage and each other. Doug’s academic and professional life has been dedicated to exploring and teaching Korean-American studies, further influenced by his parents' remarkable journey from Korea to the United States in 1949, as part of a small group of Korean immigrants. His work at San Francisco State University and his long tenure as Director of SaeJong Camp reflect his commitment to educating others about Korean history and culture. Doug often reflects on the strength derived from understanding one’s roots and the adversities faced by ancestors, a perspective that has guided him through his own journey of self-discovery and cultural advocacy.
Keywords: immigration; identity; East Asian studies; SaeJong Camp; Japanese Occupation; medical school; family; South Korean cultural values; cultural advocacy; self-discovery; Judo; Korean heritage; Midwest;

Dr. Young Son Kim, born in Jeonju, South Korea in 1928, experienced a challenging childhood marred by personal loss and the backdrop of the Japanese occupation. At just 10 years old, he faced the death of his father and later his sister, a series of events that profoundly shaped his aspirations. Coming from a large family of eight children and enduring years of financial hardship, Young Son resolved to become a doctor, a dream aimed not only at improving his family’s situation but also at serving others. His journey to fulfill this dream led him to the United States, facilitated by an enduring friendship with an American GI named Wally. With Wally’s assistance, Young Son secured admission with a full scholarship to North Park College in Chicago in 1949, beginning an academic and professional trajectory that included studies at Northwestern University and medical school at the University of Minnesota. Despite his academic success and professional dedication, including working night shifts as an x-ray technician to support himself, Young Son’s desire to return to Korea and contribute more directly to his community faced political barriers. His and his late wife’s outspoken stances on human rights and democracy led to repeated denials of his visa applications by the South Korean government, thwarting his plans to work and teach in Korea. Throughout his life, Young Son remained a devout Christian, a faith inherited from his father, who converted after encounters with missionaries. This faith deeply influenced his life and service, leading him to become an elder in his Presbyterian church, where he served in various capacities, including on the church board. In sharing his story with his son, Doug, for the Legacy Project, Young Son reflects on the intertwined paths of personal ambition and advocacy, acknowledging the complex challenges of navigating identity, career, and activism across continents. His life story underscores the profound impact of resilience and commitment to one’s principles in the face of adversity.

Jin Young Choi was born in 1937 in Manchuria, under the harsh conditions of Japanese occupation. Her early years were marked by cultural and educational restrictions, where speaking Korean was banned, and all schooling was conducted in Japanese. Despite these challenges, her family celebrated the end of the occupation and returned to their native Korea. Unfortunately, their relief was short-lived as they soon found themselves amidst the turmoil of the Korean War. During the war, Jin Young's family faced severe hardships. The trauma of losing her youngest sister to starvation deeply affected Jin Young, but her mother's resilience and insistence on the importance of education remained a guiding force. This maternal encouragement spurred Jin Young to pursue academic excellence against all odds. In a historic achievement for Korea, Jin Young became the first individual to receive a Fulbright Scholarship after the war, in 1961. This opportunity took her to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill to study English Literature. During her time in the United States, she not only faced academic challenges but also navigated the complexities of racial segregation prevalent during that era. Her professors and peers were often surprised by her background and how she managed to excel despite coming from war-torn Korea. Jin Young thrived in her studies and enjoyed her graduate school experience immensely. It was also during this time that she met her future husband, a Korean mathematics student who distinguished himself from his peers through his openness and diligence. After obtaining her master’s degree in 1963, Jin Young embarked on a teaching career in North Carolina, where she offered courses in American literature, a rare feat for an Asian woman in the 1960s. Her teaching journey continued until she returned to Korea with her husband and their three children, following an offer for her husband to take up a professorship in Korea. Back in Korea, Jin Young continued to break barriers; she became a professor of English and American literature, balancing her professional commitments with her roles as a mother and a daughter. Despite her success, she often reflected on her regret for not being more attentive to her aging mother during these years, a sentiment that stayed with her throughout her life. Jin Young's legacy is multifaceted—her children and grandchildren not only achieved high academic honors, including doctoral degrees and valedictorian titles, but they also carried forward her values of perseverance, gratitude, and kindness. Additionally, Jin Young has authored several books, with one becoming a bestseller for over 40 years in Korea. Demonstrating her lifelong commitment to giving back, she donated all the royalties from this book to her religious community. Through her enduring efforts in education and her principled stance against war, Jin Young Choi has left an indelible mark on her family and the broader community, advocating for social engagement and never standing by in the face of injustice. Her story is a profound reminder of the impact one individual can have on shaping a legacy of resilience and dedication.

Chris's story is a narrative of identity, belonging, and self-acceptance. Born in Seoul, South Korea, Chris was adopted and brought to Detroit, United States, in 1985. From an early age, his adoptive parents wanted to ensure Chris was aware of his origins and encouraged him to embrace his Korean heritage, a testament to their supportive and inclusive approach to parenting. Despite their efforts, including exposure to Korean culture through books, audio sets, and local culture camps, Chris faced a complex journey of self-discovery and acceptance. The dichotomy of Chris's early life was marked by the loving environment at home and the challenges he encountered outside, particularly at school where he was often singled out for being Asian and on the smaller side. His struggle with identity deepened as he rejected his Korean heritage during his childhood and adolescence, feeling alienated even within spaces meant to celebrate it, such as Korean culture camps. High school and college presented new opportunities and challenges for Chris. He began to find a sense of community with Asian peers and joined an Asian American organization, steps that marked the beginning of a shift in his journey towards self-acceptance. However, college also highlighted the complexities of his identity; living with a Korean roommate who spoke Korean with friends made Chris feel further estranged, spotlighting the nuanced layers of his adoptee experience. Today, Chris's journey has taken a new direction as he embraces his role as a mentor for adoptees in Chicago. This decision reflects his desire to be the positive figure he felt was absent in his own youth. Mentorship has not only allowed Chris to impact the lives of others positively but has also been transformative for him, fostering a sense of accountability, respect, and confidence in himself. It's a role that emphasizes the importance of self-compassion and forgiveness, values Chris holds dear as he navigates his path to self-discovery. Chris's return to Korea in 2016, for an adoptee conference, was a significant milestone. John Hong's journey from Seoul, Korea, to the suburbs of Chicago, US, is a story of adaptation, resilience, and identity. Born in Seoul, John moved to Chicago when he was just two years old and spent his early years growing up near Wrigley Field. His childhood was marked by independence, as he learned to take care of himself from a young age while both his parents worked—his father as a salesman with commendable English skills and involvement with the Peace Corps, and his mother transitioning from a job at the US Embassy in Korea to new work in the US. Despite moving to the suburbs, where he lived near a cornfield, John's connection to his Korean heritage remained strong, especially through the Korean church he attended every Sunday, which he describes as being with "his own people." This sense of belonging and identity was further reinforced during a trip to Korea with his daughter, highlighting the deep-rooted connection they both felt to their Korean heritage. John's educational journey took him through a predominantly white high school, where he felt out of place, to the University of Illinois, where he found a sense of community with a Korean Christian group. His extracurricular activities varied from being a DJ, radio show host, and participating in a play. John's acting pursuits even led him to roles as an extra in movies and singing the National Anthem at Wrigley Field. The narrative of John's life is also one of personal and spiritual growth, notably influenced by the death of his cousin, which catalyzed his relationship with God. This event marked a turning point, leading him to embrace his faith more fully during his junior year of high school—a faith that had been part of his upbringing but not fully accepted until then. John's professional life is as varied as his personal experiences, having transitioned from practicing law to entrepreneurship. He founded a company that customizes decorations for cellphone cases, showcasing his innovative spirit. His advice to his children encapsulates the lessons learned from his life's journey: trust your network and the people who love you, embrace failure as a stepping stone to progress, and move forward without fear.

David's journey to becoming a doctor was intertwined with his family's narrative. Learning that his father had once aspired to attend medical school deepened David's commitment to his chosen path, albeit with guilt as he pursued his residency while his parents worked tirelessly at their hardware store. This period was marked by a sense of responsibility and regret, as David wished to alleviate his parents' burdens. Tragically, by the time David was financially stable enough to support his parents, his father passed away. Throughout his life, David's strong Christian faith, nurtured from a young age in the church, played a crucial role. It was this faith that partly inspired his aspiration to become a missionary doctor. Now, as a reflection of his journey and the lessons learned, David emphasizes the importance of embracing challenges and new opportunities to his family. Jay Yoo's journey from a young boy in Seoul to a successful family man in the United States encapsulates a story of resilience, growth, and eventual reconciliation with his past. Born in Seoul, South Korea, in 1977, Jay moved to Chicago with his family, leaving behind his maternal grandparents who had raised him when he was born. The transition was challenging; at just five years old, Jay found himself shouldering adult responsibilities, looking after his younger brother while their parents worked tirelessly to provide. This early imposition of adulthood left Jay with deep-seated emotional scars, a burden he carried into his adult life. Despite outward success, Jay struggled with the invisible weight of his childhood trauma. Counseling and the support of his church community and understanding wife have been crucial in his journey towards healing, yet gaps remained in his emotional wellbeing. The loneliness and anxiety of his youth, marked by racism and a constant struggle to fit in, were juxtaposed with moments of joy, such as the cherished letters from his grandmother in Korea. Jay's story is also one of perseverance and hard work. His parents, determined to build a better life, eventually owned their own businesses, a testament to their resilience and entrepreneurial spirit. However, this success came at a personal cost to Jay, who sacrificed his education and personal aspirations to support his family's endeavors. As an adult, Jay reflects on his experiences with a nuanced understanding. He recognizes the sacrifices made by his parents and the strength he gained from his challenges. Marriage and fatherhood have offered him new perspectives and motivations. He is determined to provide his children with the support and opportunities he lacked, emphasizing the importance of understanding their heritage and the struggles of their ancestors. Jay's return visits to Korea, beginning when he was nine or ten, reconnected him with his roots and offered moments of joy and belonging that were rare in his childhood. His involvement in a diverse high school and a Christian community provided a sense of belonging and acceptance that he had longed for. Today, Jay has come to terms with his past and the decisions made by his parents. He has found forgiveness and focuses on living in the present, cherishing the blessings of his family and financial stability.

Matt Fischer (Full)
Interviewee: Fischer, Matt
Born in Korea, to a mother who was unable to care for him, Matt Fischer was left on the side of the road, subsequently living in an orphanage until the age of 7 when he was adopted by the Fischers, a family in a small town in Michigan. Despite the initial joy of joining a new family, Matt's journey was fraught with challenges. He struggled with a sense of belonging, faced favoritism within his adoptive family, and endured academic and emotional setbacks imposed by his adoptive parents. The turning point in Matt's life came when he was unceremoniously expelled from his home at 18, leading to a period of instability and hardship. However, his life took a positive turn when he was welcomed into the Dennell family, who provided him with the support and love he had been denied. This new family became his anchor for over three decades, illustrating the profound impact of chosen family and unconditional support. Matt's journey through education was marked by determination and resilience. Despite being pulled out of honors classes and transferred schools to hinder his academic success, he thrived in a community college before transferring to the University of Michigan for chemical engineering. His collegiate years also allowed him to reconnect with his Korean heritage through basketball and other community activities. His personal life flourished alongside his academic and professional achievements. Meeting his wife in a biology class, their shared journey through medical school and residency, and their subsequent marriage highlight the importance of companionship and mutual support. The decision to adopt from Hope International, the same agency through which he was adopted, reflects Matt's gratitude for his own adoption and his desire to provide a child with the opportunities he was afforded. The process of adopting his daughter, Chloe, and the cautious emotional investment until the adoption was finalized, underscored the complexities and emotional nuances of adoption. Matt's commitment to multiculturalism and his desire for his children to embrace a diverse cultural identity are central themes in his life. His sons' identification with their Indian heritage, through their mother, and the family's immediate acceptance of Chloe illustrate the beauty of a multicultural family dynamic. Matt's attempt to connect with his birth parents during a visit to Korea, and his wish for his ashes to be sent to Korea upon his death, signify a full-circle moment in his journey of self-discovery and acceptance of his Korean identity. Matt Fischer's story is a testament to the power of resilience, the value of diverse cultural identities, and the profound impact of both biological and chosen families in shaping one's life.

Dan Chung was born in Seoul, Korea, in 1977 and moving to the United States at just five months old, Dan's early life was marked by a legal hurdle—living as an illegal alien due to his parents' oversight in securing his citizenship. It wasn't until his wife took the initiative years later that Dan became a U.S. citizen, a status his parents have yet to obtain. The Chung family relocated from Korea in search of a better life, driven by Dan's father's disillusionment with the militarized state of Korea at the time and a defining incident that underscored his distrust of authority. This fierce independence and skepticism towards authority were traits Dan inherited and values deeply, influencing his decision to eschew corporate life in favor of running an organization dedicated to aiding North Korean refugees. This work, challenging and illegal in China, has been a testament to Dan's ingenuity and the spirit of resistance instilled in him by his upbringing. Growing up on the South side of Chicago, Dan's childhood was far from conventional, with memories of playing with a gun in the back of his parents' dry cleaning business and an early exposure to the realities of living in a rough neighborhood. Despite the lack of academic pressure from his parents and becoming known as the "King of Detention," Dan reflects positively on the freedom and responsibility he was given to learn from his mistakes—a freedom he cherishes and extends to his own children. Dan's professional journey as the founder of Crossing Borders is inspired by his awakening to the plight of North Korean refugees during a famine, a cause to which he has dedicated nearly 17 years of his life. His adventures, including a nerve-wracking experience in China that highlighted the precarious nature of his work, underscore his commitment to this cause. Raised in the diverse suburb of Niles, Dan enjoyed a childhood where race was not a divisive issue, a stark contrast to his teenage years in Indianapolis, where he felt the sting of being a minority and learned to defend himself with humor and wit rather than violence. These experiences shaped his outlook on life and his approach to parenting, emphasizing faith, curiosity, and the value of community over material success. Dan hopes to instill in his children the importance of engaging with others, understanding diverse perspectives, and building a strong network of supportive relationships. To him, true wealth lies not in solitary achievements but in the richness of community and the bonds of love and care that unite people.

Ji-Yeon Yuh was born in Seoul, Korea in 1965. She moved to the U.S. at the tender age of five, following her parents' pursuit of higher education and professional opportunities. Her father, on a student visa studying Theology, and her mother, a medical doctor, created a new life in Chicago, navigating the challenges and opportunities of immigrant life. In the early years, Ji-Yeon's family life was deeply intertwined with the Korean American community in Chicago, primarily through their church and her father's international student connections. Despite these communal ties, her early life in the U.S. was marked by a sense of isolation from her extended family in Korea and the cultural shock of adjusting to American life. This adjustment was further complicated by language barriers within her own household, leading Ji-Yeon to seek solace and education in American children's television programs. Ji-Yeon's educational journey, from attending an elite private school where she first encountered class consciousness, to her transformative years at Stanford University, reflects her evolving understanding of her identity and societal perceptions of race and beauty. Despite facing challenges related to her immigrant status and racial identity, Ji-Yeon's academic and social experiences at Stanford marked a significant shift in her self-perception and social interactions. Her career path diverged significantly from the expectations set by her family. Initially drawn to the prospect of medical school, Ji-Yeon discovered her passion for writing and journalism at Stanford. This passion led her to explore the fields of history and journalism, focusing on immigration and the Asian American experience. Her work, particularly a widely-read column on the culture wars, reflects her commitment to filling the gaps in Asian American literature and history. Ji-Yeon's professional and personal life continued to be a reflection of her multifaceted identity as an Asian American woman, a journalist, and an academic. Her research on military brides and her subsequent role in Asian American studies highlight her dedication to understanding and teaching the complexities of immigration, race, and gender. Ji-yeon became a founding faculty of the first Asian American Studies department at Northwestern Univeristy. Her life is a testament to the resilience and adaptability of the immigrant experience, and her contributions to journalism and academia offer valuable insights into the Asian American experience.

Bonnie Bongwan Cho-Oh's remarkable journey from Seoul, Korea to the United States is a testament to resilience, intellectual pursuit, and profound personal growth amidst adversity. Born in Seoul and arriving in the U.S. during the winter of 1956, Bonnie's early life was marked by personal tragedy, notably the death of her younger brother at the age of four—a pivotal event that deeply impacted her and inspired her book, "Phoenix in a Jade Bowl." Growing up in Korea during the 1940s, Bonnie experienced the challenges of living under an authoritarian regime amid political and intellectual persecution. Her father, a pioneering human rights lawyer, faced political persecution for maintaining their Korean surname during the Japanese occupation, a stance that left young Bonnie as the sole Korean-named student in her class, subjected to punishment and isolation. These early experiences of oppression and injustice fueled Bonnie's resolve to fight against inequity, a theme that would define her life's work. Her father's transition from a persecuted lawyer to a judge advocating for unfairly punished independence activists, and their home serving as a sanctuary for released prisoners, further influenced her commitment to justice. Bonnie's academic journey in the United States began with her independent applications to prestigious colleges, including Vassar, Radcliffe, and Barnard, leading to her acceptance and attendance at Barnard College on scholarships and financial aid. Her time at Barnard not only advanced her educational pursuits but also introduced her to her future husband, setting the stage for her next life chapter. Despite initial expectations of domestic life, Bonnie's husband encouraged her to pursue graduate studies at Georgetown, an endeavor that would see her navigate motherhood, academia, and eventually a teaching role at a local Catholic girls' high school. Her academic career was punctuated by a move to St. Paul, Minnesota, and later, significant advancements including a Danford fellowship that supported her Ph.D. studies at the University of Chicago. Yuri Doolan was born in 1988 on an Air Force base in Songtan, South Korea, to an American father and a Korean mother, Yuri's earliest memories are imbued with the warmth of his mother's love amidst the backdrop of a military camp town. Despite the early divorce of his parents and an abrupt move to Cleveland, Ohio, these formative years in Korea left an indelible mark on Yuri, shaping his sense of identity and belonging. In Ohio, his now single immigrant mother raised him and his brother, with little to be seen of his father. Growing up mixed race in the United States presented its own set of challenges and revelations, particularly during his schooling years when he first became acutely aware of his unique heritage. Yuri's journey into academia was fueled by a desire to understand his own history and that of others like him. His pursuit of Asian American history at Ohio State University was not just academic; it was deeply personal. This drive led him to Northwestern University for his Ph.D., where he explored the stories of mixed-race Koreans, inspired by his own experiences and his mother's struggles as an immigrant and a woman of color. His work seeks to bridge gaps between mixed-race students and the broader Asian American community, highlighting the nuanced experiences of identity, migration, and belonging. His current book project, The First Amerasians: Mixed Race Koreans from Camptowns to America, epitomizes his commitment to telling the stories of mixed-race Koreans, tracing their journey from U.S.-occupied South Korea to adoptive American homes. Through his academic and personal journey, Yuri has not only sought to understand his own identity but has also worked to provide a platform for those with similar backgrounds to share their stories. His dedication to making academic writing impactful and accessible to a broader audience underscores his belief in the power of storytelling to foster understanding and empathy. Yuri's personal life, marked by the complexity of coming out to his deeply Christian mother, further illustrates his navigations through the intersections of identity, family, and acceptance. Each step of Yuri's journey reflects a commitment to understanding and compassion, both in his academic pursuits and personal relationships. Now an Assistant Professor in the Department of History and the Women’s, Gender, and Sexuality Studies Program at Brandeis University, Dr. Doolan continues to inspire with his dedication to exploring the multifaceted stories of Amerasians and their journeys of identity, belonging, and resilience.
