Rayanne Williams' journey from being adopted into a white American family at four months old to her present-day reflections on identity and heritage encapsulates a complex narrative of growth, discovery, and acceptance. Initially resistant to her Korean heritage, Rayanne's early years were marked by a desire to assimilate and distance herself from her Asian roots. Growing up in Vermont, she found herself to be the only Korean in her community, leading to a childhood and adolescence where she grappled with her distinctiveness. This resistance extended to her name, as she disliked retaining her Korean name as her middle name, symbolizing a connection to an identity she wasn't ready to embrace. Rayanne's perspective began to shift during her first trip to Korea at 18, facilitated by her supportive adoptive parents and the Holt International Agency. Amidst the emotional journey and the camaraderie with fellow adoptees, she faced the reality of her adoption story, including the inaccuracies surrounding her birthday and the daunting prospect of exploring her adoptee identity further. Despite these revelations, Rayanne wasn't ready to fully engage with her Koreanness, a sentiment that persisted until the more recent challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic and the rise in Asian hate, which forced her to confront her ethnicity in ways she hadn't before.Her parents' encouragement to reconnect with her Korean roots—manifested through cultural immersion and culinary explorations at home—laid the foundation for Rayanne's gradual appreciation of her heritage. Yet, her desire for a deeper connection with the Korean community has been hampered by barriers, including her non-religious stance which made integration into church-centered Korean circles challenging. This longing for belonging led Rayanne to immerse herself in studying Korean and engaging with the broader cultural community, efforts that introduced her to a diverse group of people but also highlighted the external expectations placed on her because of her appearance. Rayanne's struggle with her identity is multifaceted; she identifies as Asian without hesitation but finds the label of Korean, with its rich historical and cultural implications, more difficult to claim. Her move to Atlanta for college, where she pursued a major in music and met her husband, marked a significant chapter in her life, offering new environments and experiences yet also bringing into focus the unresolved aspects of her adoption. Rayanne's ongoing journey involves reconciling with the possibility that she may never know her biological family. Despite the pain of seeing other adoptees reunite with their relatives, she has found solace in the community of Koreans and Korean American adoptees. Through their stories, Rayanne has begun to find peace and a forward-looking perspective, embracing the uncertainties and possibilities that lie ahead.

Sarah Park (Full)
Interviewee: Park, Sarah
Sarah Park, Korean maiden name Kim Yu Jeong, was born in 1985 in Seoul, South Korea, the eldest child of two (one younger brother). She lived with her family in Korea until she completed middle school, and has memories of her parents always putting her in a place to receive the best education; she believes that she attended around 10 schools before college, an oddly high number she attributes to her parents’ wishes for her. In moving around different schools within Seoul. Sarah had an early understanding of how society was stratified, and with it a strong conviction that, wherever she was, she ought to work toward creating a more equal and fair society. Although her family originally had plans to move to the DC area, they chose to move to Atlanta instead, in part due to the city’s exposure during the Olympics, but also because they knew a few people who had immigrated to Atlanta before them. Sarah remembers conversations she had with her younger brother about how it was sad to see her parents work so hard in a new country, having to adapt to all of its stresses, but in retrospect feels that wherever her parents worked, they would have been met with equal stressors, whether it be in Korea or in the U.S. While working/volunteering at a conference in (or right after?) college, she met her future husband, who she said was one of the few people who “treated her for who she was,” rather than treat her how the rest of society did: as a young Asian woman. Her husband, who was born in America to parents who immigrated in the 1970s, would go on “volunteering dates” with her as they continued running into each other at various events. They married, and have kids together who Sarah insists on raising “not identically” to how she was raised; among her many reflections today is how she can raise good human beings, as well as which parts of her Korean and American identities she thinks they’ll take after in becoming civically responsible citizens. In her own words, she wants her kids to grow up like fish, acknowledging that there are both bigger and smaller fish out there, but that at the end of the day they should swim with the current in stride, with no more stressors than necessary. Today, she continues her volunteering and civic work in Atlanta, and when asked by her friends why she’s chosen to remain in the American South (with all of its connotations), she believes that there’s a reason God placed her family there, to carry out work for the Korean American community and the rest of the Atlanta community for future generations so that they might live in a more fair society.

David Shin was born in 1965 in South Korea and immigrated to Toronto, Canada, at the tender age of four. David's early life was shaped by the hardworking ethos of his parents—an electrical engineer father and a mother with a master’s in Math and science. Despite his father securing a job at a TV manufacturer, David’s childhood was marked by financial constraints, evident in his wearing hand-me-downs and being unable to afford Little League participation. David's perception of racism during his childhood was minimal, often encountering curiosity about his ethnicity rather than outright discrimination. His father’s endeavor in the real estate sector, starting with a 16-unit apartment complex acquired with a modest 10% downpayment, exposed David to the harsh realities of financial management and investment risks. This experience, coupled with observing his family’s frugal lifestyle despite their asset wealth, significantly influenced his career trajectory and personal life choices. Choosing to diverge from his father's path, David pursued engineering, dedicating himself to academic excellence and leadership, as evidenced by his role as president of the Korean American Student Association. This commitment to education and community engagement continued with his decision to attend law school, where he not only honed his legal acumen but also gained insight into the demanding work culture of law firms. David’s personal life has had its share of challenges, including two divorces and a departure from the church, reflecting a journey of self-discovery and changing beliefs. His move to Houston and foray into real estate—despite initial reservations—signify a departure from past influences and a step towards carving his own path. Today, David reflects on his immigrant family’s sacrifices and the financial struggles that shadowed his upbringing with a nuanced understanding. The legacy of being "asset rich, cash flow poor" has imparted in him a deep-seated caution towards spending, inherited from his parents who, despite their successes, remain frugal. David's story encapsulates the immigrant experience of striving for a better life for the next generation, navigating the complexities of cultural integration, financial stability, and personal fulfillment.

David So's journey from South Korea to the United States encapsulates the intricate tapestry of identity, community, and purpose that defines the life of a 1.5-generation immigrant. Born in 1987 in Korea and relocating to the U.S. in 1995 with his family, David's earliest memories of arrival are marked by the sweltering heat of a Louisiana summer on July 14th, a day that symbolized the beginning of a new chapter. The Korean church in Louisiana became a beacon for David's family, serving not just as a place of worship but as a vital community center for Korean Americans navigating their new lives. Despite the church's central role in his early years, David's relationship with it became fraught as he grew older. The politics and gossip that often permeated church life led him to take a break from the institution, a decision that coincided with a tumultuous period in his 20s characterized by drinking, driving infractions, and an arrest. However, David's narrative is one of redemption and growth. Recently, he has found his way back to church, seeking solace and community once more, an endeavor that coincides with a significant personal milestone: his proposal to his girlfriend of 13 years. David's commitment to his heritage and community took a decisive turn in 2015 when he attended a Korean Festival in Houston. Inspired by the vibrant celebration of Korean culture, he seized a job opportunity in Houston in 2016, immersing himself in the Korean American community. His involvement with organizations such as the Korean Festival Houston (KASH) underscored his dedication to his roots. Professionally, David has carved a niche for himself by running an insurance brokerage that demystifies the concept of insurance for Korean immigrants, a vital service given the unfamiliarity of many in the community with the American insurance landscape. Beyond his professional achievements, David's life is deeply intertwined with his family. His mother, who runs a store, and his father, who supports her while working on his doctorate, exemplify the hardworking spirit that David has inherited. Today, he stands at the intersection of his American present and Korean heritage, navigating the complexities of being a pastor’s kid and a business owner dedicated to serving his community. David dreams of expanding his business to reach a broader, multiethnic, and multilingual American audience, continuing his mission to foster a healthier business environment for immigrants.

Dona Kim Murphey's journey is a testament to resilience, advocacy, and the pursuit of inclusion in a diverse America. Born in the late 1970s in Houston, Texas, Dona's early years were marked by a notable lack of diversity in her surroundings. Growing up in Northwest Houston, an area predominantly white at the time, she rarely encountered fellow Asians, let alone Korean Americans, in her elementary school. This scarcity of diversity slightly improved during her high school years, though Korean Americans remained a rarity. Despite these challenges, Dona's ambition and intellect propelled her to Harvard University, marking her first significant departure from Houston. However, her connection to her hometown remained strong, and after completing her undergraduate studies, she returned to Houston. Before embarking on her medical school journey, Dona dedicated a year to community projects, laying the groundwork for her lifelong commitment to creating opportunities for underrepresented students. Dona's academic pursuits didn't stop at medical school; she furthered her education by obtaining a PhD. It was during her postgraduate studies and early professional career that Dona's engagement with community work deepened, a path that eventually led her to politics. Throughout her career, Dona faced an identity crisis, particularly during the Asian Hate incidents that coincided with the 2016 election. This period of reflection on her identity and heritage was pivotal, prompting her to embrace her Korean American identity more fully. Dona's personal life reflects her complex identity; married to a white man, her children are of mixed heritage. For some time, they struggled to identify with their Asian roots, a challenge that Dona navigated with care and sensitivity. Professionally, Dona is proudest of her moral stand against accepting a job offer under a department chairman she didn't respect, a testament to her integrity and principles. Returning to Houston with her husband, Dona witnessed and contributed to the city's growing diversity and development. She believes that Houston has made significant strides in fostering difficult but necessary conversations among different cultural and ethnic groups, which has enriched the community's inclusivity and resilience. In 2019, her advocacy work, especially around immigration policy, led her to run for public office, underscoring her belief in the importance of representation and stepping into challenging roles. Dona's experiences with prejudice, both as an Asian American and a woman, have shaped her career and advocacy. Her negotiation for a deserved higher position in the face of gender-based discrimination, coupled with the societal shifts around the 2016 election, steered her away from a linear academic career path towards a more impactful role in community advocacy and politics. A pivotal moment in her life was a conversation with her parents at age 16, where they emphasized the importance of understanding one's past to inform the present and future. As a neurologist and community advocate, Dona Kim Murphey hopes to inspire others to recognize the power of representation, inclusion, and the acknowledgment of the full humanity of all communities.

Dr. Kee Ok Cho (Full)
Interviewee: Cho, Kee Ok
Dr. Kee Ok Cho was born on August 22, 1927 in Gimpo, Korea. She was born a twin, but her sister tragically died during childbirth, and she remembers how poor her family was when she was younger. She had other siblings, including an older sister of nine years, all of whom were born in different regions in Korea owing to the family’s involvement with Christian charity work, which demanded that the family move around often; as such, she dictates how her hometown was not the one of her parents, who were born in South Hamgyeong (North Korea) nor of her other siblings. While the family would come into some wealth later on in her adolescence, they faced many hardships when she was younger, and she speaks about how she was told that, because her mother couldn’t produce breastmilk, she was fed gruel instead. Later, her father would buy a plot of land for sustenance farming, and Dr. Cho recounts how although food was a struggle for many Korean families during the Japanese occupation, it wasn’t an issue that her family faced after buying the plot. Her father also strongly believed that women should have access to higher education, and encouraged her to continue schooling beyond what was typical of women at the time. However, Dr. Cho felt that her options as a woman were limited to either medicine or teaching, and so following in the footsteps of her older sister who chose to study pharmacy in Japan, Dr. Cho left for Japan to study medicine in 1944, though she had to return to Korea at the war’s end. She ended up interning for a year at a hospital in Seoul, after which the Korean War broke out, and she found work as a medic and medical translator during the war. In 1954, she arrived in the United States to attend medical school and returned to Korea in 1958 to practice medicine as a pediatric cardiologist, but found the destitute conditions impossible to work in. She looked into returning to the United States once more, this time to practice medicine, but immigrating to the country proved much more difficult than applying to study there: she first had to prove her English language competency which had not been required of her when interning at Seoul National Hospital, as they came from the Japanese tradition of studying Western sciences in the German language. Rather, she studied for her certification at Severance Hospital at Yonsei, which as a school set up by American missionaries, offered English training. After completing her language training, she lived abroad in Canada for three years (as was another requirement to entry into the U.S.), before finally arriving in New York where she practiced medicine as an affiliate clinical professor at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine.

Haejung Lee was born in Cheongju in 1961 and grew up in various places due to her father's military career, finally settling in Seoul at the age of six. Haejung's dream was to have a wonderful family, even though her frailty made her doubt she could achieve it. Financial difficulties worsened after the birth of their last child, and both Haejung and her husband struggled with English, leading her husband to abandon his Nobel Prize dreams. Haejung also faced challenges in pursuing her goal of becoming an art teacher. Feeling lonely and isolated in America, Haejung's situation worsened when her husband left the family. She contemplated suicide but survived an attempt, which left her eldest daughter feeling deeply betrayed. This incident prompted Haejung to reevaluate her role as a parent and her approach to life. Her children's mental health issues, including bipolar disorder, depression, and binge eating disorder, further strained the family. Financial hardship forced her eldest daughter to work as a hostess in a Japanese bar, which initially worried Haejung because of the connotation of being a hostess in Korea. Her daughter showed her what a hostess does in an American restaurant, and she chose to trust her children's judgement after this. Her youngest son and eldest daughter both  attempted suicide, adding to her distress. Despite these challenges, Haejung's second daughter went to college, and her son joined the military, motivated by a desire not to burden his mother. Haejung realized she had raised her children with little praise, a trait inherited from her military upbringing. This realization led to an emotional reconciliation with her eldest daughter. Haejung's struggle with English has been a significant barrier, limiting her ability to connect with others and mentor her children. She has come to understand the importance of being a good role model through actions rather than words. She now believes in loving and taking care of herself as a foundation for her life in America. Overcoming the shame of her husband's departure, Haejung has learned that bad things can happen to anyone and that suffering can be alleviated by sharing it with others. She aspires to be a supportive presence for others, helping to make their suffering less lonely.

Helen Chang (Full)
Interviewee: Chang, Helen
Helen Chang was born in Seoul, Korea, in 1949. Helen's early years were marked by the aftermath of conflict and a typhoon she vaguely recalls. Despite these early memories, Helen identifies strongly as American, having emigrated to the US in 1972, yet she holds a deep pride in her Korean American heritage. Helen's journey to the United States began at 19, after meeting her first husband, a German chef, while working as a receptionist at a hotel. Their life together took her from Germany to Las Vegas, Nevada, where they started anew with just $2,000. Life in early 1970s Las Vegas was modest; Helen recalls a $175 monthly rent for their two-bedroom apartment and making ends meet with a daily wage of $25, plus tips. Despite the lack of a Korean community—only nine Koreans lived in Las Vegas at the time—and the absence of a Korean grocery store, Helen adapted, substituting kimchi with cabbage and celery seasoned with gochujang. A subsequent move to Dallas, Texas, brought Helen closer to a larger Korean community, which she found comforting. However, her life took many turns, including a divorce, a move to Houston, and the adoption of her niece. Helen's resilience shone through as she remarried, this time to a Jewish man who supported her entrepreneurial spirit, leading to the ownership of seven restaurants. This partnership also saw the adoption of her niece, further solidifying her family in the United States. Helen's background is deeply intertwined with the history of Korea itself. Her family hails from Kaesong, now part of North Korea, and her parents' migration to the South post-war underscored the value of education and the opportunities it could provide. This belief propelled Helen to success in the United States, overcoming language barriers thanks to her mother's insistence on English education. Her multicultural household, with roots in both Korean and Jewish traditions, highlights Helen's unique identity. She has been an active member of the Korean American community, serving as the first woman president of the Korean American Association, and her dual citizenship enables her to vote in both South Korean and American elections—a symbol of her deep connection to both countries. Helen Chang's story is not just one of success in business but also of cultural integration, community service, and personal growth. She has lived the American dream while maintaining her Korean heritage, becoming a symbol of success and resilience for both communities. Known affectionately as 'Miss KoTex' for her Korean-Texan identity, Helen's journey from a young hotel receptionist in Seoul to a respected community leader in Houston exemplifies her ability to make the most of life's opportunities, embodying the spirit of perseverance and cultural pride.

Michael Jhin was born in 1950 in Hong Kong to a Korean father and a Chinese mother. Michael's early years were shaped by the diverse cultural landscape of post-war Hong Kong. Despite the complexities of his mixed heritage, Michael's racial identity was not a point of contention in his youth, thanks in part to his Cantonese fluency and Chinese appearance. The backdrop of Michael's childhood was a large house nestled on a hillside opposite Victoria Peak, an undeveloped area of Hong Kong where he enjoyed the solitude and beauty of the surrounding nature. This idyllic existence was contrasted by the Western affluence he observed among the British expatriates, planting early seeds of ambition in Michael. His father's gripping narrative, involving a last-minute trip to Incheon just before the outbreak of the Korean War, subsequent capture by the Chinese army, and a dramatic escape back to Hong Kong, instilled in Michael a sense of resilience and determination. Meanwhile, his mother's entrepreneurial spirit, demonstrated through her operation of several clothing shops, provided a stable foundation for the family. The pivotal moment came when Michael's father, leveraging his connections and pleading with the Consulate General, secured visas for the family to move to the United States. Settling in a diverse yet challenging neighborhood in New York City, Michael was confronted with the realities of racial identity and the complexities of assimilation. It was here that he forged his understanding of worth and identity, embracing the notion that despite ethnic differences, all belong to the human race. Michael's journey from the hillsides of Hong Kong to the bustling streets of New York laid the groundwork for his ambitious ascent in the corporate world. At 33, he broke barriers as the first Asian CEO of a university hospital in mainland USA, taking the helm at Temple University Hospital in Philadelphia before moving on to executive positions in California and Texas. His tenure as CEO of St. Luke's Hospital in Houston was a career highlight, symbolizing not just personal achievement but the realization of his American dream.

Young Nam Park was born in 1931 in North Korea. He had a privileged childhood due to his father's education and job as head of the industrial bank, appointed by the Japanese government. After he was discharged, his US Visa to study in the US got approved and he attended Davidson College in North Carolina, where he navigated the complexities of the civil rights movement and the racial segregation of the South. Due to his involvement in a letter against the Korean government at the time, he was unable to return back to Korea for 18 years in which time, his father and mother’s passed away. Susan Jhin's life story is a testament to resilience, cultural pride, and the power of community support in the face of adversity. Born in Daejeon, South Korea, in 1961, Susan moved to the United States at the age of 9, settling in Northeast Philadelphia. Despite not knowing English upon her arrival, she found friendship and a language teacher in a fellow student named Abraham. Growing up in the 1970s, when MASH painted a singular perspective of Korea for many Americans, Susan felt the weight of her homeland's obscurity. This feeling was amplified in 1979 when, during the Pope's visit to Philadelphia, the Korean Catholic Church was initially overlooked when the Pope didn’t recognize that she was Korean—a moment that deeply impacted Susan. Driven by a desire to elevate Korean culture beyond the stereotypes, Susan has dedicated her life to cultural education and outreach. From teaching the Korean language at Smith College to leading programs on Korean culture in business school and beyond, Susan's efforts have been relentless. Karl Johnson (Full)
Interviewee: Johnson, Karl
Originally from Korea, Karl Johnson was adopted at the age of 5 months and raised most of his life in Central Minnesota. He later moved to Korea to teach English. Karl's family was extremely loving growing up, and his mother, who ran a residency program for teen moms, prioritized diversity and cultural exposure. Despite the love, Karl faced subliminal racism as a result of being different. His mother's efforts to address this included placing him in Montessori schools with diverse students. Karl's friend from childhood was born in South Africa and was Yugoslavian, contributing to his exposure to various cultures. Dealing with the challenges of being different, Karl developed resilience but struggled with the burden of not fitting in. Eventually, he shared his experiences with his parents, who, although apologetic, couldn't change the past. Attending a Korean culture camp, Camp Kimchi, Karl found it challenging to fit in despite meeting adoptees and peers. Later, at a liberal state school, he majored in Social Work, gaining insights into systems of oppression and connecting them to his own experiences. As a child, Karl craved information about his birth parents, grappling with the ambiguity of not knowing them. In college, he sought therapy for anxiety and panic attacks. He worked at the Minnesota Council of Nonprofits and went to Korea in 2019. Karl Johnson didn’t always feel a sense of ownership over his Korean heritage, which brought him back to Korea in adulthood. When he was in Korea, he found his foster mom but discovered his birth mother chose not to meet him. Despite the complexities of the adoptee experience, Karl respects individual stories, acknowledging that every adoptee's journey is uniquely personal. Karl shares his poem “Baa Baa Yellow Sheep,” which questions what you’re left with when you’re stripped of your original culture, family, and country as a transracial adoptee.

Ken Hong (Full)
Interviewee: Hong, Ken
Born in 1967, Ken Hong immigrated to the US at six and returned to Korea at 28. With his father's government connections, his family relocated to the US when Korea was under dictatorship in the 60s. Raised in North Philadelphia, Ken, the sole non-Caucasian, skipped kindergarten and faced no bullying. At Penn State, he assimilated to white culture, realizing his cultural identity in his late twenties. His father's Americanized lifestyle included minimal Korean food, aiming to assimilate. Ken noted how he didn’t have any Asian mentors growing up, which ultimately shaped Ken's upbringing as very American. An eye-opening visit from his aunt and meeting relatives ignited his curiosity about Korean culture. Moreover, after feeling self-conscious at a wedding for being the only Asian, Ken's desire to move to Korea began. After a friend's wedding, Ken, aged 26, sold his car for $2000 and moved to Jeju Island. The only Gyopo he translated despite limited Korean. A Seoul move marked a 180-degree shift, embracing an immersive cultural experience he wouldn't trade. Through the smell of beondegi and dalgona wafting through the air, Ken Hong felt instantly welcomed back to Korea despite spending many years away after his family immigrated in the 1970s. Ken, content with self-learning, rejects forcing culture on kids, emphasizing natural curiosity. In Korea, handling family funeral arrangements brought closure. Despite his parents' disinterest in Korea, Ken, now a father, cherishes his cultural journey. After many stints of living in Korea while traveling around Asia for work as a PR representative, Ken is now proud to call Korea home and provide a more rooted and immersive cultural experience for his teenage daughter, something he lacked in his childhood in America.
Keywords: immigration; North Philadelphia; American culture; assimilation; teaching English; family; identity; PR; living abroad

Mark Wilson (Full)
Interviewee: Wilson, Mark
Mark Wilson was born in Seoul, South Korea, and adopted to a small suburban town in Philadelphia at nine months old. He grew up in a two-parent household with a brother who is ten years older and was domestically adopted. As the only Asian kid growing up, Mark had a very American upbringing and noted that he lived in a bubble where he didn’t really face racism even as the only minority. Upon entering college, Mark was still trying to find where he belonged and started having more curiosity about Korea then. At times he would walk by the table of Korean students in the cafeteria but never felt connected with them.It wasn’t until he met other people in college where he realized others face racism and are treated differently. Having housemates involved in exchange programs, he ended up meeting the Korean students at a house party and became close friends with them. They invited him to their gatherings and even talked to him about going back to visit Korea. Through his adoption agency Holt International, Mark was able to take part in a homecoming program to have the chance to go back to Korea and experience work in different locations. After teaching English at academies and pursuing other side jobs, Mark switched over to fully being involved in the radio and broadcasting sector. Since arriving in Korea, Mark hopes to continue to explore his identity as a Korean American adoptee.

Nehemiah Park (Full)
Interviewee: Park, Nehemiah
Nehemiah Park's life story is a testament to the evolving identity of a Korean American navigating between two cultures. Born in Arizona in 1993 to Korean immigrant parents, Nehemiah's early life was steeped in the cultural and community support provided by the local Korean church, despite his parents not being particularly religious. This community became a cornerstone of his upbringing, shaping his aspirations and understanding of identity. At the age of four, Nehemiah and his family relocated to San Diego, California, drawn by the appealing weather and welcoming community. Growing up, Nehemiah played a critical role in his family, often helping his parents navigate language barriers in everyday situations like banking and ordering food. These experiences not only highlighted the challenges of a bicultural life but also spurred his desire to aid others facing similar identity struggles. Driven by a passion to support young people in their quest for identity, Nehemiah aspired to become a youth pastor. He envisioned attending Wheaton College in Illinois to pursue this dream. However, his path took an unexpected turn when his father, emphasizing the value of connecting with their roots, insisted that he study in Korea at Handong College. This decision, though initially met with resentment by Nehemiah, marked the beginning of a transformative decade in Korea. During his time in Korea, Nehemiah's perspective shifted significantly. He began to see his Korean American background as a source of strength, enabling him to bridge cultural gaps between Koreans and Americans, as well as between first and second-generation Korean Americans. This realization sparked a new dream: to establish a school in Korea focused on helping low-income students excel through learning English and exploring their identities. Nehemiah's story emphasizes the importance of heritage and self-discovery. He advocates for the recognition and embrace of one’s cultural roots, stressing that understanding one’s history and the people who shape it is crucial for personal development and community building. Now, as he plans to open his school, Nehemiah is poised to use his life's lessons to empower the next generation, helping them to navigate their identities with confidence and pride. Through his journey, Nehemiah embodies the potential for personal growth and societal contribution that lies in reconciling and celebrating one’s heritage, underscoring the powerful role of education and community support in shaping successful, self-aware individuals.
Keywords: church; Christianity; youth pastor; Korean American identity; Seoul, South Korea; San Diego, California; Arizona; loneliness; isolation; Handong College;

Interviewee: Joe, Robert
Robert Joe, originally from New York, moved to Korea at the age of two, and then to Texas at four, spending the majority of his formative years there. His father, a former Samsung employee, had moved the family to America in the 1970s. Growing up in a diverse then predominantly white neighborhood in Texas, Robert was active in orchestra, playing the violin from sixth grade through high school. Eunbi's attempts to seek justice involved her father contacting the tech company. Despite presenting evidence and an internal investigation, the executive denied everything, leading to the case being closed. This experience, spanning 3 to 4 months, highlighted the challenges faced by individuals, even with credible evidence and support, in confronting sexual harassment. Eunbi's story reflects the struggles of many, especially in minority communities, in speaking up against such injustices. Despite the lack of consequences for the executive, Eunbi's resilience and the support from her family stand as a testament to her strength.

Seo Young Chu
Interviewee: Chu, Seo Young
Seo Young, a 43-year-old college professor born in Virginia, now resides in Queens and teaches at Queens College. Her academic focus spans Asian American literature, science fiction, poetry, disability studies, and the Korean DMZ. She underscores the significance of Korean Americans being part of their community dialogue and having access to a shared historical archive. In 2000, shortly after turning 27, Seo Young faced a harrowing experience of sexual assault by a renowned tenured professor at Stanford University, who was also her advisor and for whom she worked as a teaching assistant. This professor, a prominent figure in the English department, also subjected her to prolonged harassment. Seo Young didn't consider pressing charges, feeling powerless and under his control, believing the professor held sway over her future. The abuse eventually came to light, prompting an investigation by Stanford, which resulted in the professor's two-year suspension without pay. In response to this traumatic experience, Seo Young changed her name from Jenny and transferred to Harvard. Only after securing tenure at Queen College CUNY in 2016 did she gather the courage to research her abuser, discovering that Stanford had concealed the extent of the abuse. She dedicated her sabbatical to writing about rape culture at Stanford and beyond, a process of coming to terms with her own experience, which had largely been met with silence. Seo Young's upbringing by immigrant parents instilled in her a sense of perpetual gratitude and the feeling of being a guest in the U.S., despite being a citizen. This background influenced her decision not to seek legal action against Stanford, heeding her father's advice to work hard and stay under the radar. However, this silence took a toll on her health, leading to significant expenses in therapy to reconcile with the assault. Struggling daily with self-forgiveness for an incident that wasn't her fault, Seo Young grapples with the conflict between the model minority stereotype and her need for honesty about her mental and physical trauma. Her family, while supportive in some ways, lacked the tools to adequately address the issue of sexual violence, especially given the language and cultural barriers. Seo Young's experience is juxtaposed with her parents' suffering during the Korean War, causing her to minimize her trauma initially. Her disclosure of the rape to her parents was met with a mix of traditional viewpoints and misconceptions about honor, forgiveness, and religious penance. Seo Young draws strength from the concept of Hwabyeong, a culturally specific syndrome, which she interprets as a form of empowering energy rather than an illness. This perspective has been instrumental in her journey to speak out and advocate for herself and others who have suffered similar violations.
Keywords: sexual harassment; sexual assualt; sexual violence; MeToo movement; Standford University; Queens College CUNY; Harvard University; professor; academic; english professor; trauma; mental health; depression; therapy; Hwabyeong; family; Korean American; Korean history;

Peter Kim was born into a large, joyful family in Seoul, South Korea. Peter's early years were filled with familial warmth, centered around his father’s thriving textile business. His family, inclusive of five older sisters, was tightly-knit, with deep roots extending back to relatives who had migrated from North Korea. At 10, Peter’s life took a transformative turn when his family immigrated to Canada, settling in London, Ontario. This transition was challenging; thrust into an unfamiliar school system, Peter struggled with integration and even faced physical confrontations on his first day. Despite these hurdles, he found solace and community within a close-knit Korean church group, where he spent much of his childhood playing with other Korean children. Education was a central theme in Peter’s life. He attended Western Ontario University, staying close to home to support his mother after the death of his father from lung to cancer. College was also a significant chapter as he met his future wife, a Korean American from Chicago, which eventually led him to relocate to the United States. Settling in Chicago, Peter initially worked as a financial consultant before venturing into manufacturing, dealing with major OEM companies like Caterpillar. Later, Peter founded an education consultancy to aid international students in their transition, drawing from his personal experiences of displacement and cultural adjustment. This role evolved over 20 years, where he learned the value of being more of a mentor than a parental figure, a lesson highlighted when a student named Nathan, whom Peter had to expel, later thanked him for setting him on a path to success. Reflecting on his personal life, Peter expresses regret over not immersing his children more in Korean culture, particularly in speaking the language. In a heartfelt discussion with his daughter, Cara, for the Legacy Project's Remote Edition, Peter explores his complex identity as a Korean, a Korean Canadian, and a Korean American. He emphasizes the importance of open communication and understanding, hoping that Cara embraces a fulfilling life while confidently shaping her own identity.

Ashley Baik, a 19-year-old native of Nashville, Tennessee, has navigated a complex journey of cultural identity and self-discovery. Born to first-generation Korean immigrants who moved to the United States in their late twenties without a college education, Ashley's upbringing in a predominantly white suburb initially led her to feel disconnected from her Korean heritage. She struggled with her dual identity, especially during her early school years when she faced bullying for bringing Korean food to lunch, prompting her to ask her parents for more typical American sandwiches instead. Despite these challenges, Ashley's perspective began to shift in high school. It was during this time that she started to truly appreciate her parents' sacrifices and the hardships they endured to provide for their family. This change was bolstered by her involvement in a Korean American church community, which played a pivotal role in helping her rediscover and embrace her Korean roots. Her brother, who never shied away from his identity and consistently supported their parents, was a significant influence and a role model for Ashley. He guided her through many challenges, including navigating the American educational system—a task they undertook together since their parents were unfamiliar with the process. The profound impact of her family's values, particularly the importance of generosity and open-mindedness instilled by her parents, deeply influenced Ashley. However, a poignant moment in her journey was learning of her grandmother's passing in Korea via a phone call, a situation that highlighted the painful distance from her extended family and the inability of her parents to say their final goodbyes in person. Despite these challenges, Ashley has grown to cherish her summers in Korea, which have become a yearly tradition since high school. These trips have not only strengthened her bonds with her cousins and other family members but have also transformed her initial reluctance—stemming from missing out on time with friends—into an eagerness to explore her heritage and connect with her roots. In reflecting on her journey for the Legacy Project, Ashley acknowledges the integral role her faith and community have played in her life. She expresses gratitude for her parents' incredible sacrifices and discusses the dual importance of her Korean and American identities, ultimately finding strength and pride in both. Through this dialogue, Ashley hopes to inspire others navigating similar cross-cultural challenges and to honor the legacy of resilience and hope her parents have bestowed upon her.

Najung Hiatt's journey from Seoul, Korea, to the United States is a narrative of passion, perseverance, and the pursuit of personal and professional fulfillment. Born and raised in Seoul, Najung grew up with an older brother and sister, absorbing the vibrant culture of her homeland. Her academic path led her to study Ceramic Art and Fine Arts at a university in Korea, where she discovered not only her love for design—ranging from interior design to painting and advertising—but also her eventual vocation in education. Najung’s life took a romantic turn when she fell in love with a transfer student from the United States. This relationship was the catalyst for her move to the U.S., where she aimed to continue both her education and her newfound love. Initially settling in Colorado Springs, Najung later moved to California and finally Texas, seeking proximity to her husband Scott’s family and greater opportunities. Transitioning to life in the U.S. was challenging; Najung experienced feelings of loneliness and displacement until she found solace and community within a Korean church. This community played a critical role in her adaptation to a new country, providing emotional and social support as she navigated her new environment. Her career as an educator, spanning 30 years, began with her role as an Art Teacher. Najung’s deep-rooted passion for the arts, particularly in early childhood education, has been a guiding force throughout her career. Despite cultural and language barriers, her dedication to education never wavered, and she has remained committed to fostering creativity and learning among young minds. The acceptance of her marriage to Scott, a white American, by her family took nearly a decade, reflecting the complex interplay of cultural expectations and personal relationships. However, her family's eventual embrace of Scott underscores a profound journey towards acceptance and love that crosses cultural boundaries. Najung and Scott have two children, a son and a daughter, whom Najung has raised to be proud of their Korean heritage. Notably, her daughter has learned to read and write in Korean, symbolizing a connection to their cultural roots. Scott's dedication to attending a Korean-speaking church every Sunday for ten years, despite the language barrier, highlights his commitment to his family's heritage. However, their recent switch to an English-speaking church was a mutual decision that catered to Scott's desire to engage more fully with his own faith, a change that Najung welcomed enthusiastically. In her reflection for the Legacy Project, Najung emphasizes the importance of cultural heritage, expressing hope that the Korean American community will continue to embrace and pass down their traditions and values. Her story is a testament to the resilience required to bridge cultures, foster inclusive family dynamics, and nurture an enduring sense of identity among immigrants and their descendants.

Carol Park (Full)
Interviewee: Park, Carol
Carol Park's interview is a personal narrative intertwined with the broader tapestry of Korean-American history, particularly against the backdrop of the 1992 Los Angeles Civil Unrest, commonly referred to as the Rodney King Riots. Born in La Palma, California, to South Korean immigrant parents who owned five gas stations, Carol faced a life-altering moment at the tender age of ten when her father passed away, leaving her family to navigate their new reality. Carol's early years were marked by significant responsibilities as she helped manage the family's gas station in Compton, a task that exposed her to the harsh realities of racism and violence. The 1992 civil unrest, a pivotal moment in Carol's life, brought these issues into sharp focus. As she watched the escalating violence on television on April 29, 1992, the fear for her family's safety and livelihood became all too real. Despite the chaos, Carol's mothers attempt to secure the safety of their gas station—a symbol of her family's hard work and dreams—highlighted the deep-seated fears and tensions within the Korean American community during this period. The media's portrayal of the events, which Carol criticizes for exacerbating racial tensions and oversimplifying the complex socio-economic dynamics at play, further influenced her perspective and experiences. Carol's reflections on these events are poignantly captured in her book, "Memoir of a Cashier: Korean Americans, Racism, and Riots," where she narrates her experiences of working in the gas station amidst the backdrop of racial tensions and her personal encounters with racism and violence. These experiences were not only formative in her understanding of her identity and community but also propelled her towards academic and professional pursuits that aimed to explore and address these issues. Her engagement with Korean American history through oral history projects and her studies in ethnic studies at the University of California, Riverside, demonstrate her commitment to understanding and documenting the nuanced narratives of Korean Americans. Carol's journey is also a testament to resilience and healing. Confronting the trauma and violence she experienced, Carol sought therapy to process these events, illustrating the importance of mental health in overcoming the scars of past traumas. Her transition from a young girl working long shifts at her family's gas station to a full-time journalist and a doctoral candidate in ethnic studies reflects her growth and determination to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complexities of race, identity, and community in America. As Carol commemorates the 30th anniversary of the 1992 LA Civil Unrest, her story serves as a reminder of the ongoing need to critically examine media representations, engage with the past honestly, and strive towards a more inclusive and understanding future.

Jung Koo Kang (Full)

Jung Koo Kang's journey from South Korea to Los Angeles spans over four decades, marked by resilience, hard work, and a commitment to community service. Arriving in LA in 1975, he embarked on a challenging path, initially working in a sewing factory and eventually establishing his own. His dedication caught the attention of his landlord, who entrusted him with managing three wholesale clothing stores, propelling him further as a young entrepreneur. He became actively involved in the LA Senior Citizens Society, contributing his time and resources to support the elderly and even serving as president for a period. Inspired by his time as president, he founded the Hanmi Silver Club, fostering a supportive network for retired Korean seniors. He was even tasked with managing the March 1st movements anniversary organising amongst other community projects. The upheaval of the 1992 LA riots profoundly impacted Mr. Kang and his community. As the unrest unfolded, he witnessed the devastation firsthand, yet he was inspired by his pastor's call for unity and outreach. Reflecting on his journey, Mr. Kang recalls the challenges of immigrating with his wife and three young children, driven by a desire for their education. Despite facing hardships and the heartbreaking distance from his family in Korea, he persevered, pouring his energy into his work and community involvement. Mr. Kang's experiences during the LA riots underscored the importance of Korean Americans' engagement in politics and social cohesion. He advocates for compassion and love as antidotes to future unrest, emphasizing the need for unity and understanding among diverse communities. In his twilight years, Mr. Kang sees a hopeful future guided by the kindness and affection of Korean Americans, urging the younger generation to continue spreading love and creating a better world for generations to come. Through his remarkable journey, he exemplifies the transformative power of resilience, service, and unwavering dedication to building a stronger, more compassionate society.

Soonja Rhee's life is a testament to resilience, community, and the enduring spirit of hard work. Born in 1949 as the seventh of eight siblings, Soonja's journey led her to immigrate to the United States in 1981 with her husband and two daughters. Settling in Koreatown, Los Angeles, she found solace in the close-knit community and solidarity among its residents. When the LA riots erupted, Soonja's instinct to help others kicked in immediately, despite her husband's initial hesitation. Despite facing eviction and financial struggles, Soonja never wavered in her determination to overcome adversity. Throughout her trials, Soonja's commitment to hard work remained unwavering. She fondly reminisces about simpler times sharing food with loved ones and laments the changes brought about by modern life and the COVID-19 pandemic. Yet, she finds strength in her enduring friendships and the values instilled in her from childhood. For Soonja, the key to survival lies in community, hard work, and the unwavering belief that helping others is the greatest purpose one can have in life.

Benjamin Kim Oser (Full)
Interviewee: Kim Oser, Benjamin
Benjamin Kim Oser’s life story is a poignant narrative of identity, cultural reconnection, and leadership within the Korean American adoptee community. Born in Mapogu, Seoul, South Korea, in 1984, Benjamin was adopted and brought to Central New Jersey at just three months old. His early life in the United States was shaped by his adoptive family's love and support, yet his heritage remained an integral part of his identity. At 25, Benjamin traveled to South Korea not with the intention of finding his birth family but to immerse himself culturally and socially. However, a serendipitous connection with the adoption agency led to an unexpected reunion with his birth father, who had been looking for him. This reunion was swiftly arranged; Benjamin wrote a letter to his father, and within two weeks, they met for the first time. The encounter, filled with deep emotional undercurrents, involved a lunch with his aunt and birth father, facilitated by a translator. During this poignant meeting, Benjamin confronted complex emotions and had the opportunity to ask his father the painful question of why he was given up for adoption. The day ended in tears, marking a profound moment of connection and closure. The narrative became even more complex when Benjamin reached out to his birth mother. Her initial reluctance was rooted in a secret kept from her current husband about Benjamin's existence. When they finally met, she revealed her side of the story, which contrasted sharply with his father’s account, adding layers of complexity to Benjamin’s understanding of his origins. His birth parents had never married and had separated after his adoption, a revelation that was challenging for Benjamin to process. Back in the U.S., Benjamin's adoptive parents initially harbored fears about his search for his birth parents, concerned it might lead him to drift away from them. Over time, however, they grew more comfortable with his journey. His adoptive family also includes a younger sister, also adopted, though not biologically related to him. Benjamin's experiences have deeply influenced his career path. Encouraged by his parents to connect with his roots, he attended the Holt adoptee camp in the '90s, a decision that sparked his long-term commitment to the adoptee community. Starting as a camp counselor, he pursued this passion through graduate school and eventually assumed leadership roles, culminating in his current position as the director of Sejong Camp. Through his work, Benjamin seeks to empower other Korean American adoptees, helping them navigate their own complex identities and cultural heritage. Reflecting on his life, Benjamin acknowledges the profound impact of both his adoptive and birth families on his identity. His journey underscores the intricate tapestry of relationships and the enduring quest for self-discovery among adoptees. As director of Sejong Camp, he channels his experiences into nurturing and leading the next generation of Korean Americans, emphasizing the importance of understanding and embracing one’s roots.

Hope Sacco (Full)
Interviewee: Sacco, Hope
Hope Sacco was born in Hartford, Connecticut, and raised primarily in Baltimore, Maryland, Hope navigated the complexities of a biracial identity with an Italian-Irish father and a Korean mother who was adopted at the age of five. Lacking a direct cultural lineage due to her mother's adoption, Hope often felt disconnected from both her Korean and white heritage, a feeling that profoundly shaped her personal and educational pursuits. During her high school years, Hope took a proactive role as the lead editor of her school's newspaper, using the platform to reach out to and represent underserved communities, particularly the Asian community. This role was not just about leadership but was also a response to her ongoing quest for cultural connection and understanding. Her engagement deepened during a Civil War field trip, which starkly highlighted the racial dynamics and history in the U.S., spurring her to want to contribute more meaningfully to community dialogues. Hope's journey toward embracing her Korean roots led her to Sejong Camp, an experience she has repeated for the past four years. Although the camp has been a sanctuary for exploring her Korean identity, it has also been a place of cultural tension, where she sometimes feels that her biracial identity is not fully relatable. Despite these challenges, Hope has found solace in mentoring younger biracial campers, fostering a supportive network and enriching her connection to her Korean heritage. Her familial relationships reflect a blend of cultures as well. While she finds comfort and familiarity on her father's side, thanks to their shared American cultural background, this also extends to her mother's side, given her mother's upbringing by white parents. These dynamics have made her familial connections on both sides feel natural and integral to her identity. In 8th grade, Hope demonstrated her creativity and entrepreneurial spirit by winning a national business competition with a coloring book featuring women superheroes, earning her a scholarship. This achievement not only highlights her creative talents but also her drive to empower and inspire, qualities that have been nurtured by her diverse family background and her own introspective journey. Through her academic and extracurricular endeavors, Hope Sacco continues to navigate her complex identity, drawing strength from both her Korean and European heritage while contributing to a broader understanding of what it means to be biracial in America today. Her story is one of resilience, identity exploration, and the ongoing quest to find balance and community in a diverse world.
Keywords: Camp Sejong; biracial; multicultural; Italian; Irish; Korean; Baltimore, Maryland; Korean heritage; adoptee; family; campers; newspaper editor; identity; racial dynamics;

Julia Park (Full)
Interviewee: Park, Julia
Julia Park, born in Daegu and raised in Seoul, South Korea, immigrated to the U.S. at the age of 13, joining her father who had been running a grocery store in Flatbush, Brooklyn for seven years. The move was a culture shock for Julia, who had never before experienced a predominantly Black community. Her early life in America was marked by challenges, including a significant language barrier and missing out on typical teenage experiences due to work obligations at her father's store. Despite her father's initial belief that formal education was unnecessary, Julia's mother advocated for her schooling, leading Julia to complete 8th grade after skipping 7th. High school presented further difficulties, but she persevered and later graduated from college in 3.5 years, eager to achieve financial independence. Her early career saw her working as a bank teller and then an accountant at a textile company. Julia found a sense of community and social life through her church, where she also met her husband, an immigration lawyer involved in nonprofit work. The challenges of parenting led her to take a parenting class, which profoundly influenced her understanding of communication and emotional expression. Later in life, Julia became deeply involved in social services and cultural education, founding Sejong Camp, a cultural camp for Korean American youth. This role allowed her to help children realize their potential and connect with their heritage. At 56, Julia returned to school for a degree in Social Work, graduating top of her class with a 4.0 GPA. Today, Julia works in social service and serves as the executive director and trip director of Sejong Camp. Right at age 57, Julia reflects on her life's journey from a struggling immigrant to a community leader, underscoring her commitment to giving back and supporting future generations.

Laura-Ann Jacobs was born in Incheon, South Korea, in 1987 and adopted the day she was born. She arrived in Atlanta, Georgia, at four months old and enjoyed a positive upbringing. Seo Hee Kelleher (Full)
Interviewee: Kelleher, Seo Hee
Seo Hee Kelleher, originally from Seoul, South Korea, moved to Washington, D.C. in 1991 as a 15-year-old. Her initial experiences in the U.S. included adapting her name from “Sea-oh” to “Suh” to accommodate her peers, an early lesson in modifying her identity to fit into American society. Seo's journey in the States began with her and her sister arriving as international students with a plan to return to Korea, which changed when their parents later moved to the U.S. This transition led to 30 years of life in America, where she managed independence and challenges like paying bills and finding a sense of community, a stark contrast to her financially comfortable and community-rich life in Korea. Seo's professional life has been a journey of significant transformation. Initially embracing a corporate career in marketing, she realized in her 30s that despite following a traditional path, she was not fulfilled. This realization prompted her to leave her corporate job and start a fitness business focused on helping women transition through major life changes. Her work evolved from fitness coaching to life coaching, focusing on mindset shifts and personal growth. Her spiritual awakening began with an exploration into meditation, energy work, and intuition, which led her to shamanic healing. Inspired by the indigenous practices of a tribe in Peru, she completed a year-long program in shamanic healing. A subsequent vision prompted her to travel to Seoul and Jeju Island in Korea, where she connected deeply with the land and unexpectedly found two shaman teachers. This experience solidified her path as a shaman, embracing her indigenous spirituality to help others heal. Seo’s spiritual journey is deeply tied to her cultural roots, a connection reinforced when she discovered her shamanic gift was inherited from her maternal line, tracing back to her mother's birth in North Korea. This discovery was supported by her mother, adding a profound familial dimension to her practice. Now a Korean American shaman and a publisher, Seo is committed to sharing the wisdom of her ancestors. She seeks to make traditional Korean spiritual knowledge accessible to non-Korean speakers through her writing and publishing, addressing the gap she once faced. Seo’s life and work reflect a powerful narrative of embracing cultural identity, overcoming personal and professional challenges, and helping others through spiritual healing.

Tommy Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, Tommy
Tommy Lee, now 22, was born in Ann Arbor, Michigan but spent much of his childhood in Virginia, living in a bustling household with nine family members including his grandparents, parents, aunt, uncle, cousin, and younger sister. This close-knit family environment provided a comforting constant in his early life, especially since his grandparents took care of him while his parents worked, often cooking traditional Korean meals. This dynamic changed dramatically when Tommy's parents divorced when he was still young, leading to a move with his mother and sister to Maryland. This period was initially marked by personal unprocessed changes which later surfaced during his college years at the University of Michigan. It was in college where Tommy began to reflect deeply on his parents' separation and its profound effects on his views towards both his mother and father. In Maryland, Tommy and his family lived for about four to five years before moving back to Virginia during his high school years. College at the University of Michigan was a transformative time for Tommy; he majored in Philosophy, discovered his interests in graphic design and animation, and underwent significant personal growth. Tommy's engagement with his Korean heritage deepened through his involvement with Camp Sejong, a community that played a pivotal role in his cultural identity development. Initially joining as a camper and later serving as a counselor for five years, Camp Sejong helped Tommy realize the flexibility in defining one's Korean identity, which he describes as a personal journey without a fixed endpoint.Tommy has faced challenges related to identity and expression, particularly highlighted by his experiences as an Asian actor where he initially felt unable to fully be himself. Over time, however, he has grown more comfortable in expressing his true self. The aftermath of his parents' divorce initially seeded resentment towards his father, but with time, Tommy has worked towards understanding and improving their relationship. His mother now works at the FDA while his dad is a lawyer at Marriott Hotels. In this special Legacy Project series, Tommy reflects on his evolving relationship with his parents post-divorce, his evolving passions, and his deep connection to Camp Sejong. This camp not only grounded him in his cultural identity but also taught him the importance of community and personal definitions of heritage. As he moves forward, Tommy is committed to practicing radical empathy and contributing positively to his community, continuing to explore his identity and personal definitions of being Korean.

During her third year of college, she taught nutrition at nursing schools in Korea, caused by a boom in nurses needed in Germany at the time. After graduating, she worked as a nutritionist at a hospital, and dreamt of studying more about nutrition in the United States, Canada, or Sweden, then coming back to share what she learned to more students in Korea. She met her now husband in 1974, coming to the United States through San Francisco in Spring of 1975, and finally settling in Columbia, South Carolina. Mrs. Park describes her experience applying to an American school to continue her education, to which she found incredibly difficult. She became employed at a hospital in the same year, her husband at IBM as an engineer. After 2 years, her husband was able to start a business with the help of his peers in Broadway, New York. It was then when she became pregnant with her first son, and came to realize that New York was not her place to be. As she had two more children of her own, she became a South Carolinian. South Carolina being a Deep South state, she describes the prejudice she experienced being a Korean. She explains her experiences as a result of ignorance rather than racism, and how she wanted to educate them instead of actively combating them.

Peter Han, born in 1968 in Gimpo, South Korea, navigated a life marked by significant transitions and cultural shifts. Growing up in near-poverty conditions, Peter's early life was challenging. His father secured a financially stabilizing job at Northwest when Peter was around 7 or 8, but tragically passed away from leukemia two years later. Following his father's death, Peter's mother remarried an American military man, prompting a move to the U.S. when Peter was 12. In the U;S, Peter was struck by the new comforts he encountered—air conditioning, lush greenery, readily available hot water, and soft toilet paper—all novelties that marked his new life in Florida. However, adapting to American life took time; it took Peter six months to begin effectively communicating with others. Peter's transition to American life was filled with creative and spiritual exploration. He took up breakdancing, excelling in the art and winning several competitions. His journey later took a spiritual turn when he converted to Christianity, attended Hartland College, and majored in Pastoral Evangelism, eventually becoming a Bible teacher and lecturer. Despite his successes, Peter's dual heritage often left him feeling caught between two worlds, a sentiment common among 1.5 generation immigrants who feel not fully accepted by either culture. Nevertheless, Peter views his bilingual and bicultural abilities as assets, especially now that he has returned to live in Korea. Embracing his unique identity, Peter enjoys the safety, food, and language of Korea and advocates for living life on one's own terms, beyond the confines of cultural labels. His life story underscores a universal truth: at the end of the day, we are all human beings, navigating our paths and seeking connection.

Janet Russell (Full)
Interviewee: Russell, Janet
Janet Russell's life story is a tapestry of multicultural identities and experiences. Born in Germany as a military child to a Korean mother and a Belizean father, Janet initially grew up without a deep connection to her Korean heritage. Her early years were marked by frequent moves, including a significant portion of her childhood in Fayetteville, North Carolina. While Janet's father was often away on active duty, her mother was a constant presence, heavily involved in her upbringing. However, growing up, Janet and her family predominantly identified with their Black heritage, influenced by her father's roots and the community around them. Despite the strong presence of her mother, societal perceptions often challenged Janet's sense of identity. During her time in Germany, for instance, her mother's involvement in school activities led others to mistake her for a hired nanny due to their differing appearances. These experiences fueled Janet's early struggles with her identity, as she did not see herself as Korean, nor did she have many Korean friends. Janet's academic path led her to Fayetteville State University, a setting that mirrored her earlier environments with a predominately Black student body and few Korean peers. She pursued a degree in business, which steered her into roles in banking, finance, and accounting. However, the routine nature of her career left her seeking more fulfilling experiences. This search for meaning eventually drew Janet to South Korea in May 2010, a move prompted by a friend's suggestion to teach English abroad. Despite her initial reservations and her father's objections—stemming from his desire to keep her close—Janet embarked on this journey alone, settling in the city of Guanjo, Wonju. Her transition to life in Korea was not without challenges, particularly in social interactions, where she noticed differences in treatment from locals based on her mixed-race appearance. Over time, Janet encouraged her mother to visit Korea, which led to a heartfelt reunion with her Korean relatives in 2012. This trip was pivotal, helping Janet reconnect with her mother's heritage and allowing her to embrace a fuller understanding of her identity. One of Janet's most significant accomplishments is being the first in her family to graduate from college, a milestone that holds great pride for her. Janet's experiences in Korea have profoundly impacted her, fostering a connection with a part of her heritage that had once felt distant. Her story is a compelling reminder of the importance of embracing one's entire self and the complex interplay of race, identity, and family in shaping our lives.

Tony Chung's journey from Kentucky to Korea is a profound testament to his deep-rooted faith and commitment to community. Born in Kentucky and raised predominantly in Maryland, Tony experienced a childhood shaped by the influence of his immigrant parents who arrived in the U.S. in 1972. His father, a doctor, established a medical practice in Maryland, providing Tony with a stable, albeit sheltered, upbringing. Educated in a Christian elementary school, Tony faced challenges, including experiencing racism, but found solace and community within his local Korean church. Tony’s collegiate path took him to Wheaton College, where he majored in Bible Theology, deeply influencing his life's trajectory. His summers at Yonsei University’s Korean language program not only deepened his linguistic skills but also his affection for Korea. It was during college that Tony felt a calling to ministry, a decision that would shape his future in profound ways. After college, he furthered his education at a seminary in Vancouver, which solidified his pastoral ambitions. For 13 years, Tony served as a pastor in Maryland, where he also started his own family, marrying and having two children. However, the pull towards Korea remained strong. Motivated by Korea’s dynamic church scene and moved by the country’s high rates of suicide and depression, Tony felt called to serve there. In 2014, he and his family relocated to Korea, where he initially struggled to find his place, applying unsuccessfully to English teaching positions. However, destiny had a different plan for Tony. After attending a pastoral meeting, he learned of an opening at Jubilee Church. He joined the church in August 2014, a role he has since embraced, serving a congregation largely comprised of expatriates and internationals. This role, initially unintended, has allowed Tony to provide a much-needed pastoral presence for a diverse community. In Korea, Tony has connected deeply with the concept of "Yeoyu," reflecting on the pressures Korean people face from societal and familial expectations. This understanding has fostered a greater compassion within him, particularly towards immigrants and those struggling within rigid social structures. Living in Korea has not only allowed Tony to minister to others but also to grow in his empathy and understanding. Through his ministry, Tony aims to create inclusive spaces for Korean Americans and others to explore their faith, addressing the hurts often associated with religious communities. His story is one of adaptation, faith, and the continuous pursuit of creating a welcoming community for all.

Matthew Pellegrino's life story is a profound exploration of identity, culture, and belonging. Born in Chungcheongnam-do Province, South Korea, in 1984, Matthew was adopted by a white American family and moved to Long Island, New York, when he was just six months old. Growing up in a predominantly white area, he had a comfortable childhood with his parents, an adopted older sister, and a family dog. Despite these comforts, he faced significant challenges, including bullying and discrimination, which impacted his sense of self and identity. In high school, Matthew discovered a passion for music that would shape his future. Inspired by the soundtracks of movies and TV shows, he decided to pursue a career in music. He attended a music school for his undergraduate studies, majoring in music composition with a focus on oboe performance. His academic journey continued at Johns Hopkins University, where he completed both his master’s and doctorate in music composition. It was during his time at Johns Hopkins that Matthew experienced a significant culture shock. Surrounded by a diverse student body, including other Korean students, he began to confront his Koreanness for the first time. This period marked a turning point; he delved into Korean culture, exploring K-pop and Korean cuisine, and even started dating a Korean girl. His interest in his heritage deepened, and he began learning the Korean language. Driven by stories of other adoptees reconnecting with their birth families, Matthew initiated a search for his birth mother. The process was swift, and within a month, he was able to establish contact. In 2018, he traveled to Korea to meet her—a poignant reunion that was both emotional and transformative. His birth mother, a cellist, welcomed him with a performance, and their first exchange was filled with apologies and declarations of love. This encounter led to Matthew meeting his extended family, though only some relatives were aware of his existence. Currently residing in Korea on a Fulbright Scholarship, Matthew is exploring traditional Korean music and the narratives of Korean adoptees through his dissertation. His academic and personal journey is intertwined, as he continues to navigate his relationships with his newfound family and reconcile his dual identities. His time in Korea has been a complex blend of joy, sorrow, and therapeutic healing, as he and his family contemplate revealing his existence to the younger cousins. Matthew’s life narrative underscores the intricate dynamics of adoption, the search for identity, and the deep connections that can emerge unexpectedly. His experiences highlight the challenges and rewards of living between two cultures, fostering a unique appreciation for his roots and the family that raised him.

Corey (Full)
Interviewee: Corey
Corey's journey from a troubled youth in Iowa to embracing his Korean American identity in South Korea is a story of resilience, discovery, and transformation. Born in Seoul in 1982 and adopted at 1.5 years old with his twin brother, Corey faced significant challenges growing up in an environment where they were the only Asians in their community. His adoptive parents struggled to manage his behavioral issues, which were compounded by his unresolved trauma and identity confusion, leading to periods in foster care. His teenage years were marked by a distant relationship with his twin brother, although they later reconciled as adults. Feeling isolated and without a future in Iowa, Corey enlisted in the Marines after high school. The discipline and structure of military life provided him with a sense of purpose and belonging that he had longed for. After his service, Corey moved to California, where he found himself closer to a vibrant Korean American community. This exposure reignited his interest in his roots and at the age of 32, spurred by a calling, he traveled to Korea with an adoptee group. This initial trip was transformative, leading him to sell his belongings and move to Korea permanently. In Korea, Corey's journey into his heritage deepened. He enrolled in a Korean language program at Yonsei University, though he found the pressure overwhelming and eventually dropped out. However, his involvement in a local church led to an opportunity to exchange gym training for Korean lessons, which evolved into Corey establishing his own gym. This venture not only fulfilled him professionally but also embedded him within the community. Corey's work extends beyond the gym; he is also involved with a nonprofit organization focused on mentoring students, helping relieve the pressures they face—reflecting his own experiences of needing guidance and support. His relationship with his adoptive parents, strained by his decision to move to Korea and their lack of support, is something he continues to work on. Despite initial setbacks in connecting with his biological family—his attempted reunion with his birth mother was fraught, and a DNA test with his supposed birth father was negative—Corey has found a sense of family and belonging through his Korean American friends in Korea. Today, Corey confidently identifies as a Korean American, finding solace and strength in the community and the shared experiences of those around him. His life's journey underscores the importance of support systems for adoptees and the profound impact of connecting with one's heritage.
