Edwin Kim's journey is both a story of resilience and a quest for belonging. Born in Seoul, Korea, Edwin spent his childhood immersed in books and piano practice. His parents, recognizing a need for a change of environment, moved him to the U.S. when he was 14, despite the language barriers. Initially settling in Palisades Park, New Jersey, Edwin went to Juilliard's pre-college program and later went to a different high school, which led him to switch homes and schools. Despite these challenges, Edwin found his way to the Peabody Institute at Johns Hopkins University, where he pursued his bachelor's, master's, and Ph.D. He lived in Baltimore for 15 years, distancing himself from a toxic social circle of fellow Koreans, focusing on his studies and personal growth. During his time at Peabody, Edwin felt an acute sense of alienation, never quite feeling at home in either Korea or the U.S., a sentiment that persisted even as he achieved professional milestones. Edwin's musical career, defined by his identity as a pianist, took a significant turn in 2017 when he won a pivotal competition in Australia. This victory marked the end of his competitive career and opened numerous doors, culminating in the completion of his doctorate in early 2020. However, the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic thwarted his concert plans, prompting a return to Korea where he reconnected with his first piano teacher and produced his first solo album. Edwin's life reflects a deep commitment to his craft, evident since his youth when he displayed a natural talent for perfect pitch, which was initially met with skepticism and accusations of plagiarism in the U.S. Overcoming immense personal and cultural hurdles, Edwin has become known as a "jack of all trades" in the music industry—concert pianist, singer, composer, arranger, and writer—always pursuing his passions and defining his path despite feeling perennially between worlds. His story is one of enduring the challenges of displacement and the relentless pursuit of artistic fulfillment.

Interviewee: Votapek, Kayla Kim
Kayla Kim Votapek, originally from New Jersey, is an anti-racist facilitator and theatre producer. Born in Taechon, South Korea, she is a Korean American adoptee whose birth mother worked in a textile factory and had an affair with her boss, resulting in Kayla's birth. Adopted at four months old, she was raised in an Italian family, where her neighbors were considered family, and she was closest to her dad. Her sister is also a Korean adoptee. Growing up, her parents would visit her school to educate students about adoption, explaining "airplane day" and what a non-normative family looked like. Although she initially felt most included in the arts community, this changed in high school when her involvement in theatre highlighted her differences. She often felt conflicted about connecting with her Korean heritage, fearing it would be seen as a betrayal to her adoptive family, a sentiment her mother also shared, fearing Kayla might choose her birth mother. Kayla's involvement in anti-racist healing work allowed her to meet other adoptees for the first time, where she felt truly understood. Within six months, she traveled to Korea to explore her heritage further. Her interest in learning about her lineage was influenced by her father, who was passionate about family histories. Her artistic inclinations were nurtured by her aunt, and she was encouraged by her drama teacher to pursue theatre. She triple-majored in theatre, psychology, and education at Rutgers University, aiming to become a theatre teacher. Her work as an anti-racist facilitator focuses on taking action rather than just education and approaching conflict with humility. Kayla pursued a master’s degree in London to enhance her facilitation skills, and during this time, she organized a walkout in response to racist remarks by the head of the school. This activism enabled her to engage more deeply in anti-racist work and explore her AAPI identity. Kayla believes that anti-racism work is a path to self-actualization. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she moved to Korea to learn more about her heritage. Holt, the adoption agency, found her birth mother but reported that pursuing contact was detrimental to her birth mother's health. Although she intended to continue her search, the death of her adoptive mother led her to put it on hold. She remains determined to find more about her origins while ensuring her birth mother's well-being. Ultimately, Kayla strives to be seen as a complete human being beyond just her identity.

Kyu Lee's story is a compelling journey of cultural rediscovery and professional success, straddling the worlds of Seattle and Seoul. Born on a U.S. military base in Yongsan, Korea, Kyu was a U.S. citizen from birth due to his father's position in the U.S. Army. His family relocated to Mercer Island, Washington, drawn by the promise of good education and a nurturing environment for raising a family. Growing up in a predominantly Jewish neighborhood with few Asian Americans, Kyu’s early exposure to his Korean heritage was limited. Kyu's love for sports led him to the University of Washington, where he played football—a testament to his integration into American culture. His career began at Sony in 2001, but it wasn't until 2004-2005, during his encounter with the Korean film "The Brotherhood of War," that Kyu truly connected with Korean cinema. This film not only introduced him to the depth of Korean content but also sparked his mission to bring Korean films to a global audience. His enthusiasm for the film led to its distribution by Sony, marking a significant step in promoting Korean cinema in the U.S. In 2009, Sony recognized Kyu's passion and expertise by transferring him to Korea to handle local language production. However, his return was met with cultural shocks and the realization that his acceptance was more due to his professional position than his personal identity. Despite these challenges, Kyu continued to forge ahead in the industry. His career took a dramatic turn in 2012 with the global phenomenon "Gangnam Style." Kyu played a pivotal role in introducing Psy to Scooter Braun, leading to a series of opportunities that propelled his career in the media industry. This experience not only heightened his profile but also solidified his role as a cultural bridge between Korea and the U.S. By 2013, Kyu's influence and experiences culminated in the publication of a motivational book in Korean, aimed at inspiring youth. Today, Kyu continues to work in film and distribution, navigating the highs and lows of the industry with a commitment to uplift and create opportunities for others. His journey from a young boy in Mercer Island to a key player in international media is a testament to the power of embracing one's roots and the impact of cultural exchange.

Michael Hurt's story is a rich narrative that spans continents, cultures, and academic disciplines. Born in Germany and raised in Ohio, Michael, of Korean and African American descent, grew up in a diverse community which shaped his early interest in mixed-race identities. His academic journey led him to Korea on a Fulbright scholarship after college, sparking a long-term commitment to the country that began in 1994. During his stay with a host family and later academic pursuits at Berkeley, Michael delved deeply into Korean national identity, which culminated in his dissertation on the portrayal of national identity in Korean textbooks—a project completed in 2014. Michael's academic interests are intertwined with his passion for photography, particularly street and fashion photography, which he pursued actively from 2002 to 2007. Michael's work extends beyond the visual, as he critically engages with social issues in Korea. His research on the significant yet controversial topic of prostitution and sex work in Korea, which once constituted a notable part of the country's GDP, led to public exhibitions and scholarly articles. These efforts, however, were met with resistance from locals who felt his work cast a negative light on their society. Identifying as a visual sociologist, Michael combines his talents in photography with his academic interest in race, gender, and societal observation. His unique position as both an insider and outsider in Korea provides him with a distinctive perspective that enriches his work, allowing him to navigate and document the complex interplay of cultural identity in a modern and rapidly changing society. His story underscores the challenges and enrichments of living between cultures, exploring how personal identity and societal roles converge in the globalized world.

Christine Pennell (Full)
Interviewee: Pennell, Christine
Christine Pennell, born in 1969, was discovered at a railroad station in East Daegu, South Korea, around the age of 2 and was adopted to the United States at 3.5 years old. Raised in a white family, Christine felt a strong sense of belonging, never treated differently despite her awareness of her Korean roots. Her first significant interaction with another Korean occurred in Montreal in 1976, which marked the beginning of her journey to embrace her ethnic identity, even as she grappled with being fetishized by white men. Christine married at 21 to a man whose sister was her friend and whose family was well-known to her father, a local teacher. The relationship blossomed from these close family ties. However, inspired by the documentary "Lion," Christine joined a Korean American Adoptee Facebook group in 2018, which led her to a DNA test and the subsequent discovery of her sister living in Belgium. The sisters, who coincidentally both had children the same years, forged a deep connection, sharing photos, engaging in video chats, and eventually meeting in person. Christine's visits to Belgium became monthly occurrences, and she grew increasingly attached to her Korean heritage, leading her to spend more time in Korea. After 50 years in the United States, she decided to relocate permanently to Korea, supported by her family back in the States with whom she keeps in touch via frequent video calls. Now a dual citizen, Christine enjoys her life in Korea with her four children and a granddaughter, though she admits the transition from an American mindset presents ongoing challenges. Christine's story is one of rediscovery and connection, bridging continents and cultures as she finds peace in her Korean American identity. After her divorce in 2013 and her experiences of reconnecting with her biological roots, Christine has embraced her full identity, finding satisfaction and peace in her dual heritage and the new chapters of her life in Korea.

Denny Hong, born in Korea on a U.S. army base, spent his childhood oscillating between the United States and Korea due to his father's military assignments. This nomadic lifestyle took him to various cities like Memphis, North Carolina, and Atlanta, alongside stints in Seoul. Denny finally settled in Memphis during his high school years, where he faced racial slurs that were initially unfamiliar to him. However, after physically confronting some of his bullies, these incidents subsided. Denny attended Valparaiso University, and post-graduation, at 21, he moved back to Korea, planning only a year-long stay to work for his uncle before pursuing seminary school. Yet, living in Korea sparked a change in Denny's path. Realizing he did not want to become a pastor, he found himself teaching English and embracing the flow of continuous new opportunities that kept him in Korea. Denny's journey led him from Busan, where he lived for 5-6 years, to Seoul, where he stumbled into a broadcasting career, a field he has remained in ever since. In Seoul, Denny has been particularly struck by the dynamism and the plethora of opportunities, something he doubts would be as accessible in the states. Over the past 20 years, Denny has built his life in Korea, finding community among gyopos—other Korean expatriates who have returned from abroad—and embracing his identity as a "third culture kid." This unique blend of cultural experiences has helped him craft a personal culture that defies traditional definitions. Now well integrated into Korean society, Denny states that apart from his immediate family in the U.S., including his parents and brother, there are few ties pulling him back to America. He has learned to let go of the expectations others have placed on him, as well as the ones he had for himself. Today, Denny lives comfortably undefined by others, embodying a hybrid identity that resonates with many expatriates navigating life between cultures.

Zach Benson, born in Busan, South Korea, was adopted at three months old and raised in Iowa. He lived there until after graduating from college. Zach's adoptive family provided a nurturing environment, particularly as he faced learning disabilities and a speech impediment during his childhood. Despite these challenges, Zach grew very close to his adoptive mother, who played a crucial role in his educational development. He was surrounded predominantly by white peers and, apart from his aunt and uncle's adopted Korean children whom he met at family reunions, he had little exposure to Korean culture or friends of Korean descent. Zach’s life took a significant turn after college when he moved back to Korea with a plan to find his birth mother. His adopted mother initially felt uneasy about this plan, creating some tension between them. However, this eased when Zach found his birth mother in 2011 with assistance from Holt International, a remarkable reunion that also led to his adopted mother meeting her and feeling a sense of familial connection. Living in Korea, Zach felt at home despite the language barrier, calling Korea his true home. He embraced his roots, integrating into the community and even teaching English in Busan, where he also met and connected with his birth mother. This encounter sparked a desire to find his birth father as well, learning that his birth mother had remarried and he had half-siblings. Zach's academic and personal growth became evident through his high school and college years. Despite a rocky start with a 1.6 GPA in his freshman year of high school, he graduated with a 3.7 GPA. He discovered a passion for breakdancing, which not only boosted his confidence but also led to the formation of a dance crew and a breakdancing club at Central College. This hobby turned into a significant part of his identity, with performances across the United States. Post-college, Zach volunteered at World Relief, where he met a North Korean that inspired him to return to Korea. His time in Korea extended as he lived in various places, including Busan and Daejeon, working as an RA at a Korean international school to stay close to his birth mother. His journey also took him abroad to Spain and Mexico for four years, and his extensive travels to over 70 countries have led him to feel at home in hotels as much as anywhere else. Now, having lived in Korea for 6-7 years, Zach's journey from Iowa to Busan has been a profound exploration of identity, heritage, and the complex dynamics of family, both adopted and biological.

Despite the geographic distance from his family, which he regrets due to his father's recent passing, Aaron has found a strong sense of identity and pride in his Korean heritage. Now more comfortable in his own skin, Aaron prefers to use his Korean name, Yoonsuk, more frequently. As a filmmaker, director, producer, and DJ, Aaron has successfully bridged his American upbringing with his Korean roots, fully embracing his dual identity and encouraging others to experience the richness of living in Korea.

Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Samuel Sang Gook
Dr. Samuel Sang Gook Lee was born in Daegu, South Korea, in 1935. The oldest of five, he was born in the midst of the Japanese occupation and recounts seeing many Japanese soldiers around his town and school. His elementary school, which was modeled after the Japanese schooling system, had a mix of both Japanese and Korean teachers, and began the day with a recitation of a pledge of loyalty toward the emperor. Once a week, students would walk up a mountain to a Japanese shrine and pray facing east, where the emperor’s throne lay. In every home was a kamidana, a mini-shrine meant for Shinto worship, which was encouraged by the teachers. Dr. Lee also remembers how the Japanese would take all of what the Koreans produced, particularly the rice, which some families tried to hide to perform jesa. With little food to go around, many families resorted to eating the scraps discarded from pressing soybeans into oil, and when faced with a shortage of oil, Korean men were forced to cut pine trees for their resin. During the occupation, Dr. Lee’s given Japanese name was “Iwamoto Sang Gok,” and Japanese was spoken at home by everyone except for his grandmother. It was at church that his Sunday school teachers would try to teach in Korean, which at the time he didn’t understand the gravity of. His paternal great-grandfather was the first Christian in his family, and his maternal grandfather participated in the Samil Independence movements both from Manchuria and Korea, where he’d send money to independence fighters. Dr. Lee’s mother he recalls as being a very sensitive person who passed away at the young age of 41, and from whom he believes he inherited his own depression and anxiety which he says never truly went away. The youngest of her family, she had two sisters and brothers, and was popular in her town for having been educated in Seoul during a time when it was uncommon for women to be highly educated at all, much less in the capital. His father, on the other hand, ran a bike shop, and married his mother when he was 20; she was 19-20. After his mother passed, his maternal aunt lived and took care of his family for a year before returning home. During the Korean War, Dr. Lee was a “house boy” who took care of menial tasks for a general and major, safe and away from the frontline, where for three years he worked for the American military; he was 15-16 at this time.

Kwon Sook Young (Full)
Interviewee: Kwon, Sook Young
Kwon Sook Young was born in North Gyeongsang Province, five years before liberation from Japanese occupation. She remembers how her family bought a brewery from the Japanese as they left, a business they operated until she was 10 years old, which was around the time that the Korean War broke out. At the insistence of her grandmother, the family fled to Andong, North Gyeongsang, before deciding to go south to Busan squeezed into a freight train carrying cargo. As the train headed south, it was met with bombardment, the effects of which knocked a water kettle on her, and buried her underneath a bags of rice, resulting in a broken rib. Although her family believed her to have died, she managed to crawl out from underneath the rice, and was able to make it to Busan where, to her (and her grandfather’s) dismay, there was very little to do. Her grandfather asked her and her older sister to at least try selling some pears, though this was met with little success, both because other, more older vendors had established themselves in the markets, and also because she and her sister would eat all of the pears. She notes how, during the war, she saw very little damage to church structures. Eventually, she enrolled into school in Daegu, where she spent her time while the war passed; upon expressing a desire go to Seoul to continue her education, her family deemed it unnecessary for a girl to continue schooling. She remembers how whenever she went back to visit her family, she’d be careful not to wear her school uniform to not agitate the older, conservative generation. Soon, she met her husband—a future doctor—and it was he who wanted to immigrate to the United States to pursue medicine, moving the family to New York in 1973 with three kids in tow. She recalls how difficult life in America first was, unable to help her children with homework not because it was difficult, but because she didn’t understand English yet. She also remembers the apartment the family moved into: a small two-bedroom, the rent for which took up 2/3 of the family’s monthly income. To make ends meet, she bought a used sewing machine to repair clothes, then to sew dresses; sometimes, her children would help her after school. She doesn’t remember all of the jobs she worked, simply because she worked too many odd jobs to remember. What kept her going was hope that her husband’s career would soon pan out, and as he finished up his internship and residency, the family eventually moved to Scarsdale. Her children, though, attended Bronx Science, because that was where all of their friends were going. During this time, too, she had been working at a newly opened YWMCA, looking after children. When her son, HJ, married and had his first child with Theresa, she moved in to live with them for a while, and recounts how she’d occasionally butt heads with her daughter-in-law over generational differences, though she’s grateful that things have smoothed out over time. In her golden years, Kwon says that she often reflects on the time she has left on this Earth, and while she’s not afraid of death, it’s something she’s constantly reminded of as she sees her loved ones pass, watch news of others’ passings, and witness who still remains at her church.

She initially struggled with English but excelled in math and made friends with other migrant children, despite one Korean Australian boy being embarrassed by her presence. In the Bay Area, she started using dating apps to find a partner but eventually met her husband, Chris, through a friend's introduction. Issun Park, born in October 1942 in North Korea, spent her early years in Hangyumdo before moving to Seoul in 1944. Due to communist influences at Seoul National University, her father took a job with the US Army in Japan as an interpreter, and the family joined him after traveling by boat and train. They kept their ethnicity a secret due to mistreatment from the Japanese. He was later transferred to Okinawa, where Issun attended an American high school on the base, enjoying her time there despite the cultural differences. In 1962, the family moved to San Francisco to join her brother, who was pursuing a PhD in journalism. Issun audited a class at Berkeley before moving to Illinois, where she attended Southern Illinois University. That same year, her future husband, a medical doctor, arrived in the US. Initially hesitant about marrying him, she was convinced by her siblings after he proposed following their second date. Issun eventually settled in San Antonio, Texas, and despite not living long in Korea, she considers herself Korean American. Though she feels at home in the US, her youngest son, after visiting Korea, expressed a desire to move there, enjoying the experience of not being a minority. She has never felt out of place in America and believes she is not a traditional Korean, allowing her sons to choose their professions freely. She and her husband speak Korean at home and have attended the same Korean church for 40 years. Her happiest memory is the birth of her first child, while the saddest is her mother's death. Myung Kun Park (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, HJ, interviewer, Park, Myung Kun
Myung Kun Park was born in Hwanghae, North Korea, in 1934. His childhood memories are marked by the Japanese occupation, which lasted until he finished elementary school. During World War II, he witnessed Japan's initial successes and eventual defeat. In 1945, with Japan's surrender, Korea was liberated, and he began learning Hangul from his father. However, Korea's impending division cast a shadow over the celebration. His family faced turmoil; his father was imprisoned for criticizing the communist party, complicating their plans to move south. Myung Kun attended middle school under a harsh communist regime, which caused him significant stress and a stutter that later disappeared. For high school, he transferred to another county where his background was unknown, excelling academically and joining the Young Men’s Communist Group. During the Korean War, Myung Kun evaded the draft with the help of non-communist hospital staff. When UN troops liberated his hometown, he joined the South's defense forces at 16. He served in a reconnaissance battalion, finding faith during his service. After being wounded, he was discharged at 17. With his parents trapped in North Korea, he reunited with surviving siblings in Suwon. Despite hardships, Myung Kun completed three years of high school in one year while working as a security guard for a US military unit. He passed the college entrance exam and entered Seoul National University’s premed program, eventually excelling in medical school. Supporting himself as a live-in tutor, he later moved to the US for better opportunities, working in Poughkeepsie and meeting his future wife during his fellowship. Due to visa issues, he returned to Korea before securing a job in Washington, D.C., but faced a hiring freeze. He then worked in Canada as an intern before settling in Eastern Washington as a family practitioner, eventually obtaining a green card. Myung Kun later joined the University of Kansas as a teaching professor and then the University of Texas, where he became head of the Pediatric Cardiology Unit. Grateful for his wife, whom he credits to God's grace, Myung Kun is proud of his three sons who attended Ivy League schools. He reflects on his parents' absence during his success, which saddens him. One of his happiest moments was being accepted into Seoul National University, a prestigious school he later realized. Despite not identifying as a man of faith, he considers himself a believer and appreciates the life he has built.

Interviewee: Choh, Ann, interviewer, McLuen, Bree Yoo-Sun
Bree Yoo-Sun McLeun's life is a testament to resilience and identity exploration across cultural boundaries. Born in Seoul, Korea, in 1986, Bree was adopted at just 3.5 months old and immigrated to Minnesota, where she was raised in a predominantly white community. Her father, a Baptist Minister, ran a nonprofit for youth in Minneapolis, and her family was deeply involved in the church, shaping much of her early environment. Growing up, Bree experienced a profound sense of isolation, intensified by her attendance at a wealthy public school where she often felt the pressure to show gratitude for her adoption, summed up in the family mantra, "don't bite the hand that feeds you." This environment contributed to Bree's struggles with anger during her childhood, marking her as a high-risk kid. Despite these challenges, she found solace and success in sports, eventually choosing figure skating as her focus and turning professional at the age of 17. Her interest in her Korean heritage was supported at home; she attended Korean culture camp, and her maternal grandmother was particularly keen on exploring Korean culture with her. This familial support played a crucial role in her identity formation and later influenced her academic and professional choices. Bree pursued an undergraduate degree in English from North Park with the initial intention of going to law school but later shifted her focus to social work, inspired by her own experiences as an adoptee. During her time at grad school at Loyola, she faced an unexpected pregnancy with her son Carter, which led her to defer and later reapply to her program. Carter's birth marked a turning point for Bree, deepening her engagement with the Korean American community to ensure her tri-racial son—Black, Korean, and Native American—had a strong sense of identity and community support. Her professional journey included an internship with Hanul Family Alliance, driven by a desire to provide Carter with more resources and opportunities. The challenges Bree faced in connecting with her biological family, including a birth search at age 13 that ended in disappointment, further motivated her dedication to helping others navigate their own journeys of cultural and personal discovery. Today, Bree's life story encapsulates the ongoing journey of embracing one's roots while forging a path forward, underscored by her commitment to her son and her community. Her experience highlights the complex dynamics of adoption, the search for belonging, and the powerful impact of motherhood on personal healing and community connection.

Matthew Miller (Full)
Interviewee: Choh, Ann, interviewer, Miller, Matt
Matt Miller's life narrative is a poignant illustration of identity, community, and self-discovery. Born near Anyang Province, Korea, in May 1974, Matt was adopted at nine months old and flown to Chicago, Illinois. Raised in Elgin, Illinois, Matt is the youngest of four children in a family that included two biological children of his adoptive parents and his birth sister, who shared early memories of their birth mother and took care of Matt, giving him a unique connection to his origins despite their new surroundings. Matt's adoption through Holt International introduced him to adoptee gatherings, which played a role in his upbringing. However, it wasn't until his early to mid-twenties, during his involvement with a Korean American church in Naperville, that Matt experienced a profound sense of belonging. This community was pivotal in helping him embrace his Korean heritage, providing a sense of family and acceptance that was both healing and transformative. During his graduate studies, a significant encounter further shaped his identity. Matt met a Korean scholar who studied adoption, and during a conversation where Matt expressed his concerns about not knowing the Korean language, history, or culture, the scholar reassured him that "there isn't one Korean experience." This affirmation was a turning point for Matt, helping him to hold onto his Korean identity with pride rather than longing. Matt's academic career has largely focused on the experiences of Asian Americans, with his dissertation exploring how Asian Americans navigate cultural experiences. He has published extensively on the subject and has become a mentor and guide for many Asian American students, creating a safe space within predominantly white academic environments. Married for 22 years and the father of three children, Matt met his white wife at a small, conservative bible college with a notably low Asian presence. His journey of self-discovery and acceptance has also prepared him for a future trip to South Korea—a journey he plans with apprehension but sees as necessary for a deeper connection to his roots. Today, Matt Miller's life reflects a journey from a sense of isolation to one of community and identity affirmation. His experiences underscore the diverse tapestries of the Korean American experience and highlight the profound impact of community and personal interactions in shaping one's sense of self.

Soon-Young Oh was born in Gimhae, South Korea, a small city near Busan. Immigrated to Minneapolis, Minnesota in 1978 via international adoption when she was almost 5 months old. White family, 2 older brothers who were quite older. City was majority white. Always aware of having been adopted; parents would tell her that she was “chosen” to be a part of their family. Minnesota has a large population of Korean adoptees, and every summer Soon-Young would go to cultural camps catering to the adoptee population. She doesn’t remember any bullying or teasing as a child. In 2005, she went back to Korea for the very first time, and met her biological father, though she had no expectations of any reconciliation; she explains that this was the beginning of her journey of navigating her adult identity. Meeting her birth father, who explained the circumstances of her adoption beyond what she had known through various paperwork her parents had shown her, settled certain questions she’d had. She was unable to meet her birth mother, as her birth mother had given a false name during the adoption process, but Soon-Young says that she’s come to peace with this long ago. In 2007, attended the IKAA convention; in 2008 Soon-young moved to Korea to teach, a time she described as being challenging and fulfilling. She met her husband in Korea during this time. Her husband is also a Korean adoptee, though she says that his story was different from hers in how he was adopted into a Korean American family living in Chicago, and so grew up immersed in the language. She has a child who she reminds to take pride in his Korean heritage; in 2016, the family moved briefly to Korea, where her son attended daycare surrounded by other Korean 3-year olds. She feels that it’s very important in identifying as part of the Korean adoptee community, and the broader Korean American community, because it’s crucial in navigating one’s personal journey with others. She hopes that her son sees her as a person who worked to both be a part of, and be a builder of, such a community, even when it can be daunting to do so. When asked about what she’s most proud of, she responds by saying that she’s proud of staying in touch with the adoptee community, and putting herself in difficult situations (such as moving to Korea to teach, settling in Chicago) that encouraged her to grow as an adult. She explains that she takes pride in her name, Soon-Young Oh, which she discovered in 2005 on her first trip back to Korea; rather than going by a name given to her by an adoption agency, she felt it important to reclaim the one given to her by her birth parents.

Joseph Oh's life is a profound journey of cultural identity and familial connections. Born in an orphanage in Incheon, South Korea, Joseph and his brother were adopted at the age of 5 by a White couple in the United States. However, after the early loss of his adoptive father, Joseph was readopted by a Korean American family in Chicago. This new chapter reintroduced him to his Korean roots; his adopted parents, who were deeply immersed in Korean culture, were strict but tried to instill a strong sense of heritage. Living with his Korean grandmother, Joseph often found himself caught between two cultures, speaking English while his parents spoke Korean. The family rarely discussed the topic of adoption, and his grandmother's harsh words about "bad blood" made it difficult for Joseph to express his feelings or seek understanding about his identity. Despite these challenges, the Christian faith and the Korean church community played significant roles in his upbringing, providing him a sense of community and connection to his Korean heritage. Joseph's journey back to Korea as an adult—to teach English and search for his biological parents—marked a significant period of self-discovery. Although the search through Holt International did not lead to a reunion with his birth parents, it allowed him to connect deeply with other adoptees, helping them as a translator during family reunions. These experiences, particularly helping others meet their birth families, brought him a sense of fulfillment and an imagined connection with his own birth mother. Finding love with another Korean adoptee in Korea was a transformative experience for Joseph, giving him a profound sense of being seen, heard, and belonging. His marriage and the birth of his child have been sources of immense joy and pride, anchoring his life in the love and connection he long sought. Despite the complexity of his familial relationships, including the distance from his biological brother who now lives in Canada, Joseph has found closer ties with his adopted family following the passing of his adopted mother. His life's journey reflects a tapestry of loss, rediscovery, and deep personal growth, with his son and wife standing as his greatest sources of happiness and accomplishment.

Theresa Choh-Lee was born in Seoul, Korea, she immigrated to the U.S. in 1972, the youngest of three siblings. John Anthony Ranum (Full)
Interviewee: Ranum, John Anthony
John Anthony Ranum's life story begins in Pyongyang, North Korea, where he was born just before the tumult of the Korean War swept through the nation. At the tender age of ten, he found himself a refugee of war, tragically separated from his mother and left to navigate the harsh realities of life on the streets and in various orphanages. Despite these early hardships, John's life took a remarkable turn in Daegu, South Korea. It was there that he met his future adoptive brother, a U.S. soldier stationed at a local airbase. This chance meeting, initiated by John's kind act of helping the soldier find transportation, eventually led to John being smuggled into an airbase and later adopted by the soldier's family from Lockport, Illinois, in September 1955. Transitioning to life in the United States, John rapidly adapted and excelled in his studies, completing eight years of Catholic school in just four. His academic prowess continued through high school, culminating in his graduation in 1963. John harbored aspirations of becoming a pilot and even reached out to a senator for sponsorship to the Air Force Academy. However, his height fell short of the academy's requirements, which thwarted his initial dreams of flying. Undeterred, John joined the U.S. Air Force, eventually being stationed back in Korea at Osan Airbase, where he endeavored to find his biological mother—a quest that remained unfulfilled among the countless orphans of the Korean War. His military career also included a stint as a military police officer and later, tours in Vietnam, where he served as a non-commissioned officer of investigations. Throughout his life, John was deeply influenced by his adoptive family. His adoptive mother, a resilient woman of German and French descent, and his Norwegian adoptive father, a gentle carpenter, provided him with a stable and loving home. The profound connections he formed with his adoptive siblings also shaped his perspectives and aspirations. After retiring from a commendable 25-year tenure as a police officer in Bolingbrook, Illinois, John cherishes the family he built with his Korean wife—three daughters and five grandchildren, reflecting a life full of challenges overcome and joys multiplied. John Anthony Ranum's journey from the streets of Daegu to the suburbs of Chicago is a poignant testament to the unpredictability of life and the enduring strength of familial bonds, both given and chosen.

Becky Belcore (Full)
Interviewee: Belcore, Becky
Becky Belcore was born in Seoul and adopted into a Minnesotan family when she was one year old. Minnesota at the time had the most Korean adoptees than all the other 49 states combined. She lived there until her family moved to the southern states of Virginia and, eventually, Alabama. Her adoptive parents originally wanted to take in a White child, only to find out that there was an 8 year waitlist to do so, and then wishing to adopt a Black child but told not to do so because they would not be able to instill a sense of racial pride in them. Growing up in all-white communities was very challenging. Her parents' approach to raising Becky and her adoptive brother was that they were their children and not Korean, which affected how she saw herself when peers would harass and make fun of her appearance. Becky reflects on her self hatred and insecurities she had while growing up, even going to believe that Korea didn’t exist because she had never seen anybody who looked like her growing up, until she went to an all-womens’ college where the population was actually ⅙ Korean. Although her Korean peers wanted to connect with her, Becky was afraid of them because did not know what being Korean meant, growing up in an all-White community. But also college taught her that her background and upbringing is not exclusive to herself, but others too– which guided her passion for activism and organizing which allowed her to connect with peers like herself. But it was not until she arrived in Chicago when she discovered and got involved with her Korean heritage through the Korean American Resource and Cultural Center (KRCC). Although it was tough for her to get used to the space, the words of her mentor Curtis Muhammed and the lens of social justice she discovered at the center encouraged her to stay. Her journey taught her that we all have our individual and diverse experiences that all blend together to become one story, and hers is just one of the many stories. The present marks her 26th year of involvement with KRCC and her 6th year as the co-director for the National Korean American Service & Education Consortium (NAKASEC), forming groups to actively support Korean adoptees. These groups work socially and politically, one aspect of it being helping adoptees achieve citizenship. She hopes people find a home, a sense of joy and happiness through her organization, a place where adoptees can connect with others to uplift each other.

Soon Ki Bae (Full)
Interviewee: Bae, Soon Ki
Soon Ki Bae, who also goes by Simon, was born in Japanese-occupied Korea in 1935 in South Jeolla Province. He recalls how the country was liberated while he was in the third grade, but political turbulence continued for much longer. The Korean War broke out when Bae was in his third year of middle school, and he recalls how, in Busan, you were hounded by police during the day and by anti-communist partisans at night. Following the war, he graduated from high school; as was typical of the time, he was to enlist in the military to perform his mandatory service, but due to missing documentation his service was delayed until he was 27 years old, in 1961. As a result, he fulfilled his mandatory service around the time that Park Chung-hee’s May 16th coup took place. Due to poor job market prospects, Bae moved to Germany to work as a contracted miner; he recalls the difficult working conditions of drilling through earth to lay subway tracks, hauling buckets of water deep into the mine. Though hard at first, he credits his Korean physique as key to enduring through this period of his life. He also remembers the influx of Korean nurses, mostly women, who lived alongside the mining communities. At the end of this three-year contract, he was informed by a pastor that Germany would annually review, with the possibility to extend, the working contracts of those married to nurses, but Bae instead made arrangements to relocate to America with some friends he had made in the mines. Before leaving, he married and had a child (born January 1, 1968). When he arrived in Chicago, he estimates there having been around a hundred Korean students studying, who would have to leave the country after their university studies; the onus for building a Koreatown in Chicago landed in the hands of those who would permanently settle in the area, many of whom had been contracted miners in Germany like Bae himself. During holiday celebrations, Bae’s community—which had by then set up businesses along the North Side of the city—invited Korean students in the city to partake in festivities with them. Along the way, he’s founded and joined a number of Korean cultural organizations, the first of which was a performing samulnori (traditional Korean folk music) troup which traveled all around Chicagoland and the American midwest. As time passed and performing samulnori became difficult due to the aging members of the troup, he founded a saxophone sextet as a means of staying in touch with his arts and performance hobbies. Today, he spends his time doing all of the activities he wants to do—dancing, gardening, playing saxophone. He remembers fondly the friends he’s made who have since passed, and reflects on how he is now the oldest member in his immediate community. Even still, he maintains a youthful vibrancy which he credits to him seeking out leisurely activities.

Kyung Bin Bae (Full)
Interviewee: Kyung Bin Bae
Kyung Bin Bae was born in Seoul in 1953, at the heel of the Korean War. In childhood, he recalls having a comfortable upbringing, with his family able to afford private elementary education. In middle school, his father’s business underwent some financial troubles which forced the family to move. He remembers watching his mother struggle as she picked up work, and becomes aware of a degree of class consciousness. As the eldest son, though, his mother tries to hide the family’s finances from him to save him the burden of worry. In middle/high school, he was involved in a number of activities, and was near the top of his class. After losing a student election, he dropped to near bottom in shock. He applied to SNU but was rejected; studied for a year at Namsan library to prepare for the next application cycle, where he is rejected again so enrolls in Sungkyunkwan University to study journalism, joining the student newspaper. This is during the Yushin era (1970s). Fearful in partaking in “demos” (protests), he fulfills his part in student movements through his work with the newspaper, interviewing democratization activists and artists such as poet Kim Chi-ha. After military service, he prepares to study as an international student at Michigan State University in May of 1980 (Gwangju). Studies are expensive, but receives some amount of financial support from family back home. But still needing more funds, he road trips to New York City, which he falls in love with. He finds work in sales at a clothing business run by a Korean businessman in Brooklyn. After returning from New York, his ambitions for his career shift, and he decides that he should go into the clothing business as well. He marries his now-wife, a chemical engineer whom he met at Michigan State, and moves to Astoria, Queens. He recounts the run-down apartment that they first lived in, but only has fond memories of his time in the neighborhood. Tries to find work in Manhattan when his wife becomes pregnant; proceeds to look for work with more urgency and finds a modest job as a salesman in the clothing business, though this time the job requires him to attend a variety of fashion shows to promote his workplace’s sampling of textiles. When his daughter is born, the growing family moves to newly built rowhouse in Flushing; with a newly bought oldsmobile, they roadtrip around the United States. Looks very fondly upon this period of his life. After accumulating some savings, the family moves to Woodbridge, New Jersey, having bought a condominium. Begins attending church. One day, he receives a call from a businessman (non-Korean) who asks if he’d want to work for him as he expands his clothing business into the Asia-Pacific, an offer which he considers and later accepts. He recalls how at the time, the bulk of the clientele for Korean clothing businesses lived in Harlem and the Bronx, which required him to often drive to different parts of the city to close sales deals. At his new company, he’s given the opportunity to stop by Korea to visit some family before continuing with business trips in Hong Kong and Indonesia; in Korea (~1985), he resolves to work to bring his mother to the United States one day after seeing her working in her aging years, though this would never come to fruition. Relocates to Chicago following his daughter’s acceptance to university in the city, where he has lived in peaceful retirement ever since.

Kaein Oh (Full)
Interviewee: Oh, Kaein
Oh Kaein's journey from Seoul to Chicago is a testament to her unwavering faith, resilience, and dedication to family. Arriving in America in September 1985, she embarked on a new chapter, initially working for Estee Lauder. Despite lacking prior experience in the restaurant industry, her keen eye for improvement and determination to excel fueled her aspirations. Running a 24/7 restaurant, Oh Kaein encountered numerous challenges, including a fire that led to extensive remodeling, after which her landlords sold the restaurant. However, amidst adversity, she found solace and strength in her faith, experiencing a newfound connection with Christ. Her children, inspired by her relentless work ethic, learned invaluable lessons through her example. Following the closure of her restaurant, Oh Kaein ventured into entrepreneurship, launching a bracelet company with her sons. Facing setbacks in transitioning from service-oriented work to merchandising, she persevered, eventually finding success in her catering business. Initially, Oh Kaein hoped her son would pursue a stable career as a lawyer, aiming to spare him from the struggles she endured. He instead chose to run a restaurant with his good friend. She came to embrace his entrepreneurial endeavors, recognizing the depth of his compassion and dedication to his friends and community. Moved by her son's commitment, Oh Kaein embarked on another venture, crafting banchan dishes for his restaurant, further deepening their bond. Through financial challenges and personal trials, she maintained a steadfast commitment to her children's well-being, ensuring they never felt neglected by coming home to eat dinner with them no matter what every day. Reflecting on her journey, Oh Kaein acknowledges the lessons learned through hardship, recognizing the true value of faith, family, and contentment. Grateful for the opportunity to overcome greed and find fulfillment beyond material success, she embraces a simpler, more meaningful life, guided by love and compassion for those closest to her.

Jackie Faye (Full)
Interviewee: Faye, Jackie
Jackie Faye, born and raised in Dallas, Texas, comes from a richly diverse heritage, being Korean and Chinese. Her family history is deeply rooted in East Asia, with her mother originating from Incheon, South Korea, and her grandparents living through the Korean War. Jackie’s ethnic background is Chinese, and her family has been in Korea since the late 1800s, making them fourth-generation Chinese in Korea. This blend of cultures saw her growing up in a household where Korean was spoken, despite the Chinese ethnicity. Jackie's family ran one of the first jajangmyeon shops in Dallas, a testament to their integration and influence within the local community. Her older sister, who is six years older, was a significant influence during her upbringing, especially as Jackie was navigating her own identity and experiences. Tragically, Jackie’s father, who was pursuing a career in Taiwanese pop music, passed away when she was just nine, after her parents had divorced when she was two. Her early memories include recording music with him, an activity that deeply influenced her lifelong passion for music. Music continued to be a part of her life, with piano lessons provided by her church adding to her musical upbringing. Jackie’s connection with her grandmother, a Chinese Korean and the family matriarch, was particularly strong. Her grandmother not only ran the restaurant but also maintained an active lifestyle, which left a lasting impression on Jackie. Navigating her identity extended beyond her ethnic background to her sexual orientation. Jackie, who identifies as gay, knew about her orientation from a young age but only came out a year after college. The period of hiding her true self felt burdensome, and her eventual coming out marked a significant turning point in her life, lifting a weight off her shoulders. At 17, Jackie's journey toward self-discovery and independence took a dramatic turn when she ran away from home. This decision led her to pursue college education on her own terms. Post-college, she reconnected with her mother to come out formally, which, despite initial difficulties, led to eventual acceptance. Today, Jackie is committed to authenticity in her music career, striving to be honest in her lyrics and maintain integrity in her artistic expression. She continues to embrace her father’s legacy in music, using it as a medium to express her emotions and thoughts. Jackie’s story is one of embracing one's true self, overcoming adversity, and the power of resilience and acceptance in shaping a fulfilling life.

In her home, Tiffany was immersed in Korean culture, from the food to the traditions, thanks to her mother's influence. Tiffany's academic pursuits took her to the University of Utah, where she double majored in Broadcast Journalism and Political Science, with a minor in Spanish. Her passion for journalism was ignited in high school and further nurtured in college, where she was an active member of the school newspaper. She also had the opportunity to study abroad in Spain, which broadened her perspectives and experiences. Upon moving to Houston, Tiffany felt a warm reception from the Korean American community, further deepening her connection to her mother's heritage. Since filming the interview, her professional career as a journalist began to flourish in San Francisco, where she now works as an award-winning journalist. Tiffany is dedicated to journalism for its power to assist those in need, highlight overlooked issues, and give voice to the voiceless. Her work, including covering impactful stories like local Koreans in Houston sewing masks during the pandemic, underscores her commitment to meaningful journalism and contributes to her sense of integration and acceptance within the Korean community. Tiffany Justice's journey from a biracial upbringing in Utah to becoming a respected journalist in San Francisco encapsulates her ongoing exploration of identity, community, and professional dedication. Her story is a testament to the strength found in embracing one’s heritage and using one’s platform to effect positive change.

Interviewee: Kim, Andrew
Andrew Ungal Kim's journey from Gyeonggi-do, Anyang-si, Korea, to the outskirts of Baton Rouge, Louisiana, encapsulates a life of profound transitions and self-discovery. Born and raised in South Korea, where he spent his childhood playing soccer and badminton with neighborhood friends, Andrew moved to the U.S. at the age of 14, bringing with him dreams influenced by the allure of the American lifestyle. Initially thrilled by the prospect of a new life in America, Andrew soon faced the realities of assimilating into a vastly different culture and language environment. His relocation to Clinton, Louisiana, a place where his family was a rarity, presented unique challenges. His father, a former car mechanic in Korea, adapted by joining and eventually taking over his sister's beauty supply business. Meanwhile, Andrew navigated his adolescence with limited social opportunities due to the geographical and cultural constraints of his new hometown. The local Christian private school Andrew attended became a sanctuary of sorts, shielding him from bullying and allowing him a semblance of stability during his formative years. However, beneath the surface, Andrew struggled with a personal turmoil that contrasted sharply with his external environment—coming to terms with his sexuality. Andrew realized he was gay during his early teens, a revelation that conflicted with his Christian upbringing. For years, he prayed for change, a resolution that never materialized. It wasn't until college at Louisiana State University that he began to truly confront and accept his identity. Despite his acceptance, Andrew kept his sexuality hidden from his family and community, driven by fear of rejection and the need to support his widowed mother financially. His mother's eventual discovery of his sexuality in 2016 led to a traumatic period, with her seeking help from their church community to process the news. Remarkably, the church did not ostracize him but instead offered unexpected acceptance, marking a significant point in Andrew's journey towards openness. Professionally, Andrew pursued a career as a Control Engineer in the oil and gas industry, a role that took him to Houston in 2018—a city that promised a fresh start and more opportunities. Houston brought new freedoms and the chance to explore his identity more openly. He became involved with a LGBTQ+ based running group called Frontrunners, which helped strengthen his community ties. In 2022, Andrew married, solidifying a personal commitment that was once unimaginable to him. He lives with his husband and three dogs in a townhouse near downtown Houston, envisioning a future in a home with a yard where he can continue to care for his mother and share his life openly with his family. Andrew's story is one of resilience and transformation, reflecting the challenges and triumphs of navigating cultural shifts, personal identity, and acceptance. His life underscores the importance of community, whether found or fostered, and the enduring quest for authenticity and happiness.

Joseph Yoo's journey through life encapsulates the theme of navigating expectations and forging his own path amidst a deeply religious family background. Born in South Korea and moving to the U.S. at the age of six, Joseph experienced the nomadic lifestyle of a pastor's family, living in diverse locations such as South Carolina, Santa Barbara, and Hawaii. These moves, while challenging, helped forge a resilience and adaptability in Joseph, qualities that he values highly as an adult. Raised in a family where both paternal and maternal lines were deeply embedded in the ministry, the expectation for Joseph to follow in his father's footsteps was prevalent from his childhood. Despite this, during his teenage years, Joseph found himself resistant to the idea of becoming a pastor. However, his perspective shifted after attending a pivotal Methodist conference/retreat in Chicago, an experience that Joseph describes as a turning point in recognizing his own calling to ministry. Choosing to lead a multiethnic church rather than a Korean-specific congregation, Joseph has sought to establish professional boundaries that were often blurred in more culturally homogenous religious communities. His approach to ministry is shaped by his diverse upbringing and his father's influence, who despite the family's frequent relocations, always provided a stable and loving home environment. In 2016, Joseph moved to Houston, attracted by the affordability and job opportunities. His career took another turn here; he transitioned from being a United Methodist pastor to an Episcopalian pastor. This change marks another chapter in Joseph’s life of embracing new beginnings and reflecting on his spiritual journey. Joseph’s personal life took a transformative turn when he and his wife, after facing difficulties in having biological children, decided to become certified foster parents. They welcomed Nathaniel, an autistic child who was half white and half Hispanic. Initially facing complex issues with Nathaniel’s biological parents, they eventually adopted him, bringing immense joy and fulfillment to their lives. Despite initial reservations, Joseph’s parents became supportive of the adoption, recognizing the profound happiness Nathaniel brought into their lives. Joseph’s story is one of self-discovery, resilience, and embracing life’s unexpected turns. His narrative weaves through the challenges of living up to family expectations, finding personal faith, and building a family under unconventional circumstances. His life illustrates the beauty of adopting new cultures and traditions, as seen in Nathaniel’s love for Korean food, and underscores the profound impacts of love and acceptance. Joseph Yoo’s life journey invites reflection on the nature of calling and the transformative power of embracing one’s true path, no matter how unexpected it might be.

Jason Cho, a 43-year-old native of Houston, Texas, has roots deeply entrenched in martial arts and entrepreneurship. Growing up in a low-income neighborhood, his early life revolved around his family's Tae Kwon Do school, where discipline and structure were part of his daily regimen. This upbringing not only honed his athletic skills but also instilled in him a robust emotional resilience that later translated well into his professional life. Jason’s childhood was significantly influenced by his uncle, a renowned Tae Kwon Do master, which naturally led him to excel in sports throughout high school. His deep connection with martial arts guided him to become a Tae Kwon Do instructor himself before venturing into the hospitality industry, driven by a passion for food cultivated alongside his sister, a fellow food enthusiast. The pivot to the hospitality sector was sparked during a visit to New York where his sister introduced him to Korean fried chicken. Captivated by the dish and unable to find a similar offering in Houston, Jason was inspired to open his own restaurant specializing in Korean fried chicken. Despite his father's initial skepticism due to Jason's lack of cooking experience, Jason's determination led him to sell his house and car to finance the venture—a decision that paid off when his father, after tasting his son's cooking, gave his full support. Tragically, his father passed away as construction began, a profound loss that Jason felt deeply during this critical period of transitioning to a new business. In addition to running his restaurant, Jason manages two Tae Kwon Do schools, maintaining his ties to the martial arts community. His aspirations don't stop at the restaurant business; he dreams of shaping Houston's culinary scene by becoming a prominent figure in promoting Korean food concepts and hopes to one day establish a Koreatown in the city, continuing his father's legacy of community building. Jason's personal life also faced significant challenges, particularly when his father battled and initially overcame lung cancer, only to succumb later to complications from pneumonia. This period was one of intense emotional strain for Jason, who regrets not maintaining a more positive outlook during his father's final days. This experience taught him the power of the human mind and the impact of positivity on overcoming life’s hurdles. Today, Jason remains a devoted father to his daughters and a dedicated business owner, striving to balance his professional ambitions with personal commitments. His story is one of resilience, cultural pride, and the pursuit of dreams fueled by family legacy and personal passion.

David Hee Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, David Hee
David Lee's life is a profound story of resilience and transformation. Born and raised in Los Angeles, California, within a devoutly Christian Korean American family, David encountered significant challenges from a young age. His father, a pastor, had first come to the US in the 1970s for leukemia treatment at UCLA, and later, he brought David's mother over from South Korea. David's childhood was shaped by this deeply religious environment, which initially provided a sense of community but eventually felt stifling as he grew older. The most significant struggle in David's early life came from within his own home. His mother suffered from bipolar disorder and terminal breast cancer, conditions that led to periods of intense abuse directed at David. Growing up in a low-income household, David was acutely aware of the harsh realities of poverty, which further complicated his home life. Driven by a desire to escape the turbulence of his family life, David worked diligently in high school, earning a full scholarship to Georgetown University—a decision that marked his first major step away from his past. Once at university, far from the pressures of his family, David decided he would sever ties permanently with his birth family, a decision catalyzed by abuse, the lack of support, and understanding for his identity as a gay man. During his college years, David supported himself through multiple part-time jobs, an endeavor that underscored his independence and determination. It was also during this time that he formed a life-changing friendship with Kelly, a fellow student. When David faced the prospect of nowhere to go during the holidays, Kelly invited him to spend it with her family in Houston, Texas. This gesture of kindness evolved into a deep and lasting bond. After several years of growing closer to Kelly’s family, and experiencing the warmth and unconditional support he had longed for, David was legally adopted by them when he was 26 years old. This adoption came during a tumultuous time. David's biological mother passed away in 2017, an event that forced him to confront his past. During this period, his biological father apologized for the abuse David endured from his mother, a moment of closure that was significant yet complex. David also came out to his biological father around this time, who, unlike others in his biological family, fully accepted his sexuality. David's story is a testament to the power of chosen families and the profound impact of embracing one's true self. Now co-founding Texas Signal, he channels his experiences into advocacy and storytelling, aiming to give a voice to those who feel marginalized. His journey illustrates not only personal resilience but also the transformational love that defines family, not by blood but by bond.

As a child, she remembers being a “tom-boy,” hanging out with the other boys in her village, and enjoying playing out in the dirt. She recalls that her father owned ducks and goats, and would deliver goat milk around the village. She also recounts a harrowing story about a time when she was given an errand (going to the pharmacy), only to fall into the village well on the way back; she states that this was the first time she turned to her faith in earnest. As an only child, her older relatives would often tell her family to have a son, and growing up Terry wanted nothing else than to be a boy. On September 17, 1978, Terry’s family immigrated to Oklahoma, where her aunt had moved a year prior with her American GI husband. However, after ten months of living in Oklahoma, the family relocated to Houston, seeing as her aunt and her father didn’t get along very well. In Houston, they were taken under the care of a Presbyterian Church (Terry’s family is Catholic), who found them a room in a 2-bedroom apartment leased by another Korean person, “Anshi Ajuhssi.” She recalls driving through the Houston highways and being in awe of the layers of overpasses above her. Her parents found work cleaning the town mall, but one night her father and ahjussi went out and didn’t come back for three days; it wasn’t until the pastor of the church called Terry’s home that they found out that he had been in a car accident, put into a coma and hospitalized. Because the family had no insurance, they quickly took Terry’s father out from the ICU and brought him home, where he was bedridden for months. Terry remembers how the church took care of their family during this difficult time. Eventually, as Terry graduated high school and began college at UT Austin, she was faced with the question of her career. After trying out premed, she landed on studying fine arts. In 1988, she married her husband who she had met through by matchmaking—she wanted to early marry, seeing that her father was in poor health. After marriage, her husband’s family moved from Korea to live with her, a period she found difficult in maintaining both a traditional Korean household while also exercising her own freedoms, but she says that there’s no other person who knows her better than her husband. In their 40s, she and her husband moved to Birmingham, Alabama, for six years where they operated a sushi business, before coming back to Houston where she worked briefly at the Korean American Association and Community Center of Houston. After a year working there, she and a friend opened a nonprofit organization called Uri Juntos; with an eye towards the future, she envisions herself making more art, and translating religious texts.

Bark Boo Moon (Full)
Interviewee: Moon, Bark Boo
Bark Book Moon was born on January 1945 in Seoul. When he was five years old, an American family moved into the home just behind his, and they brought with them a child who was around the same age as Bark who would pellet him with his slingshot, despite Bark’s desire to befriend the new child. A couple of days before the war broke out, the American family moved away, and after fighting started Bark’s family sought refuge in Masan, where he encountered American and British soldiers for the first time. He recounts a funny story of him and his friends finding what they thought was a balloon on the ground, blowing it up when an American GI smacked him on the back of his head, telling him that the balloon was actually a condom. He also remembers how different soldiers treated the kids differently; whereas Americans would throw them chocolate and gum from the out the backs of their moving trucks, British soldiers would always pull over and hand the sweet treats to the children directly. He returned home for middle school and high school, where he initially found English an easy subject. While serving time in the military, a senior of his who needed to pass a written examination asked Bark if he could instead take it for him, which he did. He was caught, however, and was given the choice between serving time in jail, or serving time in Vietnam, and he chose the latter. After completing his training for Vietnam, he remembers how he and his friends received a paycheck which they used to go out and party before they were deployed, and he recounts how many of his platoon mates got STDs that night. In Vietnam, he was tasked with transporting medical supplies, and would often have to make harrowing treks through gunfire to deliver the supplies where they were needed. He remembers standing in the marshes, too, where it would often flood, and how standing chest-deep in water he felt as if he could see the ripples in the water emanating out of his heartbeat. In 1972 he arrived in the United States where his first job was in an ice cream parlor, before joining the U.S. Army at the age of 28 as infantry. He found training to be a breeze and when asked where he wanted to be stationed, he said he’d go back to Korea; back at home, he met his wife at church, and together immigrated to the United States. They had two kids, and Bark decided to leave the Army to work in the post office so he’d be able to spend more time with family, where he worked until his retirement. Today, he takes care of his ailing wife in Texas.

Dr. Sam Jae Cho (Full)
Interviewee: Cho, Sam Jae
Dr. Sam Jae Cho was born in Seoul, inside his father’s company residence. The oldest of 5, he has two younger sisers and two younger brothers; during the onset of the Korean War, the family was unable to flee south but instead hid in the basement of the company residence until the September 28 Offensive, which was when the family evacuated to Daegu. The family stayed in Daegu for the duration of the war, and Dr. Cho finished attending middle and high school there as well. After graduating from high school, Dr. Cho matriculated as a student in the Mining/Engineering Department at Seoul National University, which during his undergraduate time reorganized itslef into a Mineral Resources/Petrol Engineering Department. Following graduation, he took a job at a mining and engineering company which asked that he communte into the mines; he quickly realized that working in the mines wasn’t for him, as the air was unclean and he’d emerge daily coated in ash to the point where he was unrecognizable. He left the job to take a governmental one in the national department of energy; it was around this time that he saw a televised broadcast of President Park Chung-hee who announced that oil fields had been discovered off the coast of Pohang, and that a new intiative would be put into place for Korea to become self-sufficient in energy; every year, 100 Korean students were sent abroad to be educated in energy technologies. Dr. Cho left to study at UT Austin after studying English for two years. After graduating with his master’s, he intended to return to Korea to help the country’s fledgling petrol industry, but received a job offer that had little to do with what he had studied while in Texas, and so chose to remain in America to continue studying for a doctorate. The school asked of him to receive field experience before beginning his dissertation, and so he spent six months in New Orleans working for Texaco where as a technical assistant where he discovered a virgin (untapped) oil field. He then returned to school to complete his dissertation, and stayed in Texas to work for various Oil companies. Later into his career, he launched an organization which would provide resources, networking support, and community for international Korean students seeking to study energy sciences in Houston so that they might be able to return home and introduce emerging technologies in Korea.

Dae-Duck Cha (Full)
Interviewee: Dae Duck Cha
Dae-duck Cha was born in Gangwon Province, Hongcheon, the youngest of nine siblings. When he was six, the family moved to Seoul; during the Korean War, all of his older brothers died, leaving just him and his older sisters. As a child, he moved around a lot—he attended elementary school while living with his oldest sister, and middle school through college while living with his middle sister, and so he believes he didn’t do well in school because he never had time to adjust to one singular educational environment. His parents passed during the Korean War, not as casualties of war, but as victims of a massacre by fellow Koreans who were going around the country in search of supposed communist-sympathizers. Before Cha was born, they were both heavily involved with the independence movement, and after liberation, both parents were involved with democracy movements; before they were “taken away” by their captors, Cha rememembers them telling him that they would “see him later.” He reflects on the irony that is chinilpa, or Japanese collaborators, getting away with little to no punishment, and whose families are still well off today, whereas those individuals who were directly involved with the liberation and democratization of the country were treated like garbage. In school, he was often told that he was a gifted artist, and so he took art classes and attended Hongik University, widely known for their fine arts programs. He then completed his mandatory military service, then graduated from college, after which he left for the United States to work as a member of the Peace Corps. After his role in the Peace Corps came to an end, he met his wife at a Korean church and lived in Philadelphia for a while, operating a wig and hairstyling store. After 7-8 years, he realized that he hadn’t come to the U.S. to immigrate, but to work, and moved back to Korea for 1.5 years. However, the family—who now had two kids—decided to move back to the U.S. for their kids, and moved to Houston, where they knew nobody. Cha continued his art, and was recognized by a local news channel (Channel 2), after which he became well known in the Korean community within Houston, with his art presented in various galleries around the city. He soon opened a frame-making businesses, which he worked until retirement.

Justine Yoon (Full)
Interviewee: Yoon, Justine
Justine Yoon was born in Los Angeles, California, to parents who had come to the United States as young adults: her mother arrived when she was twenty-five, and her father arrived in America shortly after. She describes her family as being tight-knit and nuclear and describes her early childhood growing up in the Los Feliz area as lively and active. Her parents would register her and her siblings for sports camps and a variety of extracurriculars so that they might become immersed and exposed to American culture in their outside lives; she remembers biking up and down her neighborhood with her friends and being surrounded by a diverse group of children. At the same time, the family was raised speaking Korean, and as was the case for many Korean American children, sent their kids to weekend Korean school at the local Korean church. She recalls how both parents were active and well known within the Korean community, with her father operating a private practice as a clinical psychologist in the area. Both parents placed a strong emphasis on their children’s education, which Justine appreciated while understanding that the generational difference in their values could be explained by sympathizing with the fact that her parents were doing the best with what they knew, in a country they had immigrated to. She entered university at UCLA not knowing what she would study—those around her suggested business—and sampled a variety of courses before finding an interest in Sociology, which she chose as her major. Around the time of her graduation, her parents retired but made the transition to work in the restaurant business, where she’d often lend a hand. When describing what it means to her to be Korean American, she first says that there is a belief around the idea that working hard will actualize into success, and that Korean people seem to be filled with a lot of hope to begin with (the example she uses is her parents’ opening of a third restaurant, right before covid). Today (at the time of recording), she lives in Koreatown which she says was not planned, but has been “convenient” in how there’s access to good food, though she laments that the neighborhood has become increasingly gentrified since she was a child.
