Kevin Yoo, whose Korean name s Yoo Kun-Bae, was born in a small village (desig: Donam) in Banpo-myeon, Chungchungnam-do, Korea. Born in 1949, he describes his childhood as one wrought with the anxieties of the Korean War; he tells us that only dream he had was to escape his family’s poverty and live a simple life. Like many families from the country’s heartland, Kevin was able to escape the worst of the fighting, though he tells us that economic and financial restraints were precariously and constantly felt. In the first grade, he moved to the nearby metropole of Daejeon (between North and South Chungcheong provinces) to start his schooling in the first grade; even after finishing his studies, he remained in the school system, working as a schoolteacher in Korea for five years before arriving in the United States, where he continued working a variety of jobs until he was twenty-seven years old. Although Kevin is now retired from his last venture, a real estate business which he worked for over forty years, he has lived many lives in the Bay Area: he worked in the restaurant business, running Samwon Galbi and Gogi Time, as well as other smaller ventures such as selling wigs, working a grocery chain, and a health foods store. At the urging of his friend, Alex Hahn, Kevin moved from San Francisco to Oakland, bringing Samwon Galbi with him; he describes the city as a dynamic place with many people from many different backgrounds who tried their best to get along with one another (though sometimes, Kevin says that everyone can do a lot better). Having set up his business at the start of Oakland Koreatown’s growth, he has since helped organized Korean festivals across the Bay Area, including in Alameda, Concord, the East Bay, and everywhere in between. Telling us that we must dig our wells deep for water to flow in, he looks back at his life with thanks and gratitude (hoping that his children might want to take over his real estate business someday!).

Pat Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, Pat
Pat Lee, whose Korean name is Lee Kyung Hee, was born in 1951 in Seoul, Korea, the fifth daughter in a bustling household of seven children. As a young woman, she admits to having been impulsive and carefree—a spirit of youth that would ultimately shape her journey. After attending high school in Anyang and marrying young, she immigrated to the United States with her husband in 1972, landing in Oakland with no clear plan and few resources. Her husband, still in college, juggled night work to support them, often returning home past midnight. Isolated and far from her family, Pat found herself thrust into adulthood—loneliness, necessity, and survival pushing her to grow up fast. Seeking a path of her own, Pat enrolled at Laney College’s cosmetology program while raising two small children. Around the time she was set to receive her license, she made a spontaneous decision that would define her entrepreneurial future: she purchased a small neighborhood market near what would later become known as Koreana Plaza. At the time, she hadn’t grasped how difficult running a business would be, but she threw herself into the work—seven days a week, early mornings at the produce market, long evenings at the shop. Her customers were her teachers, helping her gain confidence and resilience in a new land. Over time, the area around her store began to flourish. A hairdresser, a video store, a billiards hall, and an acupuncturist opened nearby, creating foot traffic and a vibrant Korean hub. In the early days, Korean immigrants in the East Bay found each other through necessity and warmth. Without Korean restaurants or cultural centers, new arrivals were met with shared meals and open doors. “We didn’t have much,” Pat says, “but we had each other.” By the late 1980s, her business had grown immensely—at one point, customers lined up at the door, the cashier overwhelmed with demand. Even an arson fire in 1990 couldn’t stop the momentum; thanks to good insurance and sheer determination, she rebuilt. The plaza became a destination for Korean Americans across the Bay Area—from San Francisco to Fremont to Walnut Creek—who came seeking a taste of home. Today, Pat reflects on a dramatically changed Oakland and a Korean American community that has evolved. Yet she still believes in the value of hard work, honesty, and patience. “Things may not be as easy now,” she says, “but if you work sincerely, your time will come.” Her story stands as a testament to the enduring spirit of immigration, entrepreneurship, and the quiet strength of community built from scratch.

When she joined KCCEB in 2010, June was drawn to its mission of empowering Korean and other immigrant communities across the Bay Area. What began as admiration evolved into leadership. Over the years, she has helped transform the organization’s model from a program-centered structure to one grounded in community outcomes and impact. Under her guidance, KCCEB has championed a community health framework—one that integrates mental health, public benefits, and social services to meet the complex and evolving needs of immigrant communities. June’s most meaningful moments have come from witnessing this impact firsthand. She recalls a senior client battling depression who, through dramatized storytelling and peer support, was able to reclaim his agency and later became a helper to others. She shares the story of another elder, unhoused and unknown to the system during the pandemic, who was discovered through KCCEB’s meal delivery program. Through sustained support, he secured housing, regained health insurance, and transformed from suicidal despair to becoming a volunteer serving meals to other seniors. These stories, for June, are more than anecdotes—they are proof of possibility. “Empowerment,” she says, “means helping people live to their fullest potential. That’s everybody’s right.” As the needs of the Korean American community change with time, June is committed to ensuring that KCCEB changes with them—remaining a vital, trusted, and responsive force in the lives of those it serves.

Han Jik Kim, born on December 20th, 1965—Dongji, or the winter solstice—in Liberation Village, Seoul, is a doctor of Oriental Medicine who has dedicated his life to practicing and teaching traditional Korean medicine in Central Los Angeles. The eldest son of North Korean parents, with a father employed in broadcasting, Han Jik had a childhood marked by frequent moves, attending four elementary schools in total. Though soft-spoken and introspective, he remembers this period as a deeply joyful time. Early on, he developed a keen interest in questions without easy answers: in middle school, he dreamed of becoming a philosopher; in high school, a novelist. Theology even crossed his mind. Han Jik immigrated to the U.S. in 1988, joining his family who had settled in Southern California two years earlier. Though he had briefly attended Chung Ang University in Korea, he did not complete his studies before immigrating. After some hesitation and thoughts of returning to Korea, he ultimately enrolled in South Baylo University in 1991 to study Korean medicine—drawn by the rare opportunity to receive instruction in his native language. Guided by his uncle’s advice and a growing sense of vocation, he stepped onto a new path, one that blended tradition with adaptation. Now, decades later, Han Jik runs his own clinic where the majority of his patients are non-Korean. His approach to healing is holistic, blending the principles of *yin and yang*, the five elements, and food-based therapies. “I treat my patients like students,” he jokes, sharing how he insists on whole, traditional foods—especially two boiled eggs for breakfast (“you won’t be hungry until 1 p.m.”), jujube for warming the stomach, and samgyetang for summer balance. “Don’t let me catch you with protein powder,” he warns us! The core of Korean medicine, he explains, lies in understanding and respecting the body’s natural rhythms. “When people become ill, they often become slaves to their illness. My job is to guide them back to themselves.” Han Jik speaks about the importance of tending to one's relationships—whether with family, neighbors, or coworkers—as a form of healing in itself. “Sickness often begins when those bonds break,” he says. And while he acknowledges the challenges of maintaining those relationships in the social media age, he believes firmly that caring for others and oneself is the heart of well-being. Reflecting on his life, he confesses one regret: that he once believed the best way to resolve a conflict or difficulty was to remove himself from it. Today, he sees healing not as separation but as engagement, understanding, and care. “No matter how advanced AI or science becomes,” he says, “we are not just rational bodies. We are humans. And I am the master of my body.”

Sion Kim, born Kim Seokhyun in 1937 in Icheon, Gyeonggi-do, is a retired Methodist-trained pastor and avid apitherapist who has made Los Angeles’ Koreatown his home since 1980. One of six siblings, Sion spent his early years on a small rural farm, helping raise pigs, chickens, and rabbits in the mountainous countryside. From a young age, he had a deep fascination with animal husbandry, and his passion led him to study livestock care in Japan near Hokkaido, sponsored by the Gyeonggi provincial government. There, he gained firsthand experience in dairy farming—an opportunity that shaped his early aspirations. But upon returning to Korea, he learned that his father had sold the family’s land, effectively ending his dream of a farming life. He moved to Seoul, where he took on various jobs. Though he rarely attended church in his youth, Sion recalls feeling a sudden and powerful call to prayer one day. That spiritual pull led him to seminary, where he began pastoral training, eventually serving in Methodist, Presbyterian, and Lutheran congregations. In April 1980, he stepped off the tarmac at LAX and into a new chapter of his life in Koreatown, where he has remained ever since—becoming both a community fixture and witness to key moments in Korean American history, including the 1992 Saigu Uprising. In retirement, Sion found an unexpected second vocation: bee sting acupuncture, or apitoxin therapy. After witnessing its healing effects firsthand—his own toothache vanished overnight—he became a practitioner, often emphasizing that bee stings, when administered properly, can be more effective than needles. While he cautions that allergic reactions are possible, he also shares anecdotes of patients who, undeterred, returned for more treatments. Now in his later years, Sion reflects on life’s true priorities. “Health is more important than money or honor,” he tells us, mourning the loss of many friends to age and illness. His advice: pray if you can—but more than anything, live with a positive attitude. For Sion, the mind and body are deeply connected: “The way we think and speak,” he says, “manifests in how we live.”

Gwanghun Kim, 56, is a doctor of Korean Medicine who has lived in Los Angeles’s Koreatown for nearly a quarter of a century. Born in South Korea, he spent his childhood in the countryside before moving to the port city of Busan for his schooling. He recalls those years as relatively “average,” without any grand ambitions other than one day becoming a salaried worker and earning a stable income. It wasn’t until much later—after immigrating to the United States in 2000—that his life took a very different direction. Arriving in Koreatown as a first-generation immigrant, Gwanghun was in his early thirties and confronted by the intense stress and uncertainty of starting over in a new country. Though he did not develop a major illness, the toll of long hours, economic pressures, and cultural adjustment manifested physically: his body ached constantly, and fatigue weighed him down. These hardships prompted him to think more seriously about health and wellness, not only for himself but for others in similar circumstances. When he sought out acupuncture as a patient, he was struck by how much it alleviated his pain. This experience inspired him to train as a doctor of Korean Medicine, transforming personal hardship into a lifelong vocation. Today, Gwanghun’s practice extends beyond his clinic walls and into the wider community. Twice a week, he travels to Long Beach Port, where he offers free acupuncture, massage, and health advice to sailors and dockworkers who often spend months at sea and return with chronic aches and injuries. Many of these workers lack reliable access to healthcare, and Gwanghun sees his volunteer work as both a calling and a responsibility. His involvement in his local church further reinforces this mission of service; he does not see a contradiction between faith and medicine, but rather an alignment in the shared work of healing and care. Reflecting on the healthcare landscape, he notes differences between Korea, where traditional and Western medicine are treated as distinct systems, and the United States, where holistic or non-pharmaceutical treatments are sometimes recommended by Western doctors for patients seeking alternatives to medication. For Gwanghun, this blending underscores the importance of offering people choices in how they manage their health, especially in moments of anxiety or pain. Now in middle age, with children raised and his parents growing older, Gwanghun thinks often about legacy. Koreatown, he says, was built through the labor and sacrifice of his parents’ generation, who struggled to establish themselves in America and make life better for their families. His own generation, he believes, carries the responsibility of stewarding that legacy—ensuring the community remains strong, vibrant, and supportive for the generations to come. Beyond Koreatown, he sees this duty extending outward: to share skills, knowledge, and compassion wherever in the world they might be needed.

Sue Park Hur, 53, is the co-founder of ReconciliAsian, a non-profit peace center in Los Angeles dedicated to equipping Korean diaspora and Asian American communities and churches with tools for conflict transformation, restorative justice, and trauma healing. Born in Seoul, South Korea, Sue immigrated to Los Angeles with her family at the age of eight. As a 1.5-generation Korean American, she recalls her childhood ethos as one of dutiful responsibility—“to do a good job”—shaped by her parents’ experiences and the broader immigrant context. Her father, who had been a young teenager during the Korean War, carried with him both the resilience and traumas of his generation; her uncles even referred to him as “Buddha” for his wisdom and composure, yet Sue also witnessed the lingering hauntings of those past experiences in her family life. A life-changing moment came at the age of sixteen when her mother passed away. This loss prompted Sue to reflect deeply on family narratives and memory, realizing that while her mother’s life held moments of tragedy, she was also fully human—excited about dates with her husband, capable of joy and ordinary pleasures. Sue describes this process as “befriending” her mother: learning to see beyond the static stories we hold of our parents and recognizing their complexity, frailty, and humanity. This awareness of familial histories, combined with reflections on her father’s efforts—“In spite of all of that, you tried. And that is enough.”—deeply shaped her understanding of care, legacy, and accountability. Sue’s college years at UCLA marked another pivotal period. In 1992, as a sophomore, she witnessed the acquittal of the LAPD officers in the Rodney King case and observed the ensuing media narrative framing Koreans and Black Americans as adversaries. She recalls seeing her father on the rooftop of their family store with a gun during this period, a moment that crystallized for her the intersection of systemic racism, community defense, and generational trauma. These experiences prompted her to consider how structural oppression manifests not only in society at large but also within families, churches, and faith communities. With a background in sociology and theology, Sue and her husband have devoted their lives to fostering peacemaking and reconciliation within the Korean American and broader Asian American community. Joy Kim (Full)
Interviewee: Kim, Joy
Joy Kim (Lee Jeong-hyun), born in 1953 in the countryside near Cheonan, South Chungcheong Province, is a pioneering librarian and curator whose work has left an indelible mark on Korean Studies in North America. Raised in a conservative Confucian household after the early death of her father, Joy grew up under the guardianship of her grandfather, who believed that girls did not need an education beyond high school. Despite these limitations, her intellectual curiosity and love of literature drove her to pursue higher education, eventually studying Library Sciences at Ewha Womans University in Seoul. In the late 1970s, Joy immigrated to the United States to join her husband, who had gone ahead to study journalism. Her early years in America were marked by both hardship and determination. She began her life in Los Angeles as a live-in babysitter earning $75 a week, using the quiet hours of childcare to teach herself English by watching television and reading the Bible. Within six months, her language skills were strong enough for her to enter UCLA, where she completed her master’s degree in Library Sciences while also starting a family. In 1984, Joy began her professional career at the University of Southern California’s East Asian Library. Over the decades that followed, she advanced to become Curator of the Korean Heritage Library (KHL), where she was instrumental in building one of the most significant Korean Studies collections outside of Korea. Under her stewardship, the KHL not only expanded its holdings but also became a vital center for research, teaching, and cultural preservation. Beyond USC, Joy’s leadership extended nationally: in 2007 she became the first Asian woman elected President of the Council on East Asian Libraries, an acknowledgment of her trailblazing role in a historically underrepresented field. Her contributions were further recognized in 2011, when she received the National Order of Civil Merit from the President of South Korea, one of the nation’s highest civilian honors. Alongside her professional achievements, Joy has also contributed significantly to Korean American history preservation. She played a central role in USC’s Korean American Digital Archive and worked closely on the Legacy Project with Korean American Story, ensuring that the voices and experiences of Korean immigrants and their descendants would be preserved for future generations. Joy’s personal journey has been marked by resilience as well. She navigated a difficult marriage, raised two daughters—one of whom was diagnosed with Asperger’s—and made the courageous decision to pursue divorce when her children urged her toward a safer and more stable home environment. Through these challenges, she found strength in her faith and in her vocation as both a mother and a scholar. Now retired, Joy continues to be recognized as a leading authority in Korean Studies librarianship and as a trailblazer for women and immigrants in academia. Her career reflects a profound dedication to cultural preservation, scholarship, and community service, and her legacy endures in the institutions she shaped and the histories she safeguarded.

Rosa Chang, known in Korean as Jang Kyung-Hye, is the Executive Director and co-founder of the Korean American Special Education Center (KASEC), a nonprofit serving Los Angeles and Orange County. Born and raised in Seoul, South Korea, she credits her father with instilling in her two guiding principles that shaped her life’s work: that women can pursue any path regardless of gender, and that one should never live solely for oneself. Inspired by these lessons, Rosa studied psychology in college, where she first encountered clinical psychology and the study of autism and developmental disabilities. At the time in Korea, disabilities were heavily stigmatized—children with such diagnoses were rarely seen in public, and formal education on the subject was limited. Determined to expand her knowledge and serve those marginalized by stigma, Rosa came to the United States for further study. In 2000, alongside behavioral clinicians and social workers, she established KASEC to address the lack of culturally and linguistically accessible services for Korean American families. Many parents, limited by language barriers, either did not know their child had a developmental disorder or struggled to navigate care systems. KASEC became a bridge for these families, offering screenings, therapies, educational support, and a community in which parents could share both struggles and small victories. Rosa recalls moments of joy when parents cried together over incremental improvements in their children, underscoring the emotional weight of KASEC’s mission. Her advocacy was tested during a tragedy in 2015, when a student named Paul died after being left in a locked school bus on an extremely hot day. Paul’s inability to communicate his distress highlighted systemic failures, galvanizing Rosa and the community to push for reform. Their efforts led to the passage of the Paul Lee School Bus Safety Law, requiring safety devices on buses to ensure drivers check for students before locking vehicles. Reflecting on the slow pace of change, Rosa has likened her efforts to throwing eggs at a rock: progress often seems impossible, but over time, stains accumulate and change begins to take shape. Over 25 years, she has witnessed a gradual increase in awareness and empathy surrounding developmental disabilities within the Korean American community, though she emphasizes that ongoing support—particularly financial resources—remains critical to sustaining KASEC’s programs and professional staff. Her work has been sustained by her family’s sacrifices. Rosa’s husband carried the financial burdens of their household so she could dedicate herself fully to the cause, and her daughter, now studying neuroscience, grew up inspired by her mother’s work with children with autism. Rosa credits her family’s quiet support as the foundation that enabled her to persevere.Today, Rosa hopes to be remembered as a trailblazer—someone who carved a path through uncharted terrain to make space for others. For her, the core lesson remains simple yet profound: no one lives in the world alone. Her vision is of a community bound by empathy and mutual responsibility, where individuals with developmental disabilities and their families are supported, respected, and empowered to thrive.

Suki Park is a Korean-born mother whose experience of migration, marriage, and single parenthood illuminates the quiet struggles many immigrant families face—and raises the quiet possibilities for healing. Confronted with language barriers, cultural displacement, and the practical burdens of single parenthood, Suki describes feeling overwhelmed and apologetic—sorrowful that she could not create the harmonious family she had wanted for her children. Through family counseling at Family Touch, Suki discovered that talking with an empathetic, nonjudgmental professional offered relief and new tools for relating to herself and her children. Counseling reshaped her understanding of help: what she once thought of as something only for “when everything is broken” became a place to learn, reflect, and interrupt harmful patterns. A central insight for Suki was the conscious refusal to pass down generational trauma; drawing on the contrast between her own upbringing in a small Korean fishing town and the vast anonymity of life in the U.S., she learned ways to parent differently—deliberately cultivating emotional openness and repair rather than repeating the strict or silent scripts of earlier generations. Her conversations with her daughter Lauren are heartfelt and candid: Suki offers apologies for the hardships they endured, acknowledges the limits of what she could provide in a new country, and affirms shared growth. She frames the family’s journey with a sober, humane question—“Everyone has times when life flows in directions they want or don’t want… but would I be the only one feeling this way?”—inviting empathy and the recognition that struggle is often collective, not solitary. Suki’s story underscores how accessible, culturally-sensitive counseling can create space for reconciliation, intergenerational learning, and renewed family bonds—transforming remorse into repair and isolation into a shared path forward.

Emmett, Andrea, Ahri (Edited)
Interviewee: Schelling, Emmett
The Morales-Yoon family sits down for a conversation on family and joy, as well as their journeys in finding (and making) them. They start their story in 2017, which Arri and Andrea identify as a hectic but fulfilling year when their family began to come together; Andrea and Emmett had met through their work in trans advocacy in Texas, with Arri occasionally accompanying Emmett to the state Capitol in Austin. Though Andrea says that she initially didn’t want to “parent” Arri, Emmett describes how, at times, the two of are a lot closer to each other than him! Both Emmett and Andrea speak on what being parents has been like, particularly with respect to the field in which they work: Andrea recounts one episode after Arri came out where she thought her child was trying to make themselves legible to the queer community by balancing how she’d be perceived against what felt most true for them, a kind of conformity which was heartbreaking. Emmett quips that as parents, all they want is for Arri to feel empowered as they pursue love and joy. He also reflects on a newfound intentionality in engaging with his Korean heritage as a parent, something which Houston, with its clustered Korean communities, easily accommodates. For all of them, joy is what grounds both their work in organizing in the South, as well as their life as a family.

Su Pak & Sung Park (Edited)
Interviewee: Pak, Su Yon
In this entry of Queer Joy, Dr. Su Yon Pak and Mudang Sung Park share the story of how they met, the philosophies which guide their work and identity, and how seemingly ordinary people—which both Su and Sung insist they are—leave legacies of hope and perseverance for generations that follow. Su, who currently serves in an administrative-faculty role at Union Theological Seminary, met Sung at a religious campaign for LGBTQ inclusion in the mainline Protestant church, where they connected over shared experiences as 1.5 generation queer Korean American immigrants with a Christian background. Sung relays how their first meeting did not feel like their first interaction; whereas other encounters with other older Korean Americans had been informed by certain social tenets of Confucianism, Sung saw Su as a role model and mentor, someone who embodied a different kind of Korean elder—one grounded not in hierarchy or authority, but in care, curiosity, and support. In his words, he saw in their relationship a “lineage,” one which ascertained and reified the spiritual work which queer Korean Americans had been doing before him. Su, for her part, sees her life as the quotidian of “queer, cis, 1.5-generation woman who’s beloved, and a loving grandmother of two children.” A model of intergenerational kinship rooted in spirituality, diaspora, and shared queer perspectives, their dialogue invites listeners to consider how legacy is built not through grand gestures, but through moments of recognition, mutual witnessing, and the courage to live authentically within and beyond inherited traditions.

Vana Kim (Full)
Interviewee: Kim, Vana
Vana Kim is a writer, philosopher, and peace activist based in Los Angeles. Born in Seoul in 1946, her earliest memories begin with the Korean War, after which she recalls nothing of her life before the conflict—an absence she understands as the imprint of wartime trauma. As a child, she fled Seoul with her mother and grandparents, finding temporary refuge in a remote mountain village, an experience she remembers as profoundly spiritual and restorative: a landscape of stillness and starlight that continues to serve as a lifelong source of healing. After months of displacement in the South, her family settled in Busan for several years, where Vana first encountered the legacy of her grandfather, Yi Jong-man, an educator and visionary economic reformer whose commitment to self-reliance and social transformation would later shape her own thinking. Educated in philosophy at the University of Toronto, the University of Chicago, and Harvard University, Vana ultimately chose not to pursue a conventional academic career, instead dedicating herself to the work of personal and collective healing. She developed a philosophy she calls saengmyeong moseong (“life-maternity”), grounded in emotional self-reliance, ethical relation, and the belief that peace must begin within the individual. This conviction also animates her activism for permanent peace and neutrality on the Korean peninsula, an idea inspired in part by her mother’s reunion with Vana’s father in Pyongyang after decades of separation. Across her writing and organizing, Vana Kim advances a vision of peace as an inside-out practice—one that neutralizes internalized conflict, reshapes relationships, and opens the possibility of wholeness for individuals, communities, and nations alike.

Gil Sung Jun (Full)
Interviewee: Jun, Gil Sung
Gil Sung Jun is a Korean American retired pastor, grandfather of five, and survivor of war, displacement, and generational loss whose life bears witness to faith forged through sacrifice. Born in 1947 in Hamgyeong Province, North Korea, he is the son of an underground resistance leader who was imprisoned, tortured, and killed by the North Korean regime when Jun was only two years old—a legacy of moral courage that would quietly shape his life. Fleeing south with his mother and sisters during the Korean War, Jun survived famine, illness, and near death before escaping aboard what would later be remembered as the “Miracle Ship,” which carried thousands of refugees to safety on Christmas Day. Raised amid scarcity on Geoje Island, he learned resilience early, sustained by communal bonds and the belief that his father’s spirit continued to watch over him. Through an international sponsorship program, Jun formed a decades-long relationship with an American woman who supported his education and inspired his eventual journey to the United States in 1972. As a father, pastor, and later a grandfather, Jun reflects deeply on wisdom, love, and the enduring ache of absence—especially the longing for a father he never knew. His story traces the intimate intersections of war memory, Christian faith, diaspora, and intergenerational responsibility, offering a testament to how legacy endures through quiet perseverance rather than recognition.
Keywords: Korean War; diaspora; faith; legacy; pastoral; displacement; refugees; memory; fatherhood; wisdom; Christianity; resilience; sacrifice; immigration; intergenerational; trauma; belonging; survival

Jae Hee Jun (Full)
Interviewee: Jun, Jae Hee
Jaehee Jun was born in the rural village of Mongiya in South Chungcheong Province shortly before the outbreak of the Korean War, growing up in the seventh generation of the eldest line of her family. Her father began his career as an elementary school teacher before attending seminary and becoming a pastor, after which the family moved to a small island near Mokpo in South Jeolla Province—a place Jaehee remembers fondly from her childhood. Those peaceful memories were interrupted during the Korean War when North Korean forces arrested her father simply for being a Christian pastor. He was imprisoned and at one point forced to march to a beach alongside two other prisoners who were shot and killed, though he himself was unexpectedly spared and released. During his captivity, Jaehee and her family lived in a small church parsonage that had been taken over by communist forces for their meetings, praying constantly for his safe return. When he finally came home, their relief and joy were overwhelming. With the help of a church deacon who provided her father with false credentials, the family later made the dangerous journey back to their hometown, traveling only at night and walking through mountain paths to avoid detection. Back in their village, where Jaehee’s grandfather had built a small church, she met the man who would become her husband, Gil Sung Jun. At first she believed they were simply friends, often traveling together in groups with other young men and women. As the daughter of a pastor from a strict household, she was careful about how she lived and initially rejected Gil Sung when he first confessed his feelings after church one evening. However, his sincerity and persistence eventually persuaded her to give the relationship a chance. She later reflected that he was honest, dependable, and never wishy-washy, and she felt confident she had made the right choice. The couple eventually immigrated to California, where their early years were marked by hardship and sacrifice. They rented a single bedroom from a friend for $300 a month, and Jaehee rode the bus each day to work at a factory earning about $400 a month while her husband served as a pastor. To save money she washed the family’s laundry by hand, holding on to the hope that their situation would improve. Over time, what Jaehee describes as God’s grace opened new opportunities. After moving to Orange County, the family started a dry cleaning business. Although their shop opened later in the morning than most—around nine or ten—customers continued to come, and the business gradually grew into a successful livelihood. Through that work they were able to buy a home, send their children to Christian schools and college, and help establish a church that served the “1.5 generation” of Korean Americans navigating life between cultures. Later in life, Jaehee and her husband sold their business and gave the proceeds to the church, choosing to live simply in a small rented home. Each morning she would go to the church to pray, deeply grateful for the life she had been able to build in America after so many trials. Now a beloved grandmother, Jaehee says she hopes her grandchildren will remember her not for accomplishments but as a loving grandmother who was always praying for them. Reflecting on her life—from war and displacement to faith, family, and community—she says she intends to live the rest of her days in gratitude for God’s guidance.
Keywords: Korean War; Mongiya; South Chungcheong; Mokpo; faith; pastor; imprisonment; prayer; migration; California; Orange County; factory; dry cleaning; bus; church; 1.5 generation; perseverance; gratitude; grandmother; resilience

Interviewee: Jun, Grace
Gil Sung Jun is joined by his daughter, Grace, for a reflective conversation about how love is expressed and passed down within families shaped by war, loss, and faith. A question that weighs on Gil Sung’s mind is a simple but profound one: whether he was truly a loving person and a loving husband. His father was taken from him when he was just two years old, leaving him to grow up without that relationship, and much of what he knows about his father comes from stories shared by his mother. His father had once been a strong social communist during the period of Japanese colonization but later turned away from the ideology after witnessing how it was implemented under Soviet influence. Growing up in a traditional family, Gil Sung recalls that expressions of love were rarely spoken aloud, a cultural pattern that shaped how he himself communicated with his children. Looking back, he admits that while he devoted himself sincerely to ministry and service to God, believing it was the most important responsibility he carried, that devotion sometimes came at the cost of building a closer, more openly loving relationship with his own children. It is something that still troubles him. Grace listens thoughtfully and reassures him that he was indeed a good father, explaining that she sees his care and affection reflected in the way he relates to his grandchildren today. Together they reflect on a recent family trip to Korea, where Gil Sung took Grace and her children to places that carry deep historical and personal meaning, including Hyochang Park, which honors figures connected to Korea’s independence movement, and Namsan, where they looked out over Seoul and reflected on the seventy years it took for the country to rebuild after the devastation of war. Gil Sung also shared memories of his hometown of Dangseonpo, where his primary school once stood and which has since become a much more developed place, as well as the church where he and his wife were married. During the trip he also traveled near Mount Paektu, standing on the Chinese side and looking toward Lake Cheonji and the border city of Dandong, where a bridge stretches toward North Korea. From there he prayed quietly for the day when the divided land might one day be restored and healed. Through these memories and reflections, father and daughter return to a shared understanding: that while love is not always expressed perfectly or openly, the most enduring thing in life is the love we receive from others and the care that continues to move quietly across generations.
Keywords: Korean War; family; fatherhood; love; ministry; reflection; memory; Dangseonpo; Hyochang Park; Namsan; Seoul; Mount Paektu; Cheonji; Dandong; North Korea; prayer; reconciliation; heritage; grandchildren; legacy

In Sook Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, In Sook,
Born in 1938 in the countryside near Icheon, Korea, In Sook Lee remembers a childhood shaped by both the beauty of rural life and the upheaval of war. She often recalls the tall mountains surrounding her hometown and the smaller hills scattered among them, landscapes that remain vivid in her memory. Spring brought some of her happiest moments, when mulberries ripened and she and other children would pick and eat them while listening to the distinctive call of the cuckoo bird. Yet these peaceful memories exist alongside scenes from the Korean War that left lasting impressions. She remembers the day Seoul was liberated on September 28, when her brother and father were forced to live in hiding. At one point her brother asked her to hang up a poster supporting the cause, prompting an older woman in the village to jokingly remark that she was doing her part as well. As the war intensified, North Korean soldiers retreating through the area once stopped at a neighbor’s house while she was playing there. Hungry and exhausted, about ten soldiers asked for food, and the household could only offer barley rice and radish-top kimchi. The soldiers gratefully accepted anything they could get, a moment that later made her reflect on how desperate they must have been. During the January Fourth Retreat, planes flew low over the town dropping bombs, and her mother watched in fear as smoke rose from nearby homes while wounded villagers walked past bleeding. Miraculously, the only damage to their own home was the family’s kimchi shed. In the aftermath, United Nations forces—including American and British soldiers—arrived in the region, though rumors spread among villagers that foreign troops kidnapped young girls. Terrified, her older sisters hid behind a closet when soldiers approached, though in hindsight she laughs at the memory because their feet were still visible beneath the door. At another moment the family hid in a cave as British soldiers approached, while her older siblings attempted to communicate with them in English. Despite these disruptions, In Sook remained determined to continue her education. In her town most girls were not expected to study beyond elementary school, but her older sister secretly traveled to obtain textbooks in order to prepare for middle school entrance exams. When the school principal later visited their home and offered the sister a scholarship, In Sook was also allowed to attend. She walked a long distance each day to a Methodist missionary school where American missionaries occasionally visited and spoke to the students. On Saturdays, American soldiers sometimes screened movies for the children, experiences that fascinated her and sparked a dream of traveling to the United States. She prayed often that one day she might go there, saying she feared that if she did not she might end up “like a frog stuck in a well,” never seeing the wider world. In time that dream would come true when she joined her husband, Reverend Chang Soon Lee—who had once been known to her through her older sister’s classmates as a mischievous boy—after he received a green card and invited her to join him in California. When he first asked her to date him she initially refused, insisting she was not the kind of person suited to be a pastor’s wife, yet her life ultimately followed a path shaped by faith, perseverance, and the fulfillment of a childhood dream to see America.
Keywords: Korean War; Icheon; countryside; mountains; mulberries; cuckoo; retreat; bombing; cave; UN troops; missionaries; education; Methodist; scholarship; movies; America; migration; faith; resilience; memory

Rev. Chang Soon Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, Chang Soon
Born in Korea during the period of Japanese colonial rule, Reverend Chang Soon Lee reflects on a life shaped by faith, war, migration, and pastoral care. Born in 1936 and raised between Pyongyang and the countryside, he grew up during a time when Korean language and identity were suppressed under Japanese occupation. At school, students were required to speak Japanese and were punished if they accidentally spoke Korean while playing with friends. Korean families were also forced to adopt Japanese-style names. One of his most vivid childhood memories occurred during a Wednesday evening church service when Japanese police suddenly entered wearing heavy boots and arrested his father, a pastor, in front of the congregation—an experience that left the entire church shaken and terrified. Liberation in 1945 initially brought hope, and Lee remembers his father encouraging church members to begin studying English in anticipation of a new future. Yet the arrival of Soviet troops in the North quickly created new hardships, as soldiers moved through villages demanding possessions while shouting “davai, davai,” seizing watches and valuables and spreading fear among residents. When the Korean War began on June 25, 1950, Lee recalls hearing the radio announcement that conflict had broken out and initially believing, as many did, that the war would end quickly. Instead, the violence intensified around Pyongyang. American aircraft bombed strategic areas, forcing families to hide in fields during the day and return home only at night. As fighting spread, Lee’s family attempted to flee south, eventually reaching the Taedong River during the harsh winter of December 1950. With bridges destroyed by bombing, thousands of refugees searched desperately for ways to cross. Lee remembers people attempting to wade through the icy river carrying their belongings while planes strafed the area, sending crowds scattering in panic. His own family narrowly escaped separation when his mother insisted they remain together rather than crossing in smaller groups. After hours of danger and confusion, a small refugee boat finally ferried them across the river in multiple trips, a moment Lee remembers with deep gratitude, particularly for his mother’s determination that the family would survive together. Decades later, in 1971, Lee traveled alone to the United States intending to attend a seminary in Ohio before returning to Korea. However, after arriving in Los Angeles he was invited by a senior pastor to remain and assist in ministry, an opportunity that introduced him to the possibility of obtaining permanent residency. Learning that a green card would allow him to bring his family to the United States, Lee changed his plans and chose to remain in California. He later completed advanced theological training at Claremont School of Theology, earning a master’s degree and a Doctor of Ministry, and in 1979 he founded a Korean ministry within a multilingual, multiracial congregation in Los Angeles, where he served for twenty-two years as a pastor in the United Methodist Church. His work as an immigrant pastor extended far beyond preaching. Recognizing the struggles faced by newly arrived immigrants—language barriers, cultural conflicts, and complex immigration systems—Lee devoted much of his ministry to social services and advocacy. He recalls helping vulnerable individuals navigate immigration offices, including a Korean woman who had been abandoned after a fraudulent marriage arrangement left her stranded at the airport without support. Drawing on the respect immigration officials often gave clergy, Lee advocated on her behalf and helped secure her legal status. For Lee, such work reflected the central emphasis of his ministry: encouragement and care for those facing hardship in a new country. Looking back over decades marked by colonial rule, war, displacement, and immigration, Reverend Lee understands his life’s work as an extension of faith lived through service—supporting immigrants, strengthening community, and offering hope to those struggling to build new lives in America.
Keywords: Japanese occupation; Pyongyang; An-ak; Korean War; Taedong River; refugees; davai; migration; Los Angeles; Rowland Heights; Claremont School of Theology; United Methodist; ministry; immigration; advocacy; encouragement; language; community; resilience; faith

Interviewee: Lee, Bora Reed
At ninety years old, Reverend Chang Soon Lee sits before a computer to write a letter to the father he has not seen in seventy-five years, a man from whom he was separated during the chaos of the Korean War. Lee was only fifteen when the family fled Pyongyang and never saw his father again, leaving him with memories shaped more by fragments of stories than by shared life. In the letter, he reflects on the man he remembers: a deeply spiritual young minister from rural Hwanghae Province who, as a teenager, would climb hills at night to gaze at the moon in quiet meditation, searching for meaning before encountering Christianity and dedicating his life to ministry. Lee recalls one defining moment from his childhood when Japanese police stormed into a church service and arrested his father for refusing to surrender the church bell and other metal items demanded by colonial authorities for the war effort. Although his father was eventually released, the incident remained a powerful example of moral courage. Liberation from Japan brought brief hope, but war soon followed, and in October 1950, when United Nations forces entered Pyongyang and civilians fled south, Lee’s family left without their father, who had remained behind serving a congregation. They never heard from him again. Decades later, Lee reflects on that absence while speaking with his son, who joins him in considering how the silence surrounding their family history shaped their relationship. His son describes growing up feeling the distance of a father devoted to work and ministry, yet also remembers a transformative moment after college when he confronted Lee with his anger. Rather than defend himself, Lee simply apologized and asked for forgiveness—an act of humility that reshaped their relationship and became one of the most meaningful lessons his son carried into adulthood. The conversation moves between grief and gratitude, as father and son reflect on the expectations placed on Lee’s generation to provide rather than express emotion, and on how integrity, faith, and perseverance were nonetheless transmitted across generations. A later visit to Pyongyang in 2007 stirred further reflection, as Lee walked the streets of his childhood and quietly shared small acts of generosity with strangers, explaining that an elderly woman selling goods in the street could easily have been his own mother had history unfolded differently. Through memories of loss, reconciliation, and enduring faith, Lee and his son conclude that while war once defined their family through separation and silence, the legacy passed forward is one of humility, character, and a love that, though imperfectly expressed, continues to shape future generations.
Keywords: Korean War; Pyongyang; Hwanghae; separation; fatherhood; memory; letter; reconciliation; humility; ministry; Japanese occupation; church; courage; migration; family; legacy; forgiveness; character; faith; storytelling

David Soon Ho Kwon (Full)
David Soon Ho Kim was born in 1936 in Kyoto, Japan, during a time when many Koreans lived under Japanese colonial rule and discrimination. His mother, originally from Pakchon in North Pyongan Province, had been sent to Japan as a young girl to pursue schooling with relatives at a time when most Korean girls were not allowed to continue their education. While studying and working in Japan, she encountered constant discrimination, often hiding her Korean identity in order to find employment. At one point she worked as a domestic assistant in the household of a Japanese aristocrat while attending school at night, later supporting herself as a nurse’s aide and eventually qualifying as a nurse through self-study. Through these experiences she witnessed how Korean patients were often mistreated or denied care, deepening her resolve to help others in similar situations. During the final years of World War II, as Japan suffered heavy military losses in the Pacific, the government began mobilizing Korean nurses to serve in dangerous front-line hospitals in places such as Saipan and Guam. When Kim’s mother received orders to deploy to the South Pacific—an assignment widely understood to be nearly a death sentence—she made a desperate decision to flee Japan with her young son. Using the fluent Japanese she had learned while working for the aristocratic household, she dressed in a kimono and successfully passed as Japanese while convincing railway officials to issue rare train tickets during wartime shortages by claiming she needed to visit her wounded husband in Korea. Kim still remembers the crowded train ride from Kyoto to Shimonoseki, packed with soldiers, and even being lifted to the window by soldiers when he needed to relieve himself because the aisles were too crowded to reach the restroom. From there they crossed by ferry to the Korean peninsula and soon traveled onward to Manchuria, where his mother secured a position as head nurse in a rural hospital in a small village. Kim attended school there alongside Japanese children, as the family continued to pass as Japanese during the war. When Japan surrendered in 1945, however, the situation quickly became dangerous as Chinese laborers and local residents began retaliating violently against Japanese settlers. Because Kim and his mother had been living under Japanese identities, they feared they might be killed as well. They fled again, this time to Sinuiju on the Yalu River, where relatives were living across from the Chinese city of Andong. In 1946 they undertook another perilous journey south across the 38th parallel, traveling with guides through mountains and rivers while avoiding Soviet and North Korean patrols, eventually reaching Kaesong where a United States Army refugee camp provided temporary safety before they finally settled in Seoul. Kim completed his education there, attending elementary school, high school, and university, before immigrating once more in 1971, this time to the United States after changes to American immigration law opened new opportunities for skilled workers. Trained as a cost engineer, he settled in California and later worked as an accountant before retiring after decades of professional life in America. Looking back across a life marked by multiple migrations, shifting identities, and narrow escapes, Kim emphasizes the extraordinary courage and determination of his mother, whose quick thinking, education, and willingness to take great risks allowed them to survive war, persecution, and displacement so that her son might grow up free from the need to hide who he was.
Keywords: Japanese occupation; Kyoto; Pakchon; discrimination; nursing; Manchuria; Sinuiju; Yalu River; refugees; 38th parallel; Kaesong; Seoul; California; migration; World War II; identity; survival; mother; resilience; diaspora

Jean Yoon Kwon was born in Seoul during the final years of the Japanese occupation but spent much of her early childhood in Pyongyang, where her father worked as a regional bank manager. Living in a traditional company residence near the Taedong River, she remembers a childhood filled with simple joys—playing with her siblings by the riverbanks and accompanying her father on evening walks to nearby Morangbong Hill, where the family would sit on mats and enjoy the cool night air after dinner. Liberation in 1945 stands as one of her clearest early memories, though the hope it brought was soon overshadowed by instability under Soviet occupation. In early 1946, shortly after her mother had given birth to a younger sibling, two Soviet soldiers suddenly entered their home carrying submachine guns and began shouting while pointing their weapons at her mother. Though the soldiers eventually left without harming anyone, the terrifying encounter convinced her father that the family could no longer remain in the North. The very next day they packed their belongings and fled south with the help of a guide, boarding a small coastal boat from Haeju along with several other families. The boat traveled silently along the shoreline to avoid detection by armed forces, and passengers whispered that if the baby cried it might reveal their position and endanger everyone on board. Miraculously, the child remained quiet and the group reached safety in Seoul, where Jean Yoon’s grandfather owned a large house in Hoehyeon-dong. There she spent several peaceful years exploring the wooded hills behind the property, picking wild berries and playing among cousins, while observing traditional family rituals that reflected the strict Confucian customs of the time. Yet war returned once again when the Korean War erupted in 1950, and in January 1951, during the desperate January Fourth Retreat, her family was forced to flee south alongside thousands of civilians and soldiers. She vividly recalls crossing the frozen Mapo section of the Han River on foot with her mother and siblings before boarding what was said to be the last train heading south. When the train could go no further, refugees were forced to continue along the highway, moving in a massive crowd mixed with retreating South Korean troops while Chinese and North Korean forces advanced behind them. Above the road, American B-29 bombers roared overhead, dropping bombs on the approaching enemy forces that were often indistinguishable from the civilians fleeing in the same direction. Jean Yoon remembers the terror of hearing the planes approach, the explosions that followed, and the horrifying sights along the roadside—burning bodies, wounded soldiers, and desperate people begging for help as the crowd was pushed forward by the chaos of war. Her mother gathered the children beneath blankets and crouched under eaves or in grassy ditches whenever bombs fell, then urged them forward again once the explosions stopped. Despite the unimaginable destruction surrounding them, Jean Yoon’s family managed to stay together and survive the journey south, an outcome she still regards with deep gratitude. Looking back decades later, she reflects that while her childhood began with quiet evenings along the Taedong River, the memories that remained most vivid were the scenes of fear and endurance along that refugee highway—experiences that, in her words, were beyond imagination yet forever shaped her understanding of survival and family.

Rosa Kwon Family (Full)
Interviewee: Kwon, Rosa
In a candid and emotionally layered conversation, Rosa Kwon sits down with her parents, David and Jean Yoon Kwon, to reflect on a family history shaped by war, migration, and the quiet misunderstandings that often follow immigration. Both David and Jean Yoon trace their origins to the northern cities of Pyongyang and Shinuiju, leaving the region in 1946 as Soviet forces consolidated control in the North after liberation. Their early lives were shaped by upheaval: David spent time in Manchuria during the end of Japanese rule, while Jean Yoon recalls receiving communist schooling in the North before her family fled south. Decades later, disillusionment with the rigid hierarchies and male-dominated social expectations of South Korea led the couple to pursue a new life in the United States during the Yushin era of Park Chung-hee’s rule. With three young children—only seven, five, and four years old—they departed amid political uncertainty and the looming possibility that travel restrictions could close airports and separate families. In America, survival demanded adaptation. Settling in a predominantly white neighborhood, their children faced bullying while their parents focused intensely on economic stability and education. English became the family’s priority language; Jean Yoon recalls visiting libraries to gather English books so the children could succeed, believing that mastering English was essential for survival in American society. Only later did both parents acknowledge a quiet regret over the Korean language and cultural ties that were lost in the process. For Rosa, that loss shaped a lifelong sense of distance—feeling that linguistic barriers caused her parents to see her through the limitations of childhood, unable to fully express complex emotions across generations. The conversation reveals tensions between Rosa’s desire to reconnect with Korea and her father’s pragmatic questioning of its 가치, or value, after decades of building a life elsewhere. Yet it also uncovers shared vulnerabilities: Jean Yoon reflects on how immigrant parents often expect their children to embody Korean cultural values even as they themselves struggle to understand American society, while Rosa describes the pressure she felt growing up not to make mistakes as the child of immigrants. Through tears, apologies, and moments of humor—including reflections on Rosa’s marriage to her husband Mark and the family’s evolving understanding of culture—the Kwons begin to confront decades of unspoken feelings. What emerges is not only a story about migration and identity, but also about communication: a recognition that the hardships of survival left little room for emotional conversation in earlier years, and a renewed hope that honest dialogue can now bridge the distance that once existed within the family itself.

Chung Kun Lim (Full)
Interviewee: Lim, Chung Kun
Chung Kun Lim was born in 1944 in Jeonju, Korea, into a family where tradition and discipline were the cornerstones of daily life. As the seventh of eight daughters, she grew up in a household that navigated the rigid expectations of a society that prioritized male heirs. This reality was most poignantly felt when her mother’s hard-won educational legacy—a school board position and local influence—was eventually redirected to male relatives rather than the daughters who had supported the family’s work. Despite the strict curfews and the constant labor of maintaining a pristine home, Chung Kun's early years were most profoundly marked by the displacement of the Korean War. She often credits the "opening" of her powerful singing voice to the childhood terror of crying through the nightly bombings, a sound that she would eventually transform into a professional gift. Her vocal talent led her to Sookmyung Women’s University, where she majored in vocal music and trained as a soprano. However, the path of a performer was soon traded for the path of a pioneer. In 1966, Chung Kun immigrated to the United States, trading the concert halls of Seoul for the grueling physical labor of a new immigrant. Alongside her husband, she operated one of the first Korean-owned dry cleaners in America. For decades, her life was defined by twelve-hour workdays and the relentless heat of the presses—a "meaningful hardship" she embraced to ensure her children would have the opportunities she had left behind. This pursuit of the American Dream came with a quiet, lingering cost. The sheer exhaustion of her work schedule left little time for the cultural and linguistic immersion she desired for her family, leading to what she describes as her greatest regret: the loss of her children’s mother tongue. Now in retirement, Chung Kun looks back on her journey not through the lens of what was lost, but through the character and success of the family she built. She views her children as her true "wealth," finding peace in the knowledge that her silent strength provided the foundation for a generation that can now speak—and live—freely in two worlds.
Keywords: Jeonju; Korea; United States; Seoul; tradition; discipline; daughters; inheritance; displacement; bombing; soprano; vocalist; pioneer; immigrant; labor; hardship; motherhood; language; retirement; resilience

Won Yun (Full)
Interviewee: Yun, Won
Won Yun was born on May 1, 1940, in Sariwon, his early years spent following his father’s calling as a Methodist minister before eventually settling in Pyongyang. His childhood memories are a tapestry of simple, vivid joys: the taste of his grandmother’s mung bean pancakes and yakgwa, and the winter thrill of riding wooden sleds across the frozen Daedong River. This peace was severed during the January 4th retreat of the Korean War. Because his father’s identity as a pastor made him a target for the communist regime, the family was forced to split into three groups to escape. At just ten years old, Won witnessed the terrifying reality of modern warfare, narrowly surviving a B-29 bombing by sheltering in a roadside sewer hole; when he finally emerged, he discovered that those in the nearby bunker had not survived. During the frantic journey south, Won displayed a precocious protective instinct; after being tossed alone into a small boat to cross the river, he refused to move from the southern bank until the boatman returned to rescue his father and brother. While they eventually found safety in Busan and later Daegu, the victory was incomplete. His grandmother and two sisters remained in the North—a separation that became a "forever" silence, leaving his parents in a state of lifelong mourning. Won’s path eventually led him to Seoul, where he met his wife, Jung-geun, in a church choir; he sang bass to her soprano. In 1966, carrying only $100 and a ticket provided by a family friend, he immigrated to Los Angeles to build a new foundation. His early years in America were a grueling test of endurance, characterized by midnight shifts as a dishwasher in Chinatown and two-hour walks home in the dark. It was only after moving to New Jersey that he was able to practice the architecture he had studied in Korea, finally achieving a sense of stability when his wife joined him in 1967. Decades later, driven by his parents’ unresolved grief, Won risked a journey back to North Korea for a shadowed reunion with his sisters. In a bugged motel room, they navigated the danger of surveillance by communicating through handwritten notes, asking in silence about their father’s faith and the family they had lost. To protect his sisters, he flushed those notes before leaving, carrying the weight of their unspoken words back to his family in the States. Now 84, Won views these memories as a "time capsule" for the next generation, offering his story as an urgent prayer that his grandchildren might live in a world where peace is a permanent reality and friendship is held as life’s greatest asset.
Keywords: Sariwon; Pyongyang; Daedong River; Busan; Daegu; Seoul; Los Angeles; New Jersey; North Korea; minister; childhood; warfare; survival; boat; choir; immigrant; endurance; architect; surveillance; friendship

Won Yun is joined in conversation by his daughter-in-law, Cristina, and his granddaughter, Emily, in a reflection on the enduring cost of war and the fragile threads of family connection. Born into a family of faith in the early 1940s, Won’s youth in Pyongyang was abruptly shattered by the arrival of the Korean War. He vividly recalls the daily bombings that sent citizens fleeing toward Moranbong Mountain and a singular, chilling moment of survival: being pushed out of a crowded street bunker and seeking refuge in a sewer hole instead. He hid there for an hour while the city was leveled, only to emerge and find that those who had occupied the bunker he sought were killed. The political chaos of the era specifically targeted his family; as a Christian minister, Won's father was forced to hide underground for six months to escape communist purges before finally securing passage south. At just ten years old, Won was the first to be sent across the river in a tiny boat. Alone on the southern bank, he displayed a fierce, precocious resilience, refusing to leave and pleading with the boatmen until his father and brother were safely brought across. Yet, this escape was haunted by a heavy silence. His grandmother remained behind to care for his two young sisters—a separation the family believed would last only two weeks, but instead stretched into a permanent divide. Decades later, following the death of his parents, Won risked a clandestine return to North Korea to seek out the sisters who had lived only in his parents' nightly, tearful stories. In a motel room monitored by hidden cameras, he navigated a shadowed reunion where words were a liability. To protect their safety, he used handwritten notes to ask the questions that mattered most: Do you know our father was a minister? Do you still believe in Jesus Christ? After receiving their confirmation, he destroyed the evidence, tearing the papers and flushing them away. Despite the decades of separation and the dim light of the motel, the bond was undeniable—he recognized his mother’s face in his older sister’s features. Now 84, Won shares these memories not as a biography of grief, but as a "time capsule" for future generations. He offers his story as a stark reminder of the destruction war wreaks on the human spirit and as a fervent, final prayer: that his children and grandchildren will inherit a world defined by permanent peace, free from the disasters that defined his youth.
Keywords: Pyongyang; Moranbong Mountain; North Korea; minister; youth; warfare; survival; bombing; bunker; resilience; boat; separation; mourning; reunion; surveillance; notes; faith; peace; legacy; prayer

Michelle Kim Rogers (Full)
Interviewee: Rogers, Michelle Kim
Michelle Kim Rogers’ story begins in Seoul in 1961, a life initially defined by the long shadow of separation as her parents emigrated to the United States years before she and her brother, Harold, could follow. While living with her uncle in the city and spending summers at her grandmother’s farmhouse in Ichon, she inhabited a world of vivid sensory memories—the "odd" taste of fresh goat milk she was encouraged to drink for health, the scratchy warmth of hand-knit wool leggings worn over school uniforms, and the aroma of roasted chestnuts and silkworms sold by newspaper-wrapped street merchants. Even as a young girl taking public transit to a private school where her classmates arrived in chauffeured cars, she held onto a childhood fantasy that America was a place where the walls were literally plastered with dollar bills. When she finally arrived in Salt Lake City in 1970 at ten years old, that fantasy dissolved the moment she saw her parents’ faces at the airport; five years apart from her father and three from her mother had left visible marks of exhaustion and aging that no amount of money could mask. The "Golden Land" was revealed to be a place of grueling labor, epitomized by her mother’s years in a loud sewing factory where she saved every nickel to the point of denying herself a five-cent soda. The family’s early American life was a series of adjustments, from the "odd" selection of food at all-you-can-eat cafeterias to the comforting but strange smell of kimchi made with white cabbage because Napa was nowhere to be found. Their resilience was forged in small, resourceful joys: road trips in an un-air-conditioned Ford LTD, grilling Korean barbecue on a hibachi in local parks, and foraging for fiddlehead ferns in the mountains to be dried for soup and banchan. However, the transition was often harsh, particularly during a move to New Jersey where Michelle faced the cruelty of school-bus bullying—a period made bearable only by the quiet protection of a Black bus driver who sat her behind him and ensured she felt strong. This early encounter with "being different" eventually defined her adult life as a "gatherer of people," leading her to support Afghan refugees through the International Institute of New England. Today, she mentors ten-year-old girls navigating the same "newness" she once did, finding a sense of completion in her work and her family. Looking back at sixty-four, Michelle sees the total reunion of her family in 1970 as her most complete joy, even as she navigates the heartbreak of her mother’s Alzheimer’s. Her narrative remains a testament to the immigrant spirit and an urgent plea for radical kindness, curiosity, and the acceptance of those following in her footsteps.

Tae-hyok Kim is joined in conversation by his children, Michelle and Harold, and his granddaughter, Nicole, to reflect on a journey that began seventy-seven years ago in the village of Cheong-duk-gol. When Tae-hyok first left for Seoul, he had no inkling that the departure from his home and his four siblings—two older sisters and two older brothers—would become a permanent exile. During the chaos of the Korean War, the family’s hope for a quick reunion was thwarted by a brutal winter; while his brothers were able to move toward the border, the women and children could not survive the crossing in the extreme cold, forcing a separation that Tae-hyok hauntingly describes with the realization that he "didn’t know it would be forever." After eventually immigrating to the United States, his stories became the essential connective tissue for his family, especially during the long, formative cross-country drive from Salt Lake City, Utah, to New Jersey. It was during this relocation—when Harold was ten and Michelle was thirteen—that Tae-hyok began answering his children's questions about their heritage (and his past) by weaving detailed narratives of his parents, his cousins, and his life under the Japanese name Kaneko Taika.
For Tae-hyok, recounting the war and his past served as a vital form of therapy, allowing him to process displacement through disciplined storytelling rather than through vices; he lived a life of remarkable focus, where his only occasional indulgence was a lottery ticket. Although he spent decades typing out hundreds of pages of his experiences, a stroke in 2018 severely impaired his speech, fundamentally altering his ability to share these stories through voice. This challenge sparked a profound collaboration during the pandemic, as Nicole utilized Alexa to interview him for thirty minutes every day, meticulously ascertaining the dates and locations that were missing from his original manuscripts. Nicole’s commitment was fueled by a desire to bridge the gap between the casual "Korean feasts" of her childhood and the heavy historical reality of her grandfather’s life, a curiosity deepened by watching World War II documentaries and wondering what happened to those who survived the aftermath. The resulting book is more than a family tree of the Kims, Lees, and Parks; it is an embodiment of Tae-hyok’s central philosophy that has set the tone for how his descendants live their lives: the belief that one must always maintain both a goal and a dream, for once a goal is achieved, the dream must become the next goal to pursue. While Michelle admits that she once took her father’s prolific writing for granted, seeing the history rendered in print has made the family’s legacy feel "real" and permanent. The project stands as a collective act of profound gratitude—from Nicole, who thanks her grandfather for the courage to immigrate and build a new life, and from Michelle and Harold, who thank him for his tireless persistence in ensuring their story "hasn't died with this generation."

In Whan Rheem (Full)
Interviewee: Rheem, In Wan
Born on November 10, 1928, in a village near Pyongyang, In Whan Rheem was the youngest child in a family where the pulpit and the classroom were equally revered. His early life was a study in precariousness and perseverance; a frail constitution delayed his education, yet he eventually earned a place at the prestigious Pyongyang High School. His adolescence was defined by the stifling atmosphere of the Japanese occupation—where his own language was relegated to a single hour of weekly study—making the eventual moment of liberation a visceral triumph. He recalls the simple, profound act of grabbing a handful of soil and shouting, "This is our land!" as his father was finally freed from the threat of Japanese persecution. However, the dawn of liberation was quickly eclipsed by the ideological terrors of the Korean War. For the Rheem family, the cost of their faith was absolute. Both In Whan father and his twenty-six-year-old brother were martyred by the communist regime. The horror of this period was crystallized for Rheem when he discovered his father’s body among thirty mass burial pits on a hill in Yongsan, where the dead had been bound and executed. This discovery fueled a desperate, forty-day escape on foot toward the south. His journey was a gauntlet of survival: he clung to the roof of a train headed for Busan, watching in horror as exhausted refugees slipped from the metal to their deaths, and later endured a month of starvation in Jeju, where he survived by foraging for raw radishes. Seeking a sanctuary from the "perpetual state of conflict" that defined the peninsula, Rheem eventually turned his sights toward the West. His marriage to Sun Ok Hwang—arranged and officiated by their pastor at Namdaemun Church—marked the beginning of a shared life built on the foundations of mutual trauma and resilient hope. In the 1960s, he moved his ministry to Canada, a place that felt like "heaven" for its simple offerings of food and political freedom, before eventually settling in the United States. Now, looking back on a century of displacement and rebirth, Rheem offers his story as a spiritual compass for his grandchildren, praying that they will maintain their faith and cherish one another as the ultimate protection against a turbulent world.
Keywords: Pyongyang; Yongsan; Seoul; Busan; Jeju; Canada; United States; pastor; ministry; faith; education; occupation; liberation; martyr; communism; survival; refugee; starvation; resilience; marriage; sanctuary; freedom; legacy; prayer; endurance

Rheem Family (Full)
Interviewee: Rheem, In Whan
In the decades following the Korean War, the Rheem's family’s journey transformed from a desperate search for safety into a purposeful mission of service and resettlement. After surviving the initial displacement from the North, they established a temporary foundation in Seoul—a city that would become their "second hometown"—before eventually looking toward the West. Influenced by the American missionaries who had worked alongside the grandfather in Pyongyang, the family immigrated first to Canada and later to New York. These middle years were characterized by the relentless "busy-ness" of the immigrant experience; the In Whan Rheem calling as a minister provided spiritual direction but often meant navigating significant financial precarity. The Sun Ok Hwang, the grandmother, reflects on this period with a poignant mixture of pride and apology, recalling the burden of being unable to provide her children with the simple luxuries, like "pretty clothes," that she felt they deserved. Yet, what was lacking in material wealth was more than compensated for by the strength of their internal "love network." Central to her recollection is the enduring legacy of the Rheem family’s matriarch, Noh Ki-bok, a woman of extraordinary fortitude who survived the trauma of the Japanese occupation and the loss of her homeland to reach the age of ninety-three. Her example of "victory through endurance" served as a guiding light as the family integrated into North American life. Over seventy years since leaving the North, the family has come to view "home" not as a lost plot of land across a closed border, but as the collective presence of their children and grandchildren. This perspective has turned their focus from the grief of what was lost to the joy of what has been built. Today, as the elder generation’s memories begin to soften with age, they view the act of gathering—facilitated by their grandson, Daniel—as a sacred opportunity to solidify their history. They find their ultimate fulfillment in knowing that their years of "meaningful hardship" successfully paved the way for a generation that lives with freedom, faith, and the capacity to help others.
