Sun Ok Hwang (Full)
Interviewee: Hwang, Sun Ok
Sun Ok Hwang was born on February 13, 1935, in Shinchon, Hwanghae Province—a region defined by its fertile, sprawling rice fields that, for much of her youth, were a source of both sustenance and fear. Under the Japanese occupation, her father, Jin Seop Hwang, worked a self-funded night patrol at the fire department specifically to avoid the arbitrary military arrests targeting Korean men. The family lived a life of tactical secrecy, adopting the Japanese name Tomoda Joon Gyoko—carefully selecting Hanja that would surreptitiously preserve the "Hwang" lineage—and eating from porcelain bowls because their copperware had been confiscated for the war effort. Survival was a matter of quiet discipline; Sun Ok recalls her mother, Young Sung Choi, coordinating midnight pickups of white rice from local farmers, a luxury so strictly forbidden that a single grain spotted in the household’s wastewater stream could lead to a family being reported. The end of the occupation offered no reprieve, as Shinchon was soon partitioned into Communist North Korea. This era was marked by a new kind of surveillance: her father was repeatedly imprisoned and abused for his faith and anti-communist leanings, and Sun Ok remembers the stifling pressure of the schoolroom, where a single ideological slip required a humiliating public apology. The outbreak of the Korean War brought physical devastation as B-29 bombers partially leveled her home, forcing a harrowing evacuation. Led by her grandfather, a member of an anti-communist guerrilla force, the family trekked overnight through slippery, snow-covered terrain to Ongjin, eventually crossing to the island of Baeknyun-do under the protection of the U.S. Navy. After a transient year in Busan, a connection to a relative serving as a colonel finally allowed the family entry into Seoul. Sun Ok built a life of intellectual pursuit, graduating from college and working as a teacher’s assistant and lecturer. Her journey reached a definitive turning point on March 9, 1961, when she married In Whan Rheem. Their union was grounded in a unique, silent understanding—as two people who had fled the North, they shared a vocabulary of loss and resilience that required no translation. Now living in Flushing, Queens, Sun Ok views her life as a bridge between a shattered past and a stable future. While the loss of her extended family remains a laughing, bittersweet sorrow she carries to her prayers, she finds her greatest joy in the "good jobs" and steadfast faith of her children and grandchildren, viewing their success as the ultimate fulfillment of a survival that began in the rice fields of Shinchon.

Interviewee: Park, David Jungdo
Reverend David Jungdo Park, born in 1936 in the village of Madeok, Hwanghae Province, represents the resilient spirit of one of Korea’s earliest Christian families. His childhood was defined by the dual pressures of Japanese occupation—which suppressed the Korean language and forced worship at Shinto shrines—and the quiet, clandestine practice of his faith. He vividly recalls learning his ABCs and his scriptures simultaneously, as his mother read the Bible to him in secret. The euphoria of the August 15, 1945, liberation was, for young David, an experience of profound ambivalence; while his town erupted in a cacophony of trumpets, tambourines, and "Manseh!" cheers, his joy was muted by the absence of his father, who had been beaten to death by Japanese authorities and did not live to witness the freedom he had longed for. The promise of liberation was short-lived, as the encroaching communist regime soon targeted Christian believers for ideological "re-education." David’s resolve was tested early; he defied communist education authorities by refusing to attend school on Sundays, prioritizing his faith over the dictates of the party. When the front lines collapsed in the winter of 1950, David’s life became a series of heart-wrenching departures. His uncle, a member of the Armed Defense Unit, sacrificed his life to alert the family of the incoming forces. In the ensuing chaos, David’s grandfather—an elder who could not flee quickly—chose to stay behind, prompting a tearful decision by David’s mother and sister to return to their hometown. David, meanwhile, was swept into the evacuation, eventually reaching Chodo Island on January 14, 1951, before arriving in South Korea as a sixteen-year-old refugee. His early years in the South were marked by soul-crushing labor and spiritual hunger. Working as a dishwasher in a Chinese restaurant, he faced a new struggle: the demands of the "free" economy. When his employer refused to grant him Sundays off, David adapted, instituting a lifelong practice of daily dawn prayer. This discipline provided the inner architecture for his rise from a struggling refugee to a dedicated seminary student in Seoul. His transition was confirmed by a series of haunting, prophetic dreams—most notably, a vision of his mother in a white gown and a subsequent, inexplicable moment of spiritual comfort where he heard a voice that felt like his own father’s, urging him to have no fear. Guided by the counsel of his aunt, who connected him to his grandfather’s former associates, David moved through the ranks of the church, serving as a custodian and later as a member of the chaplaincy for KATUSA. His ministry would eventually bridge continents, bringing him from a friend’s home in Charlottesville to congregations in Austin and Atlanta. Today, serving as a professor of Hebrew and the Old Testament in Catonsville, Maryland, Reverend Park remains a man who speaks the ancient languages of faith with the authority of someone who survived the collapse of his own world. His life’s work—as a teacher, pastor, and scholar—is a testament to the idea that even when a family is torn apart by history, the seeds of faith and language planted in a small Madeok home can continue to bear fruit across generations.

Park Lee Family (Full)
Interviewee: Park, David Jungdo
Reverend David Jungdo Park’s conversation with his grandson, John Lee, is one of a profound exploration of life as defined by the tension between profound loss and enduring spiritual growth. Born in 1936 in Madeok, Hwanghae Province—a landscape now transformed into the salt-producing region of Yeomjeon-ri—he carries the indelible scars of a thirteen-year-old refugee who fled his home in 1950, clutching little more than a sack of rice and the haunting memory of his sister’s tears. As the son of an entrepreneurial father of faith who used dynamite to coax life-giving water from the stubborn rock of their family orchard, and a widowed mother whose midnight prayers became the bedrock of his faith, David’s story is one of radical transition. He recalls the joy of the liberation era, the sudden descent into the darkness of communist rule, and the long, wandering years that eventually led him to a life of pastoral ministry in the United States, where he raised five children and mentored a generation of grandchildren. In this conversation/interview, David emerges as a master of what he calls "spiritual carpentry"—the deliberate, patient shaping of a life according to higher callings rather than immediate circumstance. He reflects with vulnerability on the "Mr. Big Belly Button" photograph—a moniker given to him by teasing children—he could never keep, the willow tree he transplanted as a six-year-old that stands as a sentinel of his childhood, and the crushing realization of graduating and marrying without a single relative present to witness his milestones. His reflections on his daughter Hyun-ah, whose journey as a single mother mirrors the trials his own mother faced in 1940s Korea, reveal a man whose empathy has been forged in the crucible of his own displacement. He speaks to his grandson, John, not merely as an elder, but as a fellow traveler on a pilgrimage, viewing their shared heritage not as a finished history, but as a living, growing entity. Like the orchard he once tended, David’s life is a testament to the art of being "grafted"—uprooted from the soil of his birth only to find deep, unexpected anchorage in a new land. His voice serves as a bridge for the diaspora, demonstrating how the trauma of the North Korean refugee experience, when confronted with grace and the practice of storytelling, can be transformed into a narrative of victory. He challenges his descendants to look beyond their own immediate needs and toward a vocation of service, reminding them that even when a path seems blocked, there is always a second, third, or upward way forward. Through this exchange, David and John do more than exchange memories; they perform a ritual of remembrance that ensures the names of those left behind—like Park Yeon-do—and the sanctity of the hometown they once inhabited, remain vital parts of the family’s ongoing spiritual and ancestral journey.

John Young Ho Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, John Young Ho
John Young Ho Lee was born on June 25, 1936, in Pocheon, Korea, into a yangban (aristocratic) family, where he was addressed by the community as doryeon-nim (young master). His early childhood was marked by land ownership and traditional social status; his family managed agricultural plots through a tenant-farming system, and during the Japanese occupation, his family maintained a hospitable public stance, with his mother often preparing meals for Japanese soldiers passing through the area on horseback. The liberation of Korea marked a sudden reversal of his family’s social and economic standing; under the Communist Party’s land redistribution policies, the family’s landholdings were confiscated. Due to their status as landlords and his father and uncle’s history as policemen, the family became targets of local hostility. Following a warning from his maternal grandfather, John fled to Naechon-myeon with his father, and after being reported by villagers to the Communist Party, they were forced into further hiding. John recounts navigating a precarious escape through cornfields before eventually reaching the region of Sinwi, during which time he also suffered the loss of his grandparents, who were abducted. Despite the instability of his youth, John pursued a formal education, graduating from law school and eventually building a career as an accountant for the U.S. Eighth Army, a position he held for 24 years. This tenure involved significant international travel, including an assignment in Saudi Arabia, during which period he married the younger sister of a classmate. In 1980, John was granted legal authorization to immigrate to the United States. Motivated by the objective of providing his children with advanced educational opportunities, he settled in California, where his early years were marked by economic challenges, including employment in a pipe factory, work as a pizza delivery driver, and a financial loss due to a fraudulent business acquisition. John and his wife raised four children: their eldest son graduated from Columbia University and pursued a career in the priesthood, their second son resides in Seoul, and their two daughters are married. Having outlived many of his contemporaries, John remains focused on his family legacy, finding fulfillment in his role as a grandfather.
Keywords: Pocheon; Yangban; Aristocracy; Landlord; Displacement; Communism; Refugee; Law; Accountancy; Army; Saudi; Immigration; California; Education; Priesthood; Grandfather; Survivor; Adaptation; Diaspora; Resilience

Marina Lee (Full)
Interviewee: Lee, Marina
Marina Lee was born around Seoul, South Korea, and moved to Philadelphia when she was four years old with her parents and two older brothers. Her memories of Korea are centered around the unconditional love of her parents, as well as her mother’s legendary cooking, which drew the attention of neighbors who’d “invite” themselves over to Marina’s home for a taste of what her mother had prepared. Every week, it seemed, her family would inevitably host a dinner party for her parents’ friends and families. From dinner parties to rituals of making kimchi with her mother (and other ahjummas), Marina tells us that she holds not a single negative memory of life before moving to the United States. When Marina was four-years old, her father, an accountant for the US Army, was offered the chance to relocate his family to Philadelphia following the surprise recovery of a sum of money. In the midst of adjusting to immigrant life in her town—where she was the only person of color in her Kindergarten class—Marina began noticing the slow and confusing deterioration of her mother’s mental health: the self-talk, the changing nature of food on the table, and the growing emotional distance in the household. Yet in the face of a new country, where assimilation rhetoric and stigma surrounding mental health prohibited open discussion, Marina was left at a loss for how she could nurse her mother back to health, freeing her from an illness which trapped her in her own mind. When she was a teenager, she recounts how, in a rare moment of lucidity, her mother apologized to her for her condition, cementing Marina’s conviction to continue fighting for her mother. After graduating from college, she took it upon herself to learn as much as she could about her mother’s schizophrenia, whereupon she learned through other physical screenings that her mother was afflicted by several other health issues as well. Although she was able to provide treatment for her mother which improved her mental health, her mother would pass at the young age of 65.  Today, with a daughter of her own, Marina admits that she is “overly communicative,” though she urges families—particularly those from different cultural backgrounds—to have open conversations about mental health and wellbeing. Her advice for her daughter? “Don’t take life so seriously, have some fun, have a lot of fun, because you only have one.”

Soo Hugh (Full)
Interviewee: Hugh, Soo
Soo Hugh is an acclaimed television writer, producer, and showrunner currently based in New York. Born in Busan, South Korea, in 1977, she immigrated to the United States as an infant and was raised in the suburbs of Maryland, where she and her brother grew up as "latchkey kids" helping their parents run a local deli. It was during these afternoons in the family convenience store that she discovered a deep, abiding love for cinema and storytelling—a passion that would eventually lead her to graduate from Yale University and the USC School of Cinematic Arts. Her career reflects a steady rise through the ranks of the television industry, transitioning from early work in marketing to high-profile roles in some of the most ambitious series of the last decade. After contributing to shows like The Killing and Under the Dome, she made her mark as a creator and showrunner with the ABC series The Whispers and AMC’s The Terror. She is perhaps best known as the creator and showrunner of the Apple TV+ series Pachinko, an epic, multi-generational adaptation of Min Jin Lee’s novel. Hugh is celebrated for her "nonlinear" storytelling approach and her commitment to historical intimacy, often emphasizing the "shock of recognition"—that profound human moment where a viewer finds an electric connection to a character across temporal and spatial divides. Beyond her creative contributions, Hugh is a dedicated mentor who is actively working to reshape the industry’s landscape. Through her "Thousand Miles Project" at Universal Content Productions, she has launched an incubator program designed to empower aspiring AAPI writers, providing the resources and workshops she wishes she had at the start of her own career. Whether she is in the writers' room—which she prefers to call a "think tank"—or advocating for more diverse narratives in media, Soo Hugh champions the belief that storytelling is a vital human muscle, one that demands we step into the skin of others to foster a more empathetic world.

Billy Yoon (Full)
Interviewee: Yoon, Billy
Billy Yoon is a third-generation Korean American whose life narrative serves as a bridge between the foundational era of the Southern California diaspora and the contemporary landscape of Los Angeles. Born in Inglewood, California, in 1958, Billy grew up in what was then referred to as "Midtown"—a neighborhood south and west of today’s sprawling Koreatown. His family history is deeply rooted in the early 20th-century migration: his maternal grandfather, Chung-sew Park, fled the Japanese occupation in 1904 to work in Hawaiian sugarcane plantations before being summoned to Riverside by the independence activist Dosan Ahn Chang-ho. His paternal grandfather, Kyung Hak Yoon, arrived in San Francisco and worked in the rice fields of Sacramento and the peach orchards of Reedley, while his grandmother, Rosa Cho, was part of the "lost boat" contingent—Koreans sold into indentured servitude in Mexico who eventually crossed into the United States. Raised in a community that was small—at a time when fewer than 10,000 Koreans resided in all of California—Billy grew up at the intersection of diverse cultures. He recalls a childhood where his mother, trained in the culinary arts by her own mother (who had served in the royal courts of Korea), was renowned for her expertise, particularly her arduous, multi-day preparation of mung bean muk. While he was exposed to this rich heritage, his social life was defined by his neighborhood friendships and his experience as one of the few Korean Americans at LA High School, where the student body was predominantly composed of Black and Japanese American peers. Although his upbringing was shaped by high parental expectations—specifically the expectation that he would become a doctor—Billy eventually forged his own path. After two years of struggling through a pre-med program at UCLA, he embraced his lifelong passion for art, defying the discouragement of high school counselors who dismissed it as a "useless" pursuit. He earned a BFA, launching a rewarding 15-year career as a public school art teacher. During his tenure at Wilson Middle School in Pasadena, he became celebrated for his commitment to public art, guiding students to complete several large-scale murals, including a 13-foot by 70-foot historical project that earned coverage from CNN. In 2003, Billy transitioned from education to small-business stewardship, taking over Koreana Gifts and Arts. The shop, which he had frequented with his mother as a child when it was virtually the only Korean business between downtown Los Angeles and the Pacific Ocean, became his new sanctuary. Under his management, Koreana has become a vital repository of cultural history, housing the world’s largest collection of vintage Korean dolls and rare 1960s-era yut games featuring hand-painted wooden tokens. Today, Billy views his role not merely as a shop owner, but as a custodian of history and an advocate for intergenerational connection. Embodying a philosophy of radical curiosity, he frequently tells students and visitors that "everyone knows something you don't know," urging them to seek out the disparate perspectives that define the vibrancy of Los Angeles.

Kaylee Cho (Full)
Interviewee: Cho, Kaylee
Kaylee Cho is the Climate Resilience Specialist at the Koreatown Youth and Community Center (KYCC), where she works with the organization’s Environmental Services Unit to address the intersection of public health, environmental justice, and community advocacy in Los Angeles. For Kaylee, a lifelong Angeleno who has been involved with the organization since her youth, working as a climate resilience specialist has been a “full-circle moment” that allows her to leverage her academic background and personal passion in the service of her community. Throughout her tenure at KYCC, Kaylee has centered her efforts on building the institutional capacity necessary to support a vulnerable, aging population. By developing specialized training for staff and crafting robust community engagement strategies, she ensures that vital resources reach those most impacted by local environmental threats. Her work bridges the gap between complex policy and grassroots action, transforming administrative outreach into meaningful, face-to-face support that directly informs public health outcomes in one of the city's most densely populated neighborhoods. Her work is deeply informed by personal experience, having witnessed the impact that environmental and systemic stressors have left on her own family. Whether through her research at Breathe Southern California or her advocacy for tenant rights, Kaylee has emerged as a steadfast champion for those living in Koreatown’s high-density, renter-heavy landscape, where invisible dangers like mold and poor air quality often go unaddressed due to a lack of resources or fear of landlord retaliation. By focusing on the social determinants of health, Kaylee pushes for systems-level change, from the electrification of aging infrastructure to the creation of accessible green spaces. Her approach is rooted in empathy: a commitment to meeting community members where they are, ensuring that the pursuit of climate justice is realized and reflected in the health of the community.

Letter to My Hometown - Roh Family (Full)
Interviewee: Koh, Haesoon
Haesoon Koh and Moohong Roh, both born in Seoul in the aftermath of national division, reflect alongside their son Michael on lives shaped by inherited displacement, quiet endurance, and the lingering ache of separation from North Korea. Through family memory, they recount their parents’ arduous journeys south during the Korean War—by foot, train, and ox cart to Busan—and the enduring consequences of those forced migrations: a grandmother who, as the eldest of eight, never saw most of her younger siblings again; a grandfather from Pyongyang who fled alone, carrying prayers for reunification through decades of loneliness. Raised as children of North Korean refugees in South Korea, Koh and Roh describe subtle yet persistent discrimination that shaped their lives, from stalled military advancement to the necessity of forming refugee-centered banks, churches, and associations, with spaces like Young Nak Church serving as vital anchors of community and collective han. Despite building lives in Seoul, they grew up sensing it was not fully “home,” a feeling that perhaps explains why many North Korean refugees and their descendants found it easier to relocate again—to South America, or later to the United States—carrying with them both resilience and unresolved grief. Their reflections return often to silence and sorrow: a mother who rarely spoke of her hometown but wept at news of defectors, a father who drank and prayed each Chuseok for reunification, attending refugee gatherings in Myeongdong to remember those left behind. Visiting North Korea later in life became a profound moment of reckoning and hope, reinforcing their belief that younger generations like Michael may serve as bridges—not only between North and South, but between Korea and the United States—in the long pursuit of peace, reconciliation, and collective healing for divided families.
Keywords: Letter to my Hometown; Korean War; divided families; intergenerational trauma; North Korean refugees; diaspora; han; displacement; family separation; migration; reconciliation; peace; collective memory; refugee communities; inherited trauma; Korean American identity

Interviewee: Kim Vana
Vana Kim sits in conversation with her daughter and granddaughter, Una and Hana, reflecting on a family history marked by exile, political conviction, and the enduring afterlife of Korean division. She traces their connection to North Korea to her grandfather, the industrialist and entrepreneur Lee Jong-man, who made the fateful decision to leave his family in the South and migrate north in an effort to prevent the permanent partition of the peninsula. That commitment to a unified homeland shaped subsequent generations: Vana’s mother later traveled north to reunite briefly with her father and returned transformed, inheriting his devotion to peace and becoming an advocate for reconciliation in her own right. Because of their family’s proximity to North Korea, Vana recalls how they were treated with suspicion—her brother Sejin forced to pursue his education abroad, relatives gradually severing contact out of fear of retaliation—embedding silence and caution into everyday life. For Vana, whose philosophy and life’s work have been shaped by peace, this history rendered “normal” dinner conversations impossible, infusing family talk with the persistent weight of war, separation, and longing. Una and Hana, listening across generations, wonder whether this complicated relationship to homeland explains their difficulty in claiming one at all, identifying less as immigrants than as people living in exile. Yet Vana insists on the importance of sustaining “heart connections” with those who can no longer be reached through ordinary means, offering an ethic of remembrance and relational care through which divided families might continue to imagine purpose, connection, and peace across generations.
